Affordability is a key issue for voters, and Trump's tariffs have fuelled inflation across the country.
The tariffs – enforced after the August talks broke down – impacted around US$20 billion worth of goods, ranging from hockey sticks to cement.
In response, Canada imposed levies on an equivalent amount of American products, leading Trump to retaliate with another round of tariffs of as much as 50 per cent on certain goods.
Trump last week said he expected a new trade agreement with Canada to be reached "pretty soon," but offered no details.
On Sunday, Trump confirmed the latest talks with Carney, saying officials had "the concept of a very good deal with Canada."
"We have the concept of a deal that's going to be great for our farmers, great for our country, and it'll be fine for Canada, too," he told reporters ahead of a midterms campaign event in Iowa.
Trump said the trade deal would include the construction of the Keystone XL pipeline, long opposed by environmental activists and shelved under his predecessor Joe Biden.
The US president's chaotic trade policies have seen Canada deepen its engagement with other allies.

On Friday, the European Union and Canada announced an alliance that would see Ottawa become the bloc's first "associate member," although there was some disagreement within the EU over the use of that term.--AFP
e44d0364567872df: MELAKA: From the familiar sight of party flags and banners to the growing use of social media, candidates contesting the Melaka election are exploring different ways to reach voters as the campaign entered its second day yesterday.

Several of the 79 candidates vying for the 28 seats wasted little time after nominations closed on Saturday, taking their campaigns to the ground and social media to canvass support from the 687,697 eligible voters.

Some favoured traditional campaigning, meeting voters face-to-face through walkabouts at busy locations such as morning markets and restaurants, as well as taking part in community activities, including gotong-royong programmes.

Others turned to digital platforms to promote their campaigns, share their activities and reach voters beyond their constituencies. Some, meanwhile, are combining both approaches by organising smaller ceramah sessions and livestreaming them to reach a wider audience.
Many candidates in the race have also established a presence on social media, with some already familiar to users.
Among the more prominent names is Barisan Nasional candidate Datuk Mohd Noor Helmy Abdul Halem, popularly known as "YB Duyong", who is defending Duyong in the Nov 14 polls.

Despite having over 1.5 million social media followers, Noor Helmy said online popularity was no guarantee of an easy victory, recalling how he secured the seat for the first time in the previous election by just 200 votes.
He said the number of "likes" on social media did not necessarily reflect voters' actual support when they made their choices on polling day.
"If being popular on social media meant every 'like' translated into a vote, that would be a different story.
"To me, social media 'likes' do not guarantee what will happen on the ground during polling. We leave it to the people to fulfil their responsibility," he was previously quoted as saying.
Noor Helmy said he had been balancing digital and conventional campaigning throughout his five-year term, rather than adopting the approach only during the 14-day campaign period.
He is facing Pakatan Harapan candidate Poo Long Suan in his bid to defend Duyong for a second term.
With voters below the age of 50 making up about 65 per cent of Melaka's electorate, digital platforms have become an important channel for candidates to engage with voters.
They offer a convenient way to disseminate campaign messages, reach voters beyond constituency boundaries, build public profiles and respond quickly to issues.

A similar blend of digital and conventional campaigning was evident in the recent Johor and Negri Sembilan polls, where candidates relied on social media to reach wider audiences while continuing to engage voters through walkabouts, house visits, ceramah and community activities.

The experience in both states also highlighted how digital platforms could complement, rather than replace, traditional campaigning, particularly when candidates sought to build personal connections and maintain their presence on the ground.

Nevertheless, a strong digital presence alone may not be enough. Face-to-face engagement remains relevant as such encounters offer a more personal connection that voters may not fully appreciate when following candidates' activities from a distance through social media.
Universiti Teknologi Mara Faculty of Communication and Media Studies senior lecturer Dr Siti Faidul Maisarah Abdullah said the overall campaign approach remained largely unchanged.
"Conventional campaigning methods are still being practised, including ceramah sessions organised by parties, the setting up of campaign centres and direct engagement with voters.
"The sight of party flags being put up also adds to the festive atmosphere, much like Hari Raya. House visits, meetings with members of the public and community activities continue as usual.

"Engaging directly with people and communities is still considered a practical and people-friendly approach. However, social media also serves as an additional platform to promote candidates and their respective parties."

The campaign is expected to intensify in the coming days, with several political parties preparing to unveil their manifestos. With candidates having until 11.59pm on Nov 13 to win voters' support, the countdown to polling day is prompting them to make the most of every available platform and opportunity to reach the electorate.

e80bc034e82a95c7: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 2 — If Malaysia introduces a new nationwide insurance to cover the cost of long-term care of older persons, who would be paying for it?
The government via tax revenue? All Malaysians through a monthly contribution? Or a mix of both? Or some other method?
But wait, just what is long-term care insurance?
Unlike a medical card or medical insurance which covers hospital bills, long-term care insurance covers the care and support that a person — including older persons — needs outside of hospitals.
For example, if a person is unable to feed or dress himself/herself due to a stroke or other illnesses.

Social Security Organisation (Socso) Deputy CEO (Strategy and Corporate), Edmund Cheong Peck Huang said Socso or Perkeso already covers long-term care for Malaysian workers by giving them a lifelong monthly “invalidity pension” — but only if they become invalid before age 60.

“The irony of Perkeso being able to provide pension, being able to provide rehabilitation, medical benefits until the person dies is that you have to be sick or injured before 60. Then you would have proper long-term care protection.

“But the thing is that when we talk about long-term care, invalidity or sickness comes after 60. When it comes after 60, who protects you?” the social protection expert said recently at the National Long-Term Care Financing Dialogue 2026.
Cheong said this has led to a “moral hazard” where Malaysians lie and try to claim for this Socso monthly payout before they turn 60, even when they are actually not invalid.
“And to be honest, we are seeing trends of people applying for Perkeso’s invalidity pension at the ages of 55 to 60.

“Basically not because they are invalid, but basically they are trying their luck. Hoping for that lottery that Perkeso says that you are invalid and you get pension for life, you get rehabilitation for life,” he said, adding that the spouse and children would also continue to get a pension as this person’s dependants.
“People are lying so that they get protection. So, we need to have a much more sustainable model for it.”<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Edmund Cheong said mandatory contributions by all Malaysians would make long-term care insurance much cheaper, highlighting that everyone grows old and may need long-term care in the future. — Picture by Choo Choy May
‘Solidarity’: Paying for another Malaysian’s care now; getting paid when you become old in the future too
To introduce long-term care insurance for all Malaysians, Cheong proposed making it mandatory for every Malaysian to contribute to it.

“My one answer to it is one word — solidarity. Are we ready for solidarity? Because when we talk about long-term care insurance, it is a social insurance programme. When it is a social insurance programme, it is a mandatory contribution,” he said.

He pointed out that the monthly premium would be very affordable if it is a mandatory scheme involving all Malaysians, compared to a voluntary insurance scheme where the monthly premium would be very high as there would only be a small pool of contributors.

He cautioned Malaysians against being “individualistic” by viewing the contributions as “my savings”, noting that even the most prudent person would not be able to save enough for long-term care in their old age.
Cheong pointed out that everyone grows old, and that paying into this national insurance would eventually end up benefitting us when we need long-term care in the future.
“So that’s where you have to educate, today I’m paying for someone else’s grandfather, but one day, that some random Malaysian will be paying for me,” he said.

He added that a long-lasting organisation with a proper track record and proper infrastructure should be given the trust to run this national insurance scheme, as a person who has contributed for decades to the insurance can then hope to rely on it one day.

Cheong also indicated that long-term care insurance could be funded through existing social protection contributions, pointing out that the Employees Provident Fund (EPF) currently already allows EPF withdrawals via i-Lindung to buy life and critical illness insurance.

“But why can’t we just be brave enough and say, ‘Hey, let’s restructure it’,” he said, noting that social protection organisations such as Socso’s counterparts have also evolved over time to also cover employment injury and invalidity in line with changing needs and social risks.
One example that Cheong cited was Singapore’s national long-term care insurance CareShield Life, which is managed under the country’s Central Provident Fund (CPF) — the equivalent of Malaysia’s EPF.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Syarikat Takaful Malaysia Keluarga Berhad’s Group CEO Nor Azman Zainal said there is a lack of willingness among Malaysians to pay for retirement-related insurance products if it is voluntary. — Picture by Sayuti Zainudin
Why long-term care insurance may fail in Malaysia if it’s not mandatory

Syarikat Takaful Malaysia Keluarga Berhad’s Group CEO Nor Azman Zainal, who has 30 years’ experience in the insurance and takaful sector, indicated that the real challenge was convincing Malaysians that they need retirement-related insurance products.
“From an insurance perspective, I can tell you, based on my observation and our own experience, long-term care is least on the minds of our customers,” he said at the same panel.

Nor Azman pointed to the insurance and takaful sector’s unsuccessful attempts in Malaysia to introduce insurance for Malaysians in their old age, which he said shows it would be tough to introduce new products.
This included life annuity products in the late 1990s and early 2000s that were designed to be funded through EPF, and another new retirement product about 10 to 15 years ago which also failed.

He said the problem with a voluntary long-term care insurance would be “nobody wants to pay for it”, and that it would only work in Malaysia if it is a mandatory nationwide scheme with the government’s involvement similar to that in Singapore or Japan.
“So I think that’s the way forward, but if you leave it entirely to the insurance sector or the takaful sector, we are going to fail once again,” he said.
He said another challenge in Malaysia is the lack of relevant data, which is required by actuaries for cost predictions when designing a long-term care insurance product.
“So I think, in short, it’s going to be tough, but it’s doable,” he said.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

ProtectHealth Corporation’s Head of Healthcare (Sustainability and Assurance) Dr Muhammed Anis Abd Wahab said government funding for healthcare and long-term care needs to be increased. — Picture by Sayuti Zainudin
Government needs to fund long-term care in Malaysia too, advocates say

At the same panel, ProtectHealth Corporation’s Head of Healthcare (Sustainability and Assurance) Dr Muhammed Anis Abd Wahab agreed that there needs to be solidarity or shared risk in a single pool for long-term care.

While healthcare and long-term care should be a shared responsibility that also involves Malaysians, Dr Anis said the government has to “predominantly fund most” of those costs and advocated for an increase in government funding for these.

Fellow panellist and Malaysia Caregivers Association (Kendana) chairman Rashidi Yahaya stopped short of advocating for Socso to step up and handle a national long-term care scheme, but said it was capable of doing so.

Rashidi proposed a four-tier approach to financing long-term care in Malaysia, starting with prevention; having a social protection element that is tax-funded; a mandatory contributory fund with contributions from both employers and employees; and then a voluntary private top-up through insurance.

He indicated that Malaysians’ EPF funds could be tapped for long-term care: “We don’t have to go and tell the government tomorrow, ‘let’s start a new legislation, let’s start a new tax fund’, because the money is already there.”

In Singapore, Singaporeans must pay the premiums (typically using their CPF savings) for their mandatory long-term care insurance CareShield Life, but the government also gives premium subsidies for lower-income and middle-income households.
In Japan, funding for its mandatory national long-term care insurance is shared, with half being premiums paid by citizens and half being tax-funded.

The dialogue was part of the National Conference on Ageing 2026 (NCA 2026), which was organised by Universiti Putra Malaysia’s Malaysian Research Institute on Ageing (MyAgeing) together with Retirement Fund Inc (KWAP), the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) and Kendana.
6737fccfa856a263: KOTA KINABALU, Nov 2 — Security controls at Kinabalu Park are adequate, but trespassing on prohibited trails on Mount Kinabalu puts mountain guides at risk of physical injury and adds to the burden of search and rescue (SAR) operations.

Kinabalu Mountain Guides Association chairman Danson Bulangai said restricted areas had been marked with red paint along the park boundaries, with warning signs and references to the relevant legal provisions at every sub-station to deter trespassing.
“Using unauthorised trails endangers both mountain guides and the individuals involved, who face risks including physical injury, exposure to extreme weather and altitude sickness.

“Mountain guides also have to balance SAR duties with their primary responsibility of accompanying registered climbers, but we are always ready to assist whenever an incident requires SAR operations,” he told Bernama.
He said the vast area covered by Kinabalu Park, spanning about 754 square kilometres, posed a major challenge for the authorities and mountain guides in monitoring all potential routes.

Danson stressed that trespassing incidents created the wrong perception that mountain guides’ supervision was lax, despite the association having 241 registered guides, which he said were sufficient to meet the needs of official climbing activities.
He said the standard ratio for registered climbs was one guide for every five climbers, increasing to two guides for the same number of climbers if participants were under 16.
“The number of mountain guides also takes into account several other factors, including demand for specialised guiding services,” said Danson, who has worked in the sector since 2005.
He said mountain guides also paid close attention to the use of guide ropes, which were normally kept at a standard distance of three metres from climbers to prevent accidents at high altitudes.
However, the distance was reduced to less than one metre in thick fog to prevent climbers from straying from the actual trail.
“The situation becomes more challenging when white quartz veins on the granite surface resemble guide ropes, potentially confusing climbers when visibility is limited,” he said.

He said the association was actively strengthening emergency response skills through joint training with Sabah Parks (TTS) and the Malaysian Fire and Rescue Department (JBPM), particularly in rope rescue techniques.
The rescue skills programme is planned to be extended to all association members in stages in the future.
The association also welcomed the planned requirement for every mountain guide to carry a walkie-talkie once repairs to the repeater system at the Panalaban sub-station were completed.

The measures followed previous incidents involving foreign trespassers, including Croatian climber Mauro Persic, 46, who was fined the maximum RM25,000 after falling and sustaining injuries to his ribs and legs while using an unauthorised trail last September. — Bernama
9e81a3c34af30dbe: SEOUL, Nov 2 — North Korea’s TraderTraitor hacking group has been blamed by US authorities for stealing more than US$6 billion (RM24.5 billion) in virtual assets from Binance, in what is believed to be the largest crypto heist in history.

The October 29 attack is the latest in a string of high-profile cyber thefts linked to Pyongyang, which has built a formidable hacking operation, generating funds believed to help finance its weapons programme.
Here are five things to know about the group and its place in North Korea’s cyber warfare programme:
Who are they?

TraderTraitor is the name given to a North Korean hacking operation linked to the broader Lazarus Group, which gained notoriety in 2014 when it hacked Sony Pictures in retaliation for The Interview, a satirical film that mocked North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

Pyongyang has invested heavily in developing its cyber capabilities since at least the mid-1990s, building a formidable force that South Korean intelligence estimated in 2024 comprised around 8,400 personnel.
“North Korea has built a capable cyber force, funnelling many of the country’s top students into computer science and IT training,” the FBI said on its website.
Much of the hacking activity is known to have been directed by Pyongyang’s Reconnaissance General Bureau, its primary foreign intelligence agency.

“The top two students in my class were recruited to the hacking unit,” South Korean MP Park Choong-kwon, who studied at the North’s elite National Defense University before his defection, told AFP in a 2024 interview.
How do they operate?
TraderTraitor actors have been known to pose as recruiters offering lucrative jobs to trick victims into downloading malicious software.
The malware can allow hackers to infiltrate victims’ computer systems and steal sensitive information and digital assets.

In a 2024 heist involving the theft of US$308 million (RM1.26 billion) from Japanese cryptocurrency exchange DMM Bitcoin, a North Korean hacker posing as a recruiter on LinkedIn contacted an employee of a separate virtual currency wallet software company.
They sent the employee what appeared to be a pre-employment test, which actually contained a malicious line of code.
That allowed the hacker to compromise their system and impersonate the employee, the FBI said.
What have North Korean hackers done?

High-profile cyberattacks attributed to North Korean hackers include the theft of US$81 million (RM331.3 million) from Bangladesh’s central bank in 2016 and the WannaCry ransomware attack that disrupted computers worldwide in 2017.
In 2022, US authorities blamed Lazarus-linked hackers for stealing around US$620 million (RM2.54 billion) from the Ronin blockchain network.

The FBI subsequently attributed three more cryptocurrency heists in 2023 to TraderTraitor actors, involving the theft of nearly US$200 million (RM818 million) from Atomic Wallet, Alphapo and CoinsPaid.

The scale of the thefts increased dramatically in February 2025, when the FBI blamed TraderTraitor for stealing around US$1.5 billion (RM6.14 billion) in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Bybit.
“TraderTraitor actors are proceeding rapidly and have converted some of the stolen assets,” the FBI said at the time.
How does North Korea use stolen funds?

The North Korean regime launders stolen cryptocurrency and converts it into cash “through mixing services or private exchanges”, Lim Eul-chul, a professor at the Institute for Far Eastern Studies at Kyungnam University, told AFP.
“The proceeds are then channelled directly into military research, the illicit procurement of weapons components and the defence industry,” he added.
A 2024 United Nations report said proceeds from North Korean cyberattacks “reportedly helped to fund the country’s development of weapons of mass destruction”.
Why cybercrime?
Analysts say Pyongyang’s illicit cyber activity is driven by its ability to obtain vast sums of money quickly and at “minimal cost”.

“While international sanctions severely restrict North Korea’s ability to earn foreign currency through conventional trade, cyber theft allows it to acquire billions of dollars with minimal personnel and resources,” said Lim of Kyungnam University.

“Hacking offers Pyongyang a way to obtain funds outside conventional banking channels, taking advantage of the pseudonymous and borderless nature of digital assets to bypass financial restrictions,” he added. — AFP
54dbb6ef8b226610: IPOH, Nov 2 — For one private-sector employee, Deepavali celebrations are never complete without coffee snacks from Kampung Kacang Putih in Buntong, which he serves to guests at home, even if it means travelling more than 200 kilometres from Kuala Lumpur to get them. It has become an annual routine.

For P. Ravi, 56, Buntong kacang putih snacks are more than just a Deepavali treat. He said their quality was distinctly different from those sold elsewhere, while their prices were also more affordable.
“I leave Kuala Lumpur at around 7.30am and it takes me more than two hours to get here. It is not a burden because this place has been my family's choice for the past six years.

“We usually come here a week before the festival, and among our favourite items to serve guests are mixed murukku, plain murukku and tapioca chips,” he told Bernama at Kampung Kacang Putih here today.
The Melaka-born man said he usually set aside between RM500 and RM1,000 to buy various types of snacks from several shops in the area.
He said the snacks were not only served during Deepavali but were also given as gifts to relatives, neighbours and colleagues who visited their home.
“It has become a family tradition every time we celebrate the festival, as a way of strengthening ties with colleagues and neighbours,” he said.
Civil servant K. Gaayathri, 30, said the snacks were a must-have during Deepavali celebrations as they were among the favourites of guests visiting her home.
Gaayathri, who hails from Kuala Lumpur, said the wide variety of snacks and flavours made them popular among many people.
“That is why I never forget to get white these snacks here. Deepavali celebrations just do not feel complete without such snacks being served to guests,” she said.
She also hoped that this year's Deepavali celebrations would further strengthen the spirit of harmony and bring the light of goodness and joy to all Hindus in the country.
Meanwhile, DNS Kacang Putih manager S. Sathis Kumar said demand for the snacks at his premises increased by 60 per cent during the Deepavali festive season compared with normal days.
He said demand came not only from Hindu customers but also from people of various ethnic backgrounds across the country.
“Usually, we start making preparations two weeks before Deepavali as we know demand will increase and customers will want to buy the various types of snacks sold here.
“Among the products that are in high demand are spicy mixed murukku, kuih loyang, round murukku, kuih batu, as well as various types of sweets and ladoo,” he said.

Kampung Kacang Putih in Buntong here has been renowned for its wide variety of white kacang putih snacks and other delicacies, particularly in the run-up to Deepavali, for the past 60 years. The business has been passed down through three generations and remains popular among Malaysians of various ethnic backgrounds.
Among the varieties of snacks sold at the business centre are mixed murukku, pakoda, sivel, dal, aulu, poori, Sri Lankan pakoda, omom, kadalai, kacang susu and tapioca chips. — Bernama
3bdb960f9a2844b5: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 2 — Malaysia’s car-parts makers risk being left on the sidelines of the electric vehicle (EV) boom, as Chinese carmakers favour imported components and their own supplier networks, the South China Morning Post (SCMP) reported.
The squeeze is regional, with suppliers in Indonesia and Thailand also facing weaker demand for parts used in petrol and diesel cars while the barriers to entering EV supply chains remain high.

“The supply chain is very different between Japanese autos and Chinese EVs,” Bhima Yudhistira Adhinegara, executive director of the Centre of Economic and Law Studies in Jakarta, Indonesia told the Hong Kong newspaper.

Malaysia’s own experience shows how tricky it is, with BYD recently dropping plans for an assembly plant in Tanjung Malim after a dispute over export quotas and pricing conditions set by the Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry, which defended the requirements as non-discriminatory.
The Chinese carmaker has since partnered contract assembler Inokom to assemble passenger vehicles at an existing facility in Kulim, Kedah.

Local value-add remains modest, with local news outlets reporting in March that domestically assembled EVs had just 20 to 30 per cent local content, compared with up to 70 per cent for foreign-branded cars with conventional engines.

Putrajaya has tried to bridge the gap, with the Malaysian Investment Development Authority bringing 23 local parts suppliers and 12 technology suppliers together with Chery in May 2025, resulting in four commercial agreements covering components, technology transfer and joint investment.
Analysts quoted by SCMP see servicing and hybrids, which pair a petrol engine with an electric motor, as a possible lifeline.

Aiman Abdullah, managing editor of Motoring Malaysia, said domestic carmakers’ electrification programmes were gradually building local engineering expertise, and that experience with the high-voltage systems in hybrids could help vendors move into EV components.

But suppliers still need clearer planning from Putrajaya and carmakers, he said, as vendors typically need six to 18 months to prepare for full-scale production while investments take about a decade to pay off.
“Investors need to see stability and focus in terms of policy before they take out their chequebooks,” he was quoted as saying.
Smaller firms may have the vision and some technical expertise but lack the money to break into EVs, according to Aiman who proposed a fund to help them scale up.

Elsewhere in the region, Thai suppliers are at a disadvantage on cost and proprietary technology, according to Krungsri Research, while Bhima urged Jakarta to use local-content rules to make EV investments absorb small local manufacturers.
Servicing offers another way in, though with limits, according to Teoh Jiun Ee, co-founder of used-car platform Carsome and CEO of Carsome Academy.

Malaysia already has a well-established ecosystem for conventional repairs such as bodywork, tyres and suspension, he said, but high-voltage systems, battery assessments and model-specific components are far more specialised.
Carsome can inspect EVs but cannot repair or replace individual battery modules, so it refers such cases to manufacturers, especially for cars still under warranty.

“For us, the broader opportunity is to develop a more mature used-EV ecosystem here, where vehicles can be assessed consistently and safely, and buyers have greater confidence in the condition of the cars they purchase,” Teoh was quoted as saying.
8a59d9eca7ca093b: PETALING JAYA: The confidence and supply agreement signed between the Anwar Ibrahim government and seven opposition MPs will help ensure the coalition government will not be beholden to Barisan Nasional or any other coalition partners, say political analysts.

Syaza Shukri of International Islamic University of Malaysia says Anwar’s government has sufficient support in the Dewan Rakyat to remain until the end of its term, even if BN were to withdraw support, as other partners such as Gabungan Parti Sarawak are unlikely to leave.

"So there’s no immediate reason (to sign a similar pact with other parties). I think it’s more a long-term strategy to show that the Anwar government still has something up its sleeve and it would not be beholden to BN and the threats of some coalition members," she said.
"It is (also) more about the legitimacy of the current government to stave off any possible opposition call for a snap election," Syaza told FMT.

Anwar heads the unity government coalition formed by Pakatan Harapan, Barisan Nasional, Gabungan Rakyat Sabah, Gabungan Parti Sarawak, and several minor parties. The coalition commands 143 seats in the Dewan Rakyat, and has the support of Bersatu, six independents and Muda.
On Thursday, the federal coalition signed an agreement with the six Bersatu MPs and Muar MP Syed Saddiq Syed Abdul Rahman in return for two key reforms that Putrajaya must undertake.

The MPs want the government to limit the prime minister’s tenure and separate the roles of the attorney-general and public prosecutor before the end of its term. They also want to be allocated the same amount of constituency development funds that government backbenchers currently receive.
The seven opposition MPs agreed to support the Anwar government until the end of the parliamentary term and help approve the 2007 budget.
Syaza said Bersatu, in signing the pledge, was seeking new partners to "stabilise itself" following its fallout with PAS and Perikatan Nasional.

Similarly, Universiti Malaya political analyst Tawfik Yaakub said the agreement did not imply all was not well with the federal government, but could also be seen as a tactic to expand its options for political support in Parliament.

"However, it sends out a message that the government has leeway to obtain support from other parties without being overly dependent on existing coalition partners,” he said. However, there was no basis for BN or GPS to retract their support for the government.

Ahmad Zaharuddin Sani Ahmad Sabri of Global Asia Consulting said the agreement amounted to the government taking out political insurance. "You don't buy insurance because your house is burning. You buy it because you suspect someone might be holding the matches,” he said.
However, Anwar's move to secure cooperation from Bersatu could further complicate relations between Umno and Pakatan Harapan, he said.

"Umno grassroots have never been entirely comfortable with PH, particularly DAP. Bringing Bersatu-linked figures closer to the government could further complicate that relationship, especially when Umno and Bersatu are competing for essentially the same vote bank,” he said.
70d5de79303fc696: PETALING JAYA: Perjanjian keyakinan dan perbekalan (CSA) antara kerajaan Anwar Ibrahim dan tujuh Ahli Parlimen pembangkang dapat mengurangkan kebergantungan kerajaan perpaduan kepada Barisan Nasional (BN) atau mana-mana rakan gabungan lain, menurut penganalisis politik.

Syaza Shukri daripada Universiti Islam Antarabangsa Malaysia berkata kerajaan Anwar mempunyai sokongan mencukupi di Dewan Rakyat untuk kekal sehingga tamat penggal walaupun BN menarik sokongan, memandangkan rakan lain seperti Gabungan Parti Sarawak (GPS) tidak mungkin berbuat demikian.
“Jadi, tiada keperluan segera untuk menandatangani perjanjian sama dengan parti lain.

"Saya melihatnya lebih sebagai strategi jangka panjang untuk menunjukkan kerajaan Anwar masih mempunyai pilihan dan tidak terlalu bergantung kepada BN atau ancaman daripada mana-mana anggota gabungan,” katanya kepada FMT.
Syaza berkata, langkah itu juga bertujuan memperkukuh kedudukan kerajaan dan menangkis kemungkinan pembangkang mendesak pilihan raya mengejut.
Kerajaan perpaduan pimpinan Anwar terdiri daripada Pakatan Harapan (PH), BN, Gabungan Rakyat Sabah (GRS), GPS dan beberapa parti kecil.
Gabungan itu mempunyai 143 kerusi di Dewan Rakyat, selain mendapat sokongan Bersatu, enam Ahli Parlimen bebas dan Muda.

Pada Khamis, kerajaan persekutuan menandatangani perjanjian dengan enam Ahli Parlimen Bersatu dan Ahli Parlimen Muar Syed Saddiq Syed Abdul Rahman dengan dua pembaharuan utama perlu dilaksanakan Putrajaya.
Tujuh Ahli Parlimen itu mahu tempoh jawatan perdana menteri dihadkan dan peranan peguam negara serta pendakwa raya dipisahkan sebelum tamat penggal kerajaan.
Mereka juga menuntut peruntukan pembangunan kawasan yang sama seperti diterima Ahli Parlimen penyokong kerajaan.
Sebagai balasan, tujuh Ahli Parlimen pembangkang itu bersetuju menyokong kerajaan Anwar sehingga tamat penggal Parlimen dan membantu meluluskan Belanjawan 2027.
Syaza berkata, Bersatu pula dilihat mahu mencari rakan baharu bagi menstabilkan kedudukannya susulan pergeseran dengan PAS dan Perikatan Nasional (PN).

Tawfik Yaakub daripada Universiti Malaya berkata, perjanjian itu tidak bermaksud kerajaan persekutuan sedang berdepan masalah, sebaliknya boleh dilihat sebagai langkah memperluas pilihan sokongan politik di Parlimen.
“Namun, ia memberi isyarat bahawa kerajaan mempunyai ruang untuk mendapatkan sokongan daripada pihak lain tanpa terlalu bergantung kepada rakan gabungan sedia ada,” katanya.
Bagaimanapun, Tawfik berkata tiada asas ketika ini untuk BN atau GPS menarik sokongan terhadap kerajaan.
‘Insurans politik’
Ahmad Zaharuddin Sani Ahmad Sabri daripada Global Asia Consulting menyifatkan perjanjian itu sebagai satu bentuk 'insurans politik' kepada kerajaan.
“Anda tidak membeli insurans kerana rumah sedang terbakar. Anda membelinya kerana mengesyaki ada orang yang sedang memegang mancis,” katanya.
Bagaimanapun, beliau berkata langkah Anwar mendapatkan kerjasama daripada Bersatu berpotensi menjadikan hubungan antara Umno dan PH lebih rumit.

8f54f3a8e6a70b87: KLANG: When she went out shopping, Devaki Rani Munusamy would sometimes wonder whether she might bump into Rohani Ambri, her old school friend from Methodist Girls’ School in Kuala Lumpur.
Once, their conversations had filled their school recesses. Their friendship blossomed in 1969, when they would meet over shared canteen food despite being in different classes.
Their parents had been strict, so outings were rare. School was where they'd had each other.
“She was a very nice, pleasant girl. Very quiet,” Devaki, 73, remembered. Yet another thought would then follow: after so many years, would she even recognise Rohani?
What she didn't know was that Rohani had been searching, too. She'd even tried looking for Devaki on Kasipillay Road in Kuala Lumpur, where Devaki had once lived.
“She was always on my mind,” Rohani told FMT Lifestyle.
They had last seen each other at Devaki’s wedding in 1979. In the years that followed, they had raised children, moved across Malaysia for their husbands’ work, and lost touch.
Almost five decades slipped by, but neither woman forgot the friend who had once been such a big part of the other's schooldays.
Across the years and moves, Devaki had kept photographs of Rohani on her wedding day tucked inside an album. Neither woman remembers how the pictures came into Devaki’s keeping.
But those photographs would eventually help bring them together again.

A few months ago, Devaki was looking through the album, hoping to show her family how one of her granddaughters resembled Devaki as a baby. Photos of Rohani caught the attention of her son, Dr Madhusudhan Shanmugam.
“I asked who this was, and she said, ‘This is my old friend. Her name is Rohani, and I have no idea where she is now’,” recalled Madhusudhan, 43, better known as the “Teddy Bear Doctor”.

His mother remembered Rohani’s husband’s name - Ropee. It was enough for Madhusudhan to begin searching. Curious about the groom’s attire, he turned to ChatGPT, which suggested it was an army uniform.
An online search for “Captain Ropee” then led him to a blog post about Captain Ropee Adman Yahayauddin, who had fought communist insurgents and was remembered for having “the heart of a lion”.
Madhusudhan was convinced he had a promising lead. Eventually, a Facebook search led him to Rohani’s son, Rafe Azsnal Ropee Adman.
Before long, Madhusudhan had Rohani on a video call and handed his mother the phone. “Hello, my old friend Devaki,” came the greeting as Devaki looked at the screen.
At first, Devaki was unsure who she was looking at. Then her son told her it was Rohani, and recognition dawned.
“It was like a dream come true. I’m seeing my friend after so many years!” Devaki shared with joy.
“I felt like hugging her,” Rohani added. With much to catch up on, Devaki went to her room so the two could speak privately.
Rohani married in 1971 at age 18, with Devaki among her wedding guests. When Devaki tied the knot in 1979, Rohani had been there, too.
Devaki recalled how, even after Rohani was married, she would drive over to pick her up so they could spend time together.
Neither could have known it would be almost 50 years before they would meet again. Their reunion came at a tender time: Rohani’s husband had died the day before that first call.
In August, the friends finally met at Rohani’s daughter’s home in Kota Damansara, Selangor. “I was so happy,” Rohani recalled.
There were hugs, food and about three hours of catching up. The schoolgirls they remembered in each other were now grandmothers, with a lifetime of family stories to share.
Today, with Devaki in Klang and Rohani in Ipoh, they keep in touch by phone and look forward to their next meeting.
For Madhusudhan, bringing them together offered a glimpse of the friendships that connect Malaysians across racial lines.
“They’ve thought of each other for many years, and they’re still so close today. It makes me happy to see this kind of friendship,” he said.
During FMT Lifestyle's interview at Devaki and Madhusudhan’s home, Rohani, who joined by video call, asked for a clearer view of her friend’s face on screen.
“You look younger today,” Rohani remarked with a smile.
“Oh, I looked old the other day lah,” Devaki joked.
And there they were again: two old school friends, making each other laugh.
c9aa248e444f8c73: MEXICO CITY: Kimi Antonelli drove the perfect race to finish third in his Mercedes at the Mexico Grand Prix and seal his place in Formula One history as the youngest world champion.
Max Verstappen took the chequered flag but all eyes were on the young Italian who takes the crown at the age of 20 years and 68 days, more than three years younger than Sebastian Vettel in 2010.
He is the first Italian to win the title since Alberto Ascari in 1953.
"We did it. I wouldn't be here without Mercedes, without my family," said an emotional Antonelli who has won nine races so far this season.
"I am very grateful for this moment, it will be with me forever. I am speechless, just trying to process what happened.
"It's been an incredible season and to share this podium with Max and Lewis (Hamilton) is incredible. I am looking forward to some more battles in the future."
The race broke into two parts as it was suspended after 46 of the 71 laps following a crash involving Cadillac's Valtteri Bottas.
The Finn's suspension on the front left side had collapsed causing his wheel to buckle and making him a helpless passenger as his car flew backwards off the track and slammed into the barriers.
The 37-year-old Bottas was slow to emerge from his car but waved to the crowd as he walked away, with all the other cars returning to the pits to await a restart.
Antonelli, who needed just to finish in the top nine to seal the title, was running third in his Mercedes when the race was stopped behind Red Bull's Verstappen and the Ferrari of Charles Leclerc.
His nearest challenger teammate George Russell was out of the running after suffering a poor start dropping from second on the grid to fifth and struggling with his power.
Russell had to win to have any hope of prolonging the title race.

Lewis Hamilton, who started on pole and also needed to win to push Antonelli, was furious with his Ferrari teammate after an incident at the start that saw Leclerc leave the track and steal the lead. The Monegasque was handed a five-second penalty but he retained track superiority over Hamilton.
That changed on the restart when Hamilton powered past Antonelli and Leclerc and bumped wheels with Verstappen before settling into second.
There was a further yellow flag when the Racing Bull of Arvid Lindblad also crashed out 10 laps from the end after tangling with the McLaren of Oscar Piastri.

Antonelli sat tight in third as Hamilton continued to press Verstappen. It was entirely appropriate that the young Italian, in tears as he crossed the line, was led in by two of the all-time great drivers with 11 championships between them. --AFP
7b8795331cd3b5db: KYIV: The longest truce of the Ukraine war, limited to the eastern Kherson region, ended on Sunday after Russia refused the offer of an extension, Ukrainian officials said.

The rare pause in fighting, brokered by US first lady Melania Trump and which began early Tuesday, enabled a humanitarian mission to the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky as the war grinds through its fifth year.
Neither side reported violations after the truce began, in what one Ukrainian lawmaker described as the "biggest de-escalation since 2022".
"The ceasefire, which was in effect from Oct 27 to Nov 1, has ended," said Ukraine's Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights, Dmytro Lubinets.
He called the temporary truce "an important step in our joint humanitarian efforts" with Russia.
US-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine are set to resume this month, having been effectively frozen since the US and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran in February.
'Fresh air' for Kherson residents

The conflict, sparked by Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion, has destroyed parts of eastern and southern Ukraine, left hundreds of thousands of soldiers and civilians dead, and forced millions to flee their homes.
AFP spoke to several Kherson residents, one of whom said the ceasefire had been a "breath of fresh air".
"We have to use this time to get things done," said Volodymyr Omeltchenko, a 38-year-old gardener. "We're pruning the rose bushes for winter."
Pope Leo, who had pressed Russia for a truce in Oleshky, said he hoped the temporary pause would "strengthen the desire for dialogue and lead to new concrete peace initiatives".
A Ukrainian military officer, speaking on condition of anonymity, expressed concern that the fighting would be "worse than before" when it resumed.

Russian forces, positioned on the other side of the Dnipro river, had taken advantage of the calm of the past few days to amass new troops, transport ammunition stocks, and collect intelligence on Ukrainian positions using surveillance drones, the officer said.
Kherson regional governor Oleksandr Prokudin warned local people to be particularly vigilant when the ceasefire ended and to "respond immediately to warnings about Russian attacks".

Later Sunday, Ukraine's air force and anti-disinformation centre said they suspected the country's air raid alert system had been hacked, after false alerts of a radiation threat appeared on the application.
"The Air Alarm application has probably been subjected to hostile interference," the force said in a message. "There is no radiation threat."
Refinery reportedly hit
Russia and Ukraine exchanged strikes elsewhere on Sunday.
Russia said early Sunday that a drone had struck an "industrial enterprise" east of Moscow overnight.
Ukrainian media reported that Kyiv had attacked the Kstovo oil refinery, calling it "one of Russia's largest oil refineries, producing fuel and lubricants".
Kyiv has repeatedly struck Russian oil and gas sites, in what it says is fair retaliation for Russian attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
US President Donald Trump had been pressing Kyiv to stop such attacks, blaming them for rising diesel costs that analysts attribute to the Iran war.
Ukraine's energy ministry reported fresh power outages across the country Sunday, including in Kyiv, following Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
Ukrainian strikes killed five people in Russian-occupied Ukraine between late Saturday and Sunday afternoon, Russian-installed authorities said.
Both Russia and Ukraine deny targeting civilians.

Russia now occupies around a fifth of its neighbour: the Crimean peninsula, which it annexed in 2014, most of the eastern regions of Donetsk and Lugansk -- collectively referred to as the Donbas -- and large parts of the southern Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions.

d57aa8f139058555: ROME: Lazio coach Gennaro Gattuso warned his team not to get carried away after they surged three points clear of Inter Milan at the top of Serie A on Sunday with a 2-1 victory over Cagliari.
Lazio made a poor start as Cagliari took the lead through M'Bala Nzola in the 20th minute before goals in either half from Gustav Isaksen and Andrea Pinamonti gave them a sixth straight Serie A win.

With 28 points from 10 games, Lazio pulled clear of Inter after they lost the Milan derby. Unbeaten Roma sit third on 24 points and Como climbed back to fourth with a 1-0 win over rock-bottom Venezia.
Lazio last won Serie A in 2000 and this is the best start to a league campaign in the club's history, but the Roman outfit's ambitions remain modest according to Gattuso.
"Our target is to avoid relegation and we still need 12 more points," Gattuso said. "We need to get our heads down and work, and not look at the table."
Some Lazio fans aren't watching at all.

As has been the case in recent home matches, Lazio played in front of largely empty sections of the Stadio Olimpico, with many ultras and supporters continuing their boycott in protest against owner and president Claudio Lotito, whom they accuse of failing to invest sufficiently in the squad.
- JUVENTUS BREAK NAPOLI RESISTANCE -
Struggling giants Juventus got their fifth win of the season thanks to Bosnian wonderkid Kerim Alajbegovic producing a moment of magic.
The teenager broke the deadlock on 70 minutes with a thumping left-footed drive from outside the box.
Napoli were then reduced to 10 men as Luca Marianucci earned a second yellow for kicking substitute Jeremie Boga, who added a second goal with a strike that rivalled that of Alajbegovic.
That result lifted Juventus to seventh. Napoli are eighth and host leaders Lazio next weekend.
Como's victory at home over lowly Venezia on Sunday was a fifth consecutive victory across all competitions.
The hosts dominated, but needed a penalty to find the back of the net. Como captain Lucas Da Cunha converted in the 43rd minute for the French international's first goal of the season.
"This is the type of match we found hard to win last season," Da Cunha told DAZN.
Cesc Fabregas's side had slipped to fifth when AC Milan beat champions Inter 3-1 on Saturday.
Como moved one point behind Roma, who beat Udinese 5-2 on Saturday.
"This victory is really important in terms of our maturing process," said Fabregas.
"Our state of mind is irreproachable," added the 39-year-old Spaniard as Como prepare to resume their Champions League campaign against Lens on Wednesday.
Como have the best record of the Serie A clubs in the Champions League, sitting ninth in the 36-team standings, with six points from three games.--AFP

9504b4f980dc139c: BEIJING: Chinese state broadcaster CCTV did not broadcast a Real Madrid LaLiga match on Sunday after star forward Kylian Mbappe caused a furore in China with remarks he made about former leader Mao Zedong.
The match between Real Madrid and Racing Santander began at 1515 GMT but was not broadcast on either of CCTV's two sports channels, AFP reporters saw.
None of the other matches from the 11th round of LaLiga have been broadcast live on public television so far.
A viral video in recent days showed Mbappe referring to Mao as a "dictator", prompting the body overseeing CCTV to say it would halt broadcasts of the top Spanish league.
Mbappe, Real and LaLiga later all said sorry for his remarks, and China's foreign ministry said it took the player's apology "seriously".
Asked by AFP before the weekend, LaLiga said that Chinese television had previously shown all games live, without specifying which platforms hosted the broadcasts.

AFP journalists did find live broadcasts of matches on Migu, a digital streaming service owned by the state-owned China Mobile telecom network. That included Barcelona's 6-1 win over Alaves on Saturday.
However, the Racing Santander–Real Madrid match did not appear to be broadcast on Sunday on Migu.

China Media Group (CMG), which oversees CCTV, had said it had moved on Monday to suspend LaLiga broadcasts, adding that apologies from LaLiga, Mbappe and Real Madrid were "an absolute prerequisite" for moving past the furore.
The viral video showed Mbappe saying that the funniest internet meme about him he had seen was of his face photoshopped onto that of "some guy - I think he's a Chinese dictator".
This was an apparent reference to a meme of Mbappe superimposed on an image of Mao.
Mbappe later apologised for his "ill-judged" comments, LaLiga said it "deeply" regretted them, and Real followed suit.
CCTV's sports website later reported that CMG had acknowledged the apologies, but it remains unclear whether talks to defuse the situation have begun.
China is a huge market for European football, with CCTV also carrying matches from the Premier League as well as the German, French and Italian top flights.
Real Madrid coach Jose Mourinho said on Saturday that the club had "done our part" to put the controversy behind them.
It is taboo in China to crack jokes about Mao, who died in 1976 and whose drastic policies are blamed by historians for mass starvation and millions of deaths.
Major Chinese brands cancelled sponsorship deals with Mbappe after his comments.
Various overseas sports leagues and players have found themselves in hot water for comments on topics that are politically sensitive to China.
China effectively cut ties with the NBA for several years from 2019 after then-Houston Rockets general manager Daryl Morey tweeted his support for Hong Kong protesters.
d00a77f9c802999f: WASHINGTON: Republicans made a final push Sunday to prevent a predicted thumping in US midterm elections where Democrats are gunning to win Congress and impose a first political check on President Donald Trump's unprecedented pursuit of power.
Polls show Democrats are all but certain to take the majority from Republicans in the House of Representatives in Tuesday's vote and have a shot at winning the Senate.
But after a decade of Trump defying political gravity and two years of a second presidency in which he has ridden roughshod over every norm, Democrats remain nervous.
"Nauseously optimistic," Democratic Senator Raphael Warnock told CNN to describe the mood.

Those jitters increased Sunday over an ugly party rift in Michigan, a key battleground where a Democratic congresswoman defected to back Republican Mike Rogers against the Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed.
The consensus among analysts, however, is that Democrats are surging.

Trump headlined the Republicans' last-ditch charge, holding rallies for candidates in Iowa and Kansas – states where ordinarily his party should be confident of victory and not require presidential boosts.
Along with making lurid claims that Democrats will turn the country communist, Trump is dangling the promise of US$5,000 payments to everyone in the country if his party wins.
"We're going to win," he told the crowd in Iowa, painting Democrats as "extreme and dangerous radicals" who will "steal your wealth" and let in migrants to "ransack, rape and plunder."
But polls show Americans have soured on Trump's wrecking-ball presidency.
An NBC News poll released Sunday showed 60 per cent disapprove of Trump's performance, particularly over high prices exacerbated by his now eight-month, sputtering war against Iran.
- CURBING TRUMP -
While Tuesday is election day, early voting has already seen a record 54 million people cast ballots around the country, reflecting the intense political fervour.
Trump's second term has featured a relentless expansion of presidential power, aided by an ever-more docile Republican Party.

Trump has torn down part of the White House to build a ballroom, put his image on money and official buildings, disrupted the global economy with sweeping economic tariffs, and threatened to invade or annex allies like Canada and Greenland.
A big Democratic win would kick start the post-Trump era and could even begin the race to replace him in 2028.

Winning the House would put Democrats in charge of the federal budget and powerful committees set to probe allegations of mass corruption, Trump's links to infamous sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, and other explosive topics.
The outcome of the contest for the Senate remains in doubt.

Only a third of the Senate's 100 seats are being contested in these midterms and few of the races were seen as favorable to Democrats. However, with surprisingly strong challenges mounted in deeply Republican states like Texas and Kansas, pollsters now say the odds of a Democratic flip are at minimum even.
A Democratic Senate would be able to shut down Trump's lifetime appointments to courts – especially the Supreme Court.
- WILL TRUMP ACCEPT RESULTS? -
The midterms have seen about US$11 billion spent on advertising, with large chunks coming from individual mega-donors.
Elon Musk, a close Trump ally who led the so-called DOGE effort in dismantling entire government departments, has given a staggering nearly half-billion dollars to help get Republicans elected.
The campaigns have also been marked by blistering language and insults, led by Trump who falsely accused leading Democratic candidates of being everything from vegans to jihadists.
And hanging over everything is concern that Republicans will refuse to accept a loss, leading to a constitutional crisis similar to Trump's attempt to overturn his 2020 presidential election defeat.
A federal judge on Sunday tossed out an extremely unusual attempt by Trump's administration to hold up a potential victory by a Democratic candidate for Senate in Alaska.

The lawsuit contended that if Democrat Mary Peltola beats the Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan, the result should not be certified because there is a third, minor candidate also called Dan Sullivan, allegedly recruited by Democrats to siphon off votes.--AFP

7567dcacf028d3c6: KYIV: Russian strikes left hundreds of thousands of Ukrainian households without power on Sunday, President Volodymyr Zelensky said, while Russian authorities reported major damage to an industrial site following Ukrainian drone attacks on Nizhny Novgorod region.

Even as a six-day local ceasefire held on its final day around the Russian-controlled Ukrainian town of Oleshky, there was no letup in fighting elsewhere along the front line and both sides kept up long-range air attacks.
Zelensky said Russia had hit power infrastructure in four Ukrainian regions overnight, cutting electricity to hundreds of thousands of households.
"The intensity of the strikes is very high, and the Russians are seeking to maximally exploit the deficit of ballistic missile interceptors," he said on Telegram.
He said Ukraine, meanwhile, had hit the Kamensky plant in Russia's Rostov region, which he said was involved in the manufacture of Russian missiles.

The governor of Ternopil region in western Ukraine, Taras Pastukh, said a Russian attack on infrastructure in a town in the region had knocked out power to localities. Emergency crews were working to restore it.

Moscow did not comment on the reported Ukrainian attack in Rostov. In Nizhny Novgorod region, however, governor Gleb Nikitin said a large-scale overnight Ukrainian drone attack caused "significant damage" to an industrial facility.
He did not identify the site that was hit. The region is home to the Norsi oil refinery, one of Russia's largest.
Overall, Russia's defence ministry said its forces had downed 235 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions overnight.

Ukraine's air force said it had shot down 371 of 433 long-range drones launched by Russia since Saturday evening. In its morning update, the air force said dozens of Russian drones were still in the air as of Sunday morning. Six separate drone alerts had been issued in Kyiv since midnight.

Nizhny Novgorod's regional government did not identify the facility that was struck, but it said it was taking steps to ensure gas stations were supplied with fuel, urging motorists to "buy fuel only as needed and avoid panic buying," Interfax reported.

The warning suggests the damaged facility may have been linked to the region's oil-refining or fuel-supply infrastructure. Kyiv did not immediately claim responsibility for the Nizhny Novgorod attack.

On Friday, Russia said Ukraine had resumed strikes on its oil refineries and accused Kyiv of ignoring a request from US president Donald Trump to stop such attacks, which Trump has blamed for raising the cost of diesel before US midterm elections next week.
Ukraine says it supports a full ceasefire on energy targets, including its own battered power grid, but that Moscow is unwilling to agree to this.

In an interview with state TV channel Vesti on Sunday, Russian deputy prime minister Alexander Novak, who oversees the energy sector, did not mention the Nizhny Novgorod strike, but said Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries were adding to global fuel market imbalances and affecting prices.

KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia Airlines Bhd said its information technology (IT) systems have not been compromised by a cybersecurity incident involving its third-party technology provider, Amadeus IT Group S.A.
However, certain customer information may have been affected.

"The incident may have affected customer information processed through Amadeus between August 2023 and September 2026. We wish to reassure customers that Malaysia Airlines' own IT systems have not been compromised and there is no evidence that financial information has been accessed," it said in a statement on its website.
It has not disclosed how many customers may have been affected or the types of personal information potentially accessed.

The incident comes as several international airlines have reported unauthorised access to passenger reservation data held by Amadeus, a Spain-based travel technology company that provides reservation and other technology services to airlines worldwide.
On Oct 30, Cathay Pacific Airways Ltd said that 53,000 of its bookings were affected by unauthorised access to passenger reservation data held by Amadeus.
The Hong Kong-based airline said most affected records included booking references, passenger names and flight details.
A smaller number may have included email addresses, phone numbers, travel document information and frequent flyer numbers.
Cathay Pacific said there was no evidence that financial or payment information had been accessed, while its own systems and flight operations remained unaffected.
"Amadeus confirmed that it has taken actions to contain the incident, including a password reset, and has implemented enhanced monitoring and detection capabilities on its systems.
"To date, Amadeus has not identified evidence that the affected data has been misused."

Other airlines affected include Japan Airlines Co Ltd and Japan Transocean Air Co Ltd, which reported that about 92,000 customers were affected, while All Nippon Airways Co Ltd said information relating to about 37,800 customers had been accessed.
South Korea's Korean Air Co Ltd and Asiana Airlines Inc also reported unauthorised access to customer reservation information through Amadeus.

aebf7107f82aed5e: NEW YORK: Binance said that it had seen withdrawals of around US$4.7 billion on Sunday, after more than US$6 billion in virtual assets were stolen from the cryptocurrency exchange in a major hack the FBI said North Korea was responsible for.

Binance is the world's largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes. News of the hacking attack, which is thought to be the biggest-ever crypto heist, caused the prices of most major cryptocurrencies to fall sharply on Friday.
The company has offered reassurances it will cover the losses from the attack, saying it has used company funds to buy tokens to replenish 90% of what was stolen.
Binance suspended user withdrawals after the attack but said they would be resumed in phases, the first of which began on Sunday.
Between 6am GMT and 3:30pm GMT, the platform said it had processed US$4.65 billion in withdrawals and US$1.01 billion in deposits.
The net outflow of US$3.64 billion amounted to about 2.1% of the total assets the company manages.

The US Federal Bureau of Investigation accused North Korea of being behind the hack in a statement on Saturday, confirming earlier suspicions from private investigators and analysts that a Pyongyang-affiliated group called TraderTraitor was responsible.
TraderTraitor is the same group blamed for a US$1.5 billion theft from the Bybit platform in February last year.

"The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is releasing information advising the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than $6 billion USD in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about Oct 29, 2026," the statement said.

The FBI added that it had observed "TraderTraitor actors" converting stolen assets into Ethereum, and expected those assets to be laundered further by converting them using decentralized finance and instant swap services.
It said it was urging private sector entities "to block transactions with or derived from addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder these stolen assets."
US president Donald Trump cast doubt on North Korea's involvement in the hack.
"I'm not concerned. We're learning about it. We don't know if it's North Korea," Trump told reporters at his residence in Florida late Saturday.
The president often reflects with pride on summits he held with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un during his first term.
'Commitment' to cover losses
Binance said Saturday it has set aside more than US$6.34 billion in company funds to cover losses in the hack.
"Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident," the company said on X.

It said it has used company money to buy tokens to replenish 90% of the stolen funds, while the remaining 10 percent of tokens are "less liquid, which means they may take longer to source in the required amounts."
The attack on Binance came as many observers express worries that the ever-expanding capabilities of artificial intelligence models could compromise cryptography and IT security protocols.
Bitcoin plunged nearly 5% after the news of the hack, while Ethereum dropped nearly 6% and BNB, native to Binance, tumbled nearly 10%.

The sheer scale of the hack has put a spotlight on the capacity of North Korea -- which faces extensive international sanctions over its nuclear and missile programs -- to find illicit means to capture funds.

TraderTraitor is believed to be part of the Lazarus Group, which gained notoriety in 2014 when it was accused of hacking into Sony Pictures as revenge for "The Interview", a film that mocked North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

0b311b067cc9836f: Invictus here. During Friday’s sell-off, I wanted to review the major economic factors to see whether the market is foreshadowing a slowdown or worse. The TL:DR: The United States is still growing, but at a slower pace. Compared with the 1990s, growth has become increasingly dependent on a narrower range of economic activity, which may leave us more vulnerable than headline GDP figures suggest. Let’s dive in:

The American economy has a breadth problem. At first glance, the numbers seem reassuring. Real gross domestic product continues to expand (3.4% SAAR), consumers keep spending, and businesses keep investing. But beneath those headline figures lies a potentially troubling development: an unusually large share of recent economic growth comes from information-processing equipment and software.

That raises an important question: Is today’s economy as fundamentally robust as the American economy of the 1990s was, or is it running on fewer cylinders — and therefore more fragile and susceptible to shock? Let’s take a look at the various components of GDP and compare what we’re seeing today against what we saw in the ’90s.

All data comes from BEA table 1.5.2, Contributions to Percent Change in Real Gross Domestic Product, Expanded Detail, and BEA table 1.5.5, Gross Domestic Product, Expanded Detail. I uploaded those tables (Q1 1990-Q3 2026) to ChatGPT for its analytical capabilities and, frankly, to save me countless hours in Excel.
As the chart below shows, an unprecedented amount of economic activity is coming from a single sector:
Two Expansions, Two Very Different Economies
Consider two periods: the five years from 1995 through 1999, and the eight quarters ending in September 2026.

BEA data show annualized real GDP growth averaged about 4.17% during the late-1990s expansion. Over the latest eight quarters, it has averaged 2.34%. The U.S. economy is obviously growing more slowly today. Let’s look at the components of that growth and assess how robust it is. Are we seeing a multi-pronged expansion, or are we vulnerable to a sudden slowdown in one area? If that area slows, how disruptive might it be to the economy as a whole?
Will weakness in the economy’s strongest component produce a meaningful slowdown or recession?

In the late 1990s, investment in information-processing equipment and software contributed an average of 0.68 percentage points to quarterly annualized GDP growth. During the most recent eight quarters, that contribution increased to 0.81 percentage points. In other words, technology-related investment is contributing more to GDP growth today, even as overall growth has slowed considerably.
Measured relative to total growth, the contrast is striking:

1995–1999: Information-processing equipment and software accounted for the equivalent of approximately 16% of average GDP growth. 2024 Q4–2026 Q3: Their contribution was 35%.1 The table below, comparing the mid-90s to today, illustrates how the composition of GDP has shifted:

What Happens When We Subtract Technology? Let’s perform a simple thought experiment to highlight the issue: Subtract the contribution of information-processing equipment and software from overall GDP growth. 2

From 1995–1999, the rest of the economy contributed about 3.49 percentage points to annualized growth. During the latest eight quarters, that figure was just 1.53 percentage points. That’s a decline of approximately 56%.

This is not to say the “ex-IT” economy is contracting; it is to say its contribution to overall growth is substantially smaller than it was in the ’90s. Other BEA figures reinforce the concern. Residential investment contributed positively during the late 1990s but negatively during the latest eight quarters.3
Consumer spending remains an important source of growth, but it contributes far less. These are all among the important legs supporting the chair that is the US economy. A couple appears wobbly.
The late-1990s economy had multiple powerful engines. Today’s economy appears to lean more heavily on fewer of them.

The AI Question The AI question matters because the current technology investment boom is not necessarily self-sustaining — certainly not indefinitely. Companies are spending enormous sums on compute capacity, data centers, networking equipment, and software in anticipation of future demand and productivity gains.

Those expenditures contribute to GDP today. Whether they eventually generate adequate financial returns is a separate question. If expected returns disappoint, businesses may scale back investment, and we have already seen signs of this. Reduced spending would directly weaken GDP growth and could indirectly affect employment, construction, suppliers, and consumer spending, with economic consequences that could extend well beyond the technology sector.

This is not a prediction that the AI boom will collapse; I have no idea how this story unfolds (though I do have thoughts). Nor is it proof that the investment is irrational. Transformative technologies often require substantial capital expenditures before their full economic benefits emerge. But an economy unusually dependent on a particular investment cycle is exposed to that cycle’s fortunes — and I believe we are seeing fraying begin.

An Important Historical Qualification The late 1990s were hardly free of speculative excess. The dot-com bubble eventually burst, and a recession followed in 2001. Nor were all the 1990s equally strong. The early decade included a recession and a sluggish recovery. Our comparison deliberately focuses on the powerful expansion of 1995–1999.

An important distinction also exists between concentrated growth and systemic fragility. Today’s households, banks, and corporations may, at least for now, possess financial strengths that help cushion an investment reversal. The US consumer continues to defy expectations and has been remarkably resilient. GDP contribution figures alone cannot settle the concentrated growth v systemic fragility question.

Still, I believe the historical comparison is instructive. Even during an extraordinary technology boom, the late-1990s economy saw stronger contributions from the rest of its economic activity than today’s does.

The Bottom Line The question isn’t whether the American economy is growing; it is. My question is whether that growth rests on a sufficiently broad foundation to continue organic expansion for the foreseeable future. BEA data suggest today’s expansion is slower and more concentrated in information-processing equipment and software than the late-1990s expansion. That does not establish that a recession is imminent. It does suggest that a reversal in technology investment could be especially consequential.
A healthy economy requires more than a single powerful engine. The data today suggest we have become overly dependent on that single driver of economic expansion…
FOOTNOTES:

1. This is not to say that artificial intelligence accounts for 35% of economic growth; it does not. The BEA categories encompass considerably more than AI. But they capture important components of the extraordinary investment boom surrounding computing infrastructure and software.

2. Lots of AI Capex has shifted from other sectors of investment into technology because it’s the new hotness, and managers tend to chase performance. If the AI CaPex boom wasn’t happening, much of this pending capital would flow to other sectors, making this an imperfect counterfactual…

3. Despite mortgage rates comparable to those of the late 1990s, today’s housing market is burdened by home prices that have risen far faster than household incomes, making homeownership substantially less affordable. Compounding the problem, millions of existing homeowners are reluctant to sell and surrender the exceptionally low mortgage rates they locked in years ago, which is suppressing both housing inventory and transaction volume. Nonresidential structures show a similar reversal.

Data: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, National Income and Product Accounts, Table 1.5.2, revised October 29, 2026. Comparisons use averages of quarterly annualized GDP growth contributions. Information-processing equipment is line 31; software is line 38. Percentages comparing contributions with total GDP growth are descriptive ratios, not exact cumulative growth shares.

ffb4b579e8dc8cfd: LONDON: Opec+ oil-producing countries kept December production targets steady on Sunday, confirming expectations that more policy adjustments will not occur until next year, as the group continues to struggle with export disruptions from the Iran war.
Seven core opec+ members — Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Algeria, Kazakhstan and Oman — made the decision in an online meeting on Sunday, Opec said in a statement.
While Gulf members have been boosting exports that have been disrupted for months by the conflict, most are still pumping well below their targets.
Opec+ comprises the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies, including Russia.
Only the seven members — plus the UAE until it quit Opec in May — have been involved in monthly output decisions in recent years.
All members of the 21-country group are due to meet on Nov 29, when analysts expect it will decide 2027 quotas.
"Today's decision was the easy one," said Jorge Leon, an analyst at Rystad.
"The much more important test comes at the Nov 29 ministerial meeting, when Opec+ will decide its 2027 production framework," Leon said.

Oil prices jumped more than 2% on Friday, with Brent crude settling at almost US$118 a barrel, the highest since April, as traders braced for a potential escalation in the Iran war after the US midterm elections.
The International Energy Agency and other forecasters have warned of excess supply in 2027 should Gulf flows return to normal.
"Opec+ faces an extremely difficult call for 2027," Leon added.

"The group has to plan around huge uncertainty over the US-Iran war, the pace of recovery through the Strait of Hormuz, and the size of the surplus that could emerge once disrupted barrels return," Leon added.
The seven members have been boosting output targets for much of 2026 and in September completed the phased rollback of a 1.65 million-barrel-per-day supply cut first agreed in 2023.
At earlier meetings, they kept the targets steady for October and November.
Opec+ still has one more layer of production cuts of about 2 million bpd covering most members through the end of 2026.

"The group needs to complete a review of members' production capacity during the fourth quarter before setting the 2027 baselines that will determine future quotas and shape plans to unwind those cuts," sources have said.
The Iran war has disrupted projects to expand capacity across the Middle East, throwing estimates of future production potential into uncertainty, Reuters reported in October.
As a result, the review is now expected to be completed by mid-November.
