fa07f212d6065057: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 1 — A little over a decade ago, Johor FC were fighting to stay in Malaysia’s top flight; today, as Johor Darul Ta’zim (JDT), they are the country’s dominant club.
That journey is now the subject of Untamed, a 76-minute club-produced documentary that revisits its milestones, achievements and controversies.

“The whole idea behind producing these documentaries is to help everyone learn more about JDT than they previously knew, particularly what happens behind the scenes and how things operate,” chief operating officer Alistair Edwards told reporters at a special screening at TGV Suria KLCC last week.
Edwards said he is often asked on his travels how the club achieved so much in such a short time.
His answer, as the film tells it, is simple: “As you can see, it comes down to having a good team, led by one person who is behind the vision.”

The club was founded in 1972 as Perbadanan Kemajuan Ekonomi Negeri Johor (Johor State Economic Development Corporation) Football Club, became Johor FC in 1996 and was rebranded as Johor Darul Ta’zim in 2013 under owner Tunku Ismail Sultan Ibrahim, the Regent of Johor.
The league titles followed from 2014, and the Southern Tigers, as the club is nicknamed, have since become regulars in Asian competition.
Untamed draws on management voices including Edwards, finance director Datuk Seri Jaifuddin, special projects manager Kevin Ramalingam and former sporting director Martin Prest.
From the pitch come current players Arif Aiman, Bergson da Silva, Matt Davies and Corbin Ong, along with former players Safiq Rahim and Safee Sali and former head coach Bojan Hodak.

JDT chief operating officer Alistair Edwards (centre) with former players Safiq Rahim (right) and Aidil Zafuan (left) at the ‘Untamed’ screening at TGV Suria KLCC on October 28, 2026. — Picture courtesy of JDT
Former youth and sports minister Khairy Jamaluddin and rapper Joe Flizzow also appear.
The documentary is streaming on JDT+, the club’s own platform, which launched on October 22.
More is on the way, including Unbound, a series on the club’s AFC Champions League Elite campaigns, due in November.
Edwards said he hopes younger players will take the film as motivation to prepare for their careers.

“This platform allows us to share those experiences and create something positive for the next generation, both in their careers as footballers and in their lives beyond professional football,” he said.
abd4daf190a46335: MEXICO CITY, Nov 1 — While Day of the Dead is a centuries-old tradition in Mexico, its parade in the capital is a newer addition — with thanks to Bond, James Bond.
The Day of the Dead, when Mexico honours its deceased by blending pre-Columbian traditions with the Christian All Saints’ Day, is historically a family affair.
Relatives visit cemeteries and set up altars with food and other items their loved ones enjoyed in life.
Then came 007.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Miguel Angel Mancera, who served as Mexico City mayor from 2012 to 2018, organised the city's first Day of the Dead parade in 2016. — AFP pic
The 2015 Bond film “Spectre” opens with the British spy walking through a crowd dressed as the dead in downtown Mexico City.
Yesterday, giant skeletons, floats and performers in feathered headdresses and masks filled the streets of Mexico City for the 10th anniversary of the Day of the Dead parade.
Musicians and acrobats joined the colourful floats, giving the downtown avenues a carnival atmosphere.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
People take part in the Day of the Dead parade in Mexico City on October 31, 2026. — AFP pic
“Everyone started asking me, ‘What about the parade? When’s the parade?’”
Miguel Angel Mancera, who organised the first parade while serving as Mexico City mayor from 2012 to 2018, told AFP. “It was an adventure.”
City officials expect more than half a million visitors from Mexico and abroad to watch this year’s parade, which falls on the same weekend as the city’s Formula One Grand Prix race.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
People attend the Day of the Dead parade in Mexico City on October 31, 2026.
Some of the giant figures used in the film appeared in the first parade in 2016.
“It’s a very, very big thing now,” Mancera said. “It’s something I’m really proud of.”
An 11-storey Catrina — an elegantly dressed female skeleton — stands in the Zocalo, the capital’s main square, as part of this year’s festivities.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Two women wearing Catrina costumes attend the Day of the Dead parade in Mexico City on October 31, 2026.
What was once a “more intimate” celebration has become “a mass event,” said Roberto Montalvo, an academic at the Iberoamerican University.
Tourists now pack some cemeteries, competing with families for space. “Do we adapt the visit to the ritual, or does the ritual adapt to the visitor?” Montalvo asked. — AFP
6e5f0f80d999f43d: LA PAZ, Nov 1 — Bolivian President Rodrigo Paz declared a state of emergency Saturday to free up resources for dealing with the impact of the El Nino weather phenomenon, wreaking havoc around the world.

Among Bolivia’s neighbors’ Peru has seen increased temperatures and wildfires, which have already claimed the lives of at least 12 people.
Chile has experienced the rainiest October ever recorded in Santiago, the capital. —- AFP

3a82acc0c9f9d067: NOVEMBER 1 — Sundar Pichai believes AI could one day do his job, running Google.

In a BBC interview on 18 November 2025, Pichai was asked whether an AI agent could eventually do his job. His answer was striking: “I think what a CEO does is maybe one of the easier things for AI to do one day.”
Not a warehouse job. Not a data-entry job. His job. CEO of Google.
When the man at the helm of one of the world's most powerful technology companies admits that AI could one day do his job, it is time for the rest of us to sit up and take notice.

Bill Gates had an equally stark warning. In an interview with The Observer, published in late October 2026, he described AI as an “evolutionary event”, a transformation in which humans may no longer be the most intelligent beings on the planet.
His prediction for the workplace is even more unsettling. AI could replace not just routine tasks but skills of invention, white-collar work and, with humanoid robots, eventually physical labour.
Gates believes businesses have a powerful incentive to replace people with machines. As he puts it: “Hire the robot, fire the human and don't look back.”

Elon Musk takes the prediction several steps further. In a July 2026 interview with The Economist, he suggested that AI could soon perform almost any digital job better than humans, with humanoid robots eventually extending automation into physical work. He believes employment could become optional, with people working by choice rather than necessity.
But his vision of a future of abundance raises a fundamental question: who will own the wealth generated by machines, and who will benefit from it?
That is the heart of the problem. AI could generate extraordinary wealth while leaving millions of workers struggling to find their place in the new economy.

These warnings are no longer confined to boardrooms or technology conferences. They have entered offices, homes and online chats. Beneath the talk of innovation and productivity lies a growing unease: Will there still be a place for me when AI takes over?
The payroll data are beginning to show where some of this pressure is emerging.

A Stanford Digital Economy Lab study, updated in August 2026, found that young workers aged 22 to 25 are falling behind in occupations most exposed to AI. The impact is showing up not in a wave of layoffs, but in the jobs that never materialised.
Not because they were fired. Because they were never hired.

Which raises a difficult question: if AI writes the first draft, prepares the first brief and produces the first analysis, where does the human learn to do the second? How will we train tomorrow's accountants, lawyers and managers if we remove today's training ground?

Pichai's answer is that people must adapt. But adaptation is easy to advocate when you are a CEO. It is a very different proposition when you have spent years mastering a profession, only to find that software can now perform your tasks in seconds.

The threat extends beyond job losses. AI may affect workers' pay and bargaining power even before their jobs disappear. The Economist, in an article titled Ignore AI and Ask for That Pay Rise, raises the concern that fear of technological replacement may itself suppress wages.
If you believe a chatbot is waiting for your seat, do you ask for a raise? Do you leave for something better? Or do you stay quiet, grateful simply to have a job?
So are we heading for mass unemployment? Not yet.

Stanford found no evidence of widespread, economy-wide job displacement associated with AI. And the widely quoted World Economic Forum forecast of 92 million jobs displaced and 170 million created by 2030 covers several forces reshaping employment, including technological change, demographic shifts and the green transition. It is not an AI-only forecast.

Exposure to AI does not automatically mean a job will disappear. Some roles will be transformed, while others may lose tasks or eventually disappear. The uncertainty is itself becoming a source of anxiety.

We've seen this before. When ATMs became widespread in the 1980s, many predicted the end of the bank teller. They were only partly right. ATMs reduced the number of tellers needed at individual branches, but they also lowered operating costs, allowing banks to open more branches.
But AI is not simply another step in automation.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
The author argues that AI is changing the job market rapidly, threatening jobs and wages, and that governments, businesses and workers must adapt to its impact. — AFP pic

It is a technological force unlike anything humanity has encountered before. AI is rewriting the rules of work itself. It can write, reason, analyse, create and make decisions, abilities once considered uniquely human. It is sweeping across professions, industries and disciplines, challenging not just how we work but what we once believed only the human mind could do.

We are no longer talking about machines replacing human hands. We are talking about machines that increasingly appear to think and respond like intelligent beings, challenging the very boundaries between human intelligence and artificial capability.

Gates is not simply sounding an alarm. He is also proposing ways to manage the upheaval. He believes certain jobs should remain reserved for humans, particularly where human involvement is essential. He has also suggested that governments consider taxing AI use, including the tokens businesses purchase to run AI systems.
But policy alone will not be enough.

Businesses must look beyond the savings AI can deliver and consider the people whose livelihoods may be affected. Governments, in turn, must ensure that the gains from AI are shared more widely through retraining, social protection and policies that help workers adapt. Employers must also find ways to give young people the experience traditionally gained through entry-level jobs.

For young people entering the workforce, the message is not to fear AI but to understand it. Beyond being a work tool, AI is now a guide to learning, a sounding board for ideas and even a source of companionship.

Being AI-savvy will become as important as being digitally literate: learning to use these tools, question their outputs and understand their limitations. Technical knowledge alone will not be enough. Critical thinking, creativity, judgement and the ability to work alongside intelligent systems will matter. The future will belong to those who know how to work intelligently with AI, not ignore it.
AI is not waiting for us to catch up. Its capabilities are multiplying, its reach expanding and its pace accelerating. What seemed impossible yesterday is routine today.

This is the real disruption. AI is changing the world of work even as we debate what it might do. By the time governments regulate it, businesses adapt and education systems catch up, the technology may already have moved on.
That brings us back to Sundar Pichai. If AI could one day perform many of the responsibilities of a CEO, what would leadership itself look like in the future?
The question is no longer whether AI will change the world of work. It is whether we can keep pace with a technology that is changing faster than our ability to understand its consequences.

16f8de2ebd69ad0d: No lesser authority than the MIT Technology Review says that the Emacs editor has turned 50 years old. But then, it is biased — Emacs was invented in MIT's AI lab.
Simson Garfinkel's article is simply called EMACS turns 50, but the sub-heading explains why it matters more:
"How the MIT AI Lab's text editor gave birth to the free software movement."

There are multiple timelines and accounts of the origins of Emacs, and it is not a single monolithic application. The name is an abbreviation for "Editing MACroS", and the original editor for which this set of macros was developed was TECO – "Text Editor and COrrector," written by Dan Murphy in 1962. Murphy died earlier this year at the age of 83.

The inimitable Jamie Zawinski has an encyclopedic Emacs Timeline – as he mentions at the start, his interest being that he long ago maintained a fork of GNU Emacs, originally called Lucid Emacs. It's still around, under its later name XEmacs. There are a lot of forks and re-implementations of Emacs out there, and we are not going to go into all of them, or this article would become a book – one only interesting to programmer-archeologists (to use a term coined by the late great Vernor Vinge).

As for who originally wrote those Editing Macros, though, another history has quotations from several of the people involved: On the Origin of Emacs in 1976. (Note – some of the quotes still contain the | symbols that marked quoted text.)
This credits Lisp boffin Guy L. Steele Jr with the original work in 1975, but in it, Steele says:

"RMS is responsible for the names 'E' and 'EMACS'. RMS still deserves 99% or 99.9% or 99.99% or 99.999% of the credit for taking a package of TECO macros and turning it into the most powerful editor on the planet."

RMS is of course Richard Stallman, and the page also quotes some emails from RMS on October 23 and 31, 1976. Mind you, just a few years after the event, in a 1981 talk now preserved on the GNU website, Stallman said, "I began the development of EMACS in 1974 with an improvement to TECO". Like all the best FOSS, even in its very early stages, it was a collaborative effort – but around late October 1976 is when RMS took over the bulk of the development.

Of the many forks of Emacs over its half a century of development, some are still just about hanging on in there. When we looked up the link for XEmacs, we were surprised to see that there was a new release: XEmacs 21.5.37 "lettuce" appeared just last month. And even the forks have forks: in this case, SXEmacs, last updated in 2020.

Most of the changes in XEmacs and SXEmacs eventually made their way back upstream to GNU Emacs, which is still in active development, although as The Register reported in 2008, RMS is no longer the primary maintainer. GNU Emacs 31.1 appeared in August.

Cards on the metaphorical table: this vulture is not an Emacs user. We have tried. A major influence was one of the Reg FOSS desk's favorite writers, Neal Stephenson, who in 1999 published an essay called In the Beginning… Was the Command Line. (It was later republished as a rather short book, but the text is still online.) In it, he says:

"In the GNU/Linux world there are two major text editing programs: the minimalist vi (known in some implementations as elvis) and the maximalist emacs. I use emacs, which might be thought of as a thermonuclear word processor. It was created by Richard Stallman; enough said. It is written in Lisp, which is the only computer language that is beautiful. It is colossal, and yet it only edits straight ASCII text files, which is to say, no fonts, no boldface, no underlining. In other words, the engineer-hours that, in the case of Microsoft Word, were devoted to features like mail merge, and the ability to embed feature-length motion pictures in corporate memoranda, were, in the case of emacs, focused with maniacal intensity on the deceptively simple-seeming problem of editing text. If you are a professional writer–i.e., if someone else is getting paid to worry about how your words are formatted and printed–emacs outshines all other editing software in approximately the same way that the noonday sun does the stars."

Emacs is 50-plus-year-old software, and it shows. This is a huge and complicated program: decades ago, the joke was that EMACS stood for "Eight Megs And Constantly Swapping". It is not an easy program to learn. Despite lavish documentation and a built-in tutorial, this is software so old that its terminology predates microprocessors and the personal computer.

Its exhaustive manual is 804 pages long, and to pick some trivial examples, its terms for parts of the screen use “frame” to mean what’s now called a window, and “window” to mean what’s now called a pane. In the section on Keys, it discusses the Control and Meta keys. That’s a slight snag: you don’t have a Meta key, and neither do the authors of Emacs. It was a key on the now almost legendarily rare Space Cadet Keyboard, of which the Deskthority keyboard wiki says:
“It is known as the holy grail of keyboards.”

You can buy a modern replica, the Keymacs keyboard. They are hand-made in the Czech Republic, and depending on exactly what model and specifications you want, they cost from €2,998 for the Lispsaver up to €6,878 for the A624N Space Cadet.
In other words, you can have a keyboard with a real Meta key if you want, but it is going to cost you.

One of the problems with these historical terms, unfamiliar to anyone who wasn’t already programming in the 1970s, is that meanings drift. In the context of Emacs, "Meta" means Alt, or Opt on Macs. However, KDE also uses the Meta key – but what the KDE documentation calls "Meta" is the Windows key – or Command on Macs. Like most Linux folks, the GNOME documentation calls it the Super key.
Names are important. They matter. Who's right, the Emacs folks or the KDE folks? Well, neither: nobody has Meta keys any more. We have Ctrl, Alt, and Cmd/Super/Windows.

There have been valiant efforts to modernize Emacs and bring it into line with modern UI and terminology. This vulture tried to learn Aquamacs, which modernized Emacs with a native macOS UI, but sadly it's no longer maintained.

Another, which we enjoyed trying, is ErgoEmacs, which changes the key bindings and rearranges the UI into something much more like the IBM Common User Access arrangement, as used in Windows and most Linux desktops. However, it never really caught on and you need to know your way around Emacs to install it and configure it for your regional keyboard layout.

So complex is it to configure Emacs that there are multiple pre-configured distributions of Emacs, such as Doom Emacs, or the minimalist Emacs Solo. We wish someone did a "CUA-Macs" config, with ErgoEmacs integrated and able to pick up your existing keyboard config.

Come to that, the Gershwin Desktop project that we mentioned along with GhostBSD last year is in active development, and it's based around GNUstep. Maybe its developers could pick up Aquamacs, and adapt it to GNUstep.

There is a long history of such Emacs facelifts. One instance is Borland’s Sprint word-processor, one of the selling points of which was that it could emulate the user interfaces of most of the leading MS-DOS word-processors of its day (just before they all converged on IBM CUA). Before Borland acquired it, Sprint was called The Final Word, developed by musical equipment makers Mark of the Unicorn. FinalWord was based on an Emacs clone called MINCE.
The Great Rival
Another well-known Emacs distribution is Spacemacs, which adapts Emacs to have a more Vi-like user interface.

Vi is the other seminal Unix text editor, as the Stephenson quote above mentions. As this article on Origins and the Evolution of Vi & Vim notes, it too dates back to 1976. Indeed, that’s the reason we chose the year in this story: Tilde, a text editor that doesn’t work like it’s 1976. One feature of Tilde we enjoy is that it supports use of the mouse even on the Linux console – which is the headline new feature of GNU Emacs 31.1.

Vi is very much alive and well today. GNU Emacs is based on the original source code, but Vi mainly survives as re-implementations. The recreation Stephenson mentions, Elvis, lives on today in the form of nvi.

However, by far the best known is Vim, maintained by Bram Moolenaar until his death in 2023. In the grand FOSS forking tradition, it too has forks, including Neovim, as used in Omarchy, and more recently, the AI-free Vim Classic – a new project led by Drew DeVault, who just launched the similarly LLM-free AlpineBSD. ®

d91c9fc5ba430ac6: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 1 — With the national jobless rate at just 2.9 per cent, Malaysia’s labour market looks healthy on paper, yet fresh graduates say artificial intelligence (AI) is making the first rung of the career ladder harder to reach.
Andy Iskandar Baharudin, 23, a finance graduate from a public university, has applied to more than 100 companies since an internship ended in July, the South China Morning Post (SCMP) reported today.
“How are we supposed to gain experience as fresh graduates if even getting an opportunity to work is difficult?” he asked.
Marketing graduate Nafeesa Azman, 24, says she has sent out 200 to 300 applications since finishing an internship about two months ago.
She blames AI for thinning out copywriting and visual-content work, and says employers armed with the tools are lowballing on pay.
Nafeesa wants at least RM3,000 a month, she said, but many offers fall short.
The routine tasks that once trained newcomers, such as taking notes, preparing slides and compiling data, can now be done faster and more cheaply by AI, SCMP noted.
The Department of Statistics Malaysia (DOSM) put unemployment among those aged 15 to 24 at 10.1 per cent in August, or 291,300 people.
Among those with jobs, DOSM found that 35.2 per cent of employed tertiary-educated workers were in semi-skilled or low-skilled roles in the second quarter.

The Human Resource Ministry told Parliament back in June that 1.6 million graduates, or 32.2 per cent of the graduate workforce, were underemployed in 2024, and that then government was accelerating labour market reforms.

A study commissioned by the Human Resources Ministry found last year that 600,000 existing jobs were “at risk” from AI, though then minister Steven Sim said up to 60 per cent of employers across 10 key sectors expected AI to create jobs.
The International Labour Organization estimates that nearly 80 million South-east Asian workers will be affected by AI, and 11.7 million could lose their jobs or see their tasks reworked.
Its July report, however, found no evidence yet of large-scale AI-driven job losses in the region.
A similar situation appears to be developing to Malaysia’s south, in Singapore.
Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said on October 12 that AI may have already broken the “bottom rung” of the career ladder.
Singapore will subsidise firms that take on interns, and has unveiled a S$1 billion (RM3.19 billion) plan covering worker upskilling, infrastructure, hardware and research.
International Monetary Fund managing director Kristalina Georgieva warned on October 16 that young people who would once have taken professional routine jobs are now serving coffee in Starbucks.
“That is not what I think young people in the world aspire for,” she said during the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok.
For Andy, the wish is simple: “We do want to work, gain experience and build our own careers.”

0d0c3021da6afaa8: ALOR SETAR, Nov 1 — Guar Chempedak state assemblyman Abdul Ghafar Saad and his son sustained minor injuries after the sports utility vehicle (SUV) they were travelling in collided with a car in Ulu Sedaka, near Yan, yesterday.

e237dc9c68bd0142: MANAMA, Nov 1 — The UAE is hoping for a breakthrough in negotiations between Iran and the United States while being prepared for the worst, a senior official said on Sunday, following threats of a resumption of the Middle East war.
“We’re hoping that there is a diplomatic breakthrough,” diplomatic adviser to the Emirati president Anwar Gargash said during a conference in Manama.
“It is not the interest of the region to go through another round... But I think we’re also, as we’ve shown before, braced for the worst.”
Following a visit to Tehran this week by a Qatari delegation, Iran has dispatched envoys to the Gulf country to continue consultations as part of indirect negotiations with the US to end the war.
But US President Donald Trump reiterated his threats on Saturday, saying the United States still has to “take care of” one or two targets in Iran.
“We just can’t allow Iran to take this region and the global economy hostage,” US Assistant Secretary for Near Eastern Affairs Donald Blome said at the Manama conference on Sunday.
“The hand of negotiation has been extended, and those channels have continued to be open and active at the same time,” Blome said. “We’ve been also prepared to go in another direction.”
On Saturday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Trump has not made a decision about fresh strikes on Iran and that the US would be open to a diplomatic solution.
The war began on February 28 with joint US-Israeli strikes on Iran, which retaliated by targeting, among others, Gulf countries allied with Washington. — AFP
42f1d1f919113e09: MELAKA, Nov 1 — The excitement surrounding the 16th Melaka State Election is beginning to build, with a “flag war” among political parties visible along roadsides and in public hotspots following the completion of the nomination process yesterday.

A Bernama survey today found that political party flags had been put up in urban areas such as Kota Laksamana, Banda Hilir, Semabok, Duyong, Bukit Katil and Ayer Molek, featuring flags of Pakatan Harapan (PH), Barisan Nasional (BN), Perikatan Nasional (PN), Parti Bersama Malaysia (Bersama) and Parti Pribumi Bersatu Malaysia (Bersatu).
Several political parties are reusing flags from previous state elections in Johor and Negeri Sembilan for the Melaka polls.
Political party flags line the roads in Tanjung Bidara, Alor Gajah, ahead of the 16th Melaka state election on October 31, 2026. — Bernama pic
Melaka DAP chairman Khoo Poay Tiong said most of the flags were still in good condition, making their reuse a cost-saving measure to reduce expenses for the Melaka state election.
“We do not have a lot of financial resources, but putting up campaign materials such as flags, posters and banners is important to inform voters in a particular area that PH is contesting there.

“These campaign materials are also intended to introduce to voters the candidates representing PH… the main purpose is to convey that message, rather than compete over who puts up the most flags,” he told Bernama today.
Political party flags are being put up along roads in Tanjung Bidara, Alor Gajah, ahead of the 16th Melaka state election on October 31, 2026. — Bernama pic
He said the installation of PH flags, particularly in areas contested by DAP, was being carried out in stages, especially at locations frequented by the public.
He said about 2,000 flags would be put up in each state constituency contested by the party, with the number to be increased if necessary.

“We will also put up billboards and buntings. We started after the nomination process ended yesterday, and the work is still ongoing. The installation of billboards and buntings will be based on polling district areas and according to need,” he said.

Meanwhile, BN candidate for the Duyong state seat Datuk Mohd Noor Helmy Abdul Halem said the flags displayed around the constituency had also been obtained from friends in Negeri Sembilan and Johor, where the respective state elections had concluded.
“Since Melaka is the third state to hold a state election, we are using whatever flags are available, as our budget is not large,” he said.
He said the installation of flags in the Duyong constituency was still being carried out in stages and was expected to be completed within the next two or three days.
A total of 79 candidates will contest 28 state seats in the 16th Melaka state election following the close of nominations yesterday.
Early voting is scheduled for November 10, while polling day will be held on November 14.
For the latest news on the 16th Melaka state election, visit the Bernama Melaka State Election Portal. — Bernama
3331b1971324bb82: MELAKA, Nov 1 — Thailand, Brunei and Cambodia are the latest Asean countries to have expressed interest in joining Malaysia, Indonesia and Singapore in efforts to address online safety issues involving children.
Communications Minister Datuk Seri Fahmi Fadzil said he welcomed the development, describing it as a sign that Asean was moving in the same direction.

“In discussions with my counterparts from Indonesia and Singapore, we were already on the same page on this matter. So, this is even better as Southeast Asia will now move in the same direction because we will be stronger when we stand united, especially in dealing with major social media platforms.

“We believe this will help considerably, particularly as these platforms view the region as a single market. So, if the entire or majority of the Southeast Asian market starts speaking about the same issues, then it will be easier,” he said.
Fahmi was speaking at a press conference after attending the Safe Internet Campaign Programme at Multimedia University (MMU), Melaka Campus in Bukit Beruang here today.
Also present was Communications Ministry secretary-general Datuk Abdul Halim Hamzah.

Elaborating on the joint efforts to address children’s online safety issues, Fahmi said Malaysia was also drawing lessons from the way certain restrictions had been implemented in other countries, such as Australia.
“We are also following and taking note of several recent cases in the US, in New Mexico, and this is very helpful in enabling us to take action or plan our next steps,” he said.

Fahmi was previously reported as saying that Malaysia and Indonesia had agreed to establish inter-agency cooperation at the implementation level to address children’s online safety issues, with plans also underway to involve Singapore.

On the Safe Internet Campaign, Fahmi said the programme had so far reached schools throughout Malaysia, with the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission (MCMC) continuing to enhance its content from time to time. — Bernama
c9ea3b114c789dba: MELAKA, Nov 1 — Barisan Nasional (BN) is confident that the achievements and performance of the state administration over the past five years will be among the key factors considered by fence-sitters in determining their choice of candidate in the Melaka state election on November 14.

Melaka BN chairman Datuk Seri Dr Ab Rauf Yusoh said these voters would assess the party based on its ability to administer the state, as well as the effectiveness of policies and initiatives that directly benefit the people.
“Fence-sitters look at the direction of a party that will be given the mandate to administer a state or country.

“So they will look at what we have delivered to the people while administering the state before making their choice,” he told reporters after inspecting the preparations of the BN election machinery at the Telok Mas state constituency operations room here today.

Ab Rauf, who is also Chief Minister, said approaches taken by the state government to win over the group included the Wakil Rakyat Untuk Rakyat (WRUR), Hari Exco Bertemu Rakyat and Jelajah Ketua Menteri Sayang Rakyat programmes, which focus on identifying and resolving various issues faced by the people.
He said the implementation of the initiatives demonstrated the state government’s commitment to ensuring that every plan and policy was translated into action that benefits the community.
Ab Rauf said that through the WRUR programme, the state government had resolved about 75 per cent of the 4,800 complaints received involving various needs and issues faced by the community.
He said the achievement was among the results of efforts undertaken well before the election.

“We have done the work early so that the people are not sweet-talked during the 14-day campaign period. This is important because we must regard our position as elected representatives... as an opportunity to serve the people, not for the people to serve us,” he said.

Ab Rauf said among the elements frequently assessed by fence-sitters was the ability of each candidate elected as a people’s representative to understand the pulse of the community, including listening to and identifying their problems and needs.

“First, a people’s representative must be one of the people before becoming their representative. They must know the people’s problems, know their needs, listen to what they say and convey it to me so that I can formulate policies that the government can implement in the future,” he said.
Ab Rauf said BN left it to the people to assess all the efforts undertaken by the state government before deciding on their mandate on polling day.
“I hope what we have done and what we have delivered will be the best measure for them to continue working together with us in managing Melaka,” he said.
The Election Commission has set November 14 as polling day for the Melaka polls, while early voting will be held on November 10.
For the latest news on the 16th Melaka State Election, visit https://election.bernama.com/prn/melaka/2026/. — Bernama
ea5dc6d8e172919e: MELAKA, Nov 1 — The Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission (MCMC) will not interfere in social media campaigns by contesting political parties during the 16th Melaka State Election, says Communications Minister Datuk Seri Fahmi Fadzil.
Instead, he said the commission will actively monitor social media platforms and only initiate investigations or take action against posts upon receiving complaints from the public.

“To date, these are the only two mechanisms MCMC will apply to posts concerning campaigning by contesting parties on social media platforms,” he said when asked about MCMC’s online monitoring measures during the Melaka polls scheduled for November 14.
Fahmi said this at a press conference after attending the Safe Internet Programme at the Multimedia University (MMU) Melaka Campus in Bukit Beruang here today.
Elaborating, Fahmi said MCMC is also monitoring the misuse of social media accounts to spread false information, the use of deepfakes, and extremely offensive content.

“We are also tracking a trend where content is uploaded by fake accounts, which then disappear once the post is published. This happens frequently and is not something we only anticipate during the state election; it is being detected more often and is quite worrying.

“We found that much of the content containing derogatory statements against the King originated from overseas-based accounts. Upon closer examination, we found that most of them, or 98 per cent, were fake accounts, so we take this very seriously,” he said.
Asked about Pakatan Harapan’s (PH) decision to name Parti Amanah Negara vice-president Adly Zahari as its Chief Minister candidate, Fahmi said it was due to his experience.
“He is an experienced figure. He has served as a state assemblyman for two terms and was previously Chief Minister,” said Fahmi, who is also PH communications director.

PH election director Datuk Seri Amirudin Shari was previously reported as saying that Adly, who is the coalition’s candidate for the Bukit Katil state constituency, was chosen as the poster boy and Chief Minister candidate should the coalition win the Melaka polls.
The Election Commission (EC) has set November 14 as polling day for the 16th Melaka State Election, with early voting on November 10.
For the latest news on the election, visit [https://election.bernama.com/prn/melaka/2026/](https://election.bernama.com/prn/melaka/2026/?utm_source=chatgpt.com). — Bernama
f93162fb8b37719e: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 1 — Seven heritage players who were previously handed 12-month suspensions by Fifa are now free to resume all football-related activities with effect from today.
The Malaysian Football League (MFL) confirmed this in a circular dated Oct 30, stating that the suspensions imposed on the players had ended yesterday.
MFL chief executive officer Mohd Shazli Shaik Mohd confirmed the authenticity of the circular, which was also widely circulated on social media.
“That is correct, it is genuine,” he told Bernama when contacted.
The seven players are Facundo Garces, Rodrigo Holgado, Imanol Machuca, Joao Figueiredo, Gabriel Palmero, Jon Irazabal and Hector Hevel.

Of the seven players, four – Figueiredo, Palmero, Irazabal and Hevel – play for Johor Darul Ta’zim (JDT), while Holgado is on the verge of joining DPMM FC, as previously confirmed by the Brunei-based club.

The controversy involving the seven players came to light in September last year after Fifa found that falsified documents had been used to support the eligibility of the foreign-born players to represent Malaysia in international matches.
In March, the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) partially upheld the seven players’ appeals against Fifa’s sanctions over the falsification of naturalisation and eligibility documents.
In its operative decision, issued without detailed reasons, CAS ruled that the players would still serve 12-month suspensions.
However, the bans applied only to official matches and not to all football-related activities. — Bernama

* Editor’s note: Fifa stands for Fédération Internationale de Football Association, football’s world governing body. DPMM stands for Duli Pengiran Muda Mahkota, the Brunei club’s name, which refers to the Crown Prince of Brunei.

a34ac9dda36ff354: Openreach has issued a stark reminder to customers that the legacy phone network is being officially switched off on January 31, and says the deadline will not be postponed.
The infrastructure arm of BT Group, Britain’s biggest telecoms biz, circulated the warning this week in a letter to comms providers that use its network to deliver their services.
It informs them that any customers still on legacy public switched telephone network (PSTN) connections are at risk of disruption when these are retired at the end of January, 2027.

The switch-off could affect businesses and consumers alike. Beyond the plain old telephone, systems that rely on PSTN connectivity include point-of-sale terminals, fire and security alarms, and personal care alarms for elderly and vulnerable people.

The move is part of a wider government scheme to get the UK onto all-digital high-speed networks running on fiber-optic infrastructure, and the legacy phone service – with its dependency on copper cabling – was standing in the way.

Many households have now ditched landline handsets and instead use only mobile phones, yet for those who still want a landline, the changeover means plugging the phone into the back of a broadband router to access a Digital Voice service.

Openreach has been planning this move for the best part of a decade. It has already pushed back the deadline at least once, after the government asked telecoms providers not to force vulnerable customers who use phone-network systems such as TeleCare to switch until fixes are in place.

Nevertheless, public awareness seems low that analog phone services will soon be disconnected. "Openreach and all providers need to coordinate a much more cohesive campaign that reaches customers directly," said telecoms analyst Paolo Pescatore at PP Foresight.

"TV, billboards and newspaper advertising should reinforce a consistent message, supported by targeted letters, calls and door-to-door support for older and vulnerable people who need extra help," he told The Register.

"Customers need to understand what is changing, what action to take, and who will help them. Providers must take responsibility for ensuring people remain safely connected, especially those who rely on their landline or a care alarm."
Caroline Abrahams, charity director at Age UK, agreed.

"With only three months to go, the digital landline switchover is entering a critical final phase. Most people have moved over without major problems, but nobody who relies on their landline or TeleCare should be left behind," she told us.

"Anyone with concerns should contact their provider, but the responsibility cannot rest with customers alone. Providers must not give up on people who have not responded. They need to keep trying to reach them and offer practical, individual support, recognizing that some may be unwell, living with dementia, worried about scams or without anyone nearby to help."
Openreach has a webpage with information regarding the switch-off. This advises consumers to call their service provider as soon as possible to ensure service is not interrupted.

The company previously told The Register that customers without a fiber connection will likely be switched to SOTAP for Analog (Single Order Transitional Access Product), where equipment is installed in the local telephone exchange to allow them to continue to use their old phone line as before.

Openreach has warned that commercial customers delaying migration risk significant disruption and unnecessary costs - leaving it until the last minute could make it harder to secure the requisite engineering support before the deadline hits.
"Businesses and organizations that delay action are making things harder for themselves," said James Lilley, Openreach Director of All-IP.

"The straightforward migrations have largely been completed. What's left are the complex connections that underpin critical operations, requiring careful planning, supplier coordination, and thorough testing. We are urging businesses to act now, audit their remaining analog services, and work with their communications provider on a migration plan today."

Earlier this year, the firm tried to drive home the message by announcing it was stepping up its charges to service providers and companies still operating legacy business lines, who will by now be paying double the rental cost compared to last year. ®

4b39511dbb407e45: NEW YORK: Binance said Sunday that it had resumed withdrawals after more than US$6 billion in virtual assets were stolen from the cryptocurrency exchange in a major hack the FBI said North Korea was responsible for.

Binance is the world's largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes. News of the hacking attack, which is thought to be the biggest-ever crypto heist, caused the prices of most major cryptocurrencies to fall sharply on Friday.
The company has offered reassurances that it will cover the losses from the attack, saying it has used company funds to buy tokens to replenish 90% of what was stolen.
Binance suspended user withdrawals after the attack but said they would be resumed in phases, the first of which began on Sunday.
"First batch network now opened in phase one of withdrawals," the exchange posted on X .

The US law enforcement agency accused North Korea of being behind the hack in a statement on Saturday, confirming earlier suspicions from private investigators and analysts that a Pyongyang-affiliated group called TraderTraitor was responsible.
TraderTraitor is the same group blamed for a US$1.5 billion theft from the Bybit platform in February last year.

"The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is releasing information advising the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than US$6 billion USD in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about Oct 29, 2026," the statement said.

The FBI added that it had observed "TraderTraitor actors" converting stolen assets into Ethereum, and expected those assets to be laundered further by converting them using decentralized finance and instant swap services.
It said it was urging private sector entities "to block transactions with or derived from addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder these stolen assets."
US president Donald Trump cast doubt on the North Korea's involvement in the hack.
"I'm not concerned. We're learning about it. We don't know if it's North Korea," Trump told reporters at his residence in Florida late Saturday.
The president often reflects with pride on summits he held with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un during his first term.
Binance has said that it was preparing to gradually resume withdrawals, starting between 6am and 9am on Sunday.

"We are taking a phased approach by prioritising tokens based on the past week data of user demand, so that each network and asset pair can be restored carefully, with stability and security checks completed before access is reopened," it said.
'Cover the financial impact'
Binance said Saturday it has set aside more than US$6.34 billion in company funds to cover losses in the hack.
"Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident," the company said on X.

It said it has used company money to buy tokens to replenish 90% of the stolen funds, while the remaining 10% of tokens are "less liquid, which means they may take longer to source in the required amounts".
The attack on Binance came as many observers express worries that the ever-expanding capabilities of artificial intelligence models could compromise cryptography and IT security protocols.
Bitcoin plunged nearly 5% after the news of the hack, while Ethereum dropped nearly 6% and BNB, native to Binance, tumbled nearly 10%.

The sheer scale of the hack has put a spotlight on the capacity of North Korea - which faces extensive international sanctions over its nuclear and missile programs - to find illicit means to capture revenue.

TraderTraitor is believed to be part of the Lazarus Group, which gained notoriety in 2014 when it was accused of hacking into Sony Pictures as revenge for "The Interview", a film that mocked North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

b636783076b1dc09: GEORGE TOWN, Nov 1 — A vibrant splash of colours, festive decorations and lively entertainment has brought the spirit of Deepavali to life at the Penang Jom Jom Deepavali Carnival 2026 in Bayan Lepas, with the celebration also opening new doors for small businesses and aspiring entrepreneurs.

Beyond the festive atmosphere, the 10-day carnival, which runs until November 7, is providing a valuable platform for small and medium enterprises (SMEs), home-based businesses and budding entrepreneurs to showcase their products, connect with consumers and expand their market reach.

Penang Indian Business Organisation president Dr Kugilan Pushpanathan said the carnival featured about 45 stalls offering a variety of products, with nearly 95 per cent of the participating vendors making their debut at a Deepavali carnival, many of whom had previously operated from home or relied on online platforms to sell their products.

He said the initiative, organised by the Penang Indian Business Organisation, was not solely business-oriented but also aimed at highlighting the growing number of Indian entrepreneurs and encouraging more members of the community to venture into business.

“Our intention is to give small vendors an opportunity to step out and introduce their products to the public. Some have been operating from home or online, but have never had the chance to participate in a carnival like this.
“We want them to gain exposure and experience, rather than focusing solely on making profits from the event,” he told Bernama at the carnival today.

Kugilan, who is also Key Global Network Sdn Bhd chief executive officer and founder, said the carnival is targeting about 10,000 visitors throughout its 10-day programme, following an encouraging turnout of nearly 2,000 visitors on the opening day.

He said the carnival also featured various cultural and entertainment programmes, including traditional music performances, local artistes and a special platform for aspiring singers to showcase their talents after auditions.

Kugilan also thanked the Penang state government, including Chief Minister Chow Kon Yeow, for their support in making the state’s first and largest Deepavali carnival possible, while expressing hope that the carnival could become an annual fixture in Penang’s Deepavali celebrations, providing a sustainable platform for small businesses and emerging talents.

Among the vendors is 16-year-old entrepreneur Aesvan Arvind, selling decorative lights and traditional Indian biscuits, who said business at the carnival had been encouraging, with visitor turnout exceeding his expectations and customers showing strong support for the participating vendors.

He said the carnival’s spacious outdoor setting and strategic location had given vendors better visibility and made it easier for visitors to discover their products compared with some other events held indoors.
“The response has been good, with more people coming than we initially expected. This provides a good platform for us to sell our products face-to-face to customers,” he said.
Meanwhile, Batu Uban assemblyman A.Kumaresan said the carnival offered an important platform for new entrepreneurs, start-ups and small traders to introduce their products directly to consumers.

“Many entrepreneurs had been operating from home or selling their products online, and the event allowed them to gain exposure to a wider market. This initiative was also important in encouraging more members of the Indian community to venture into entrepreneurship,” he said.

Kumaresan said the initiative also provided an opportunity for entrepreneurs to explore ways to take their businesses to the next level, with support from various agencies, including the Malaysian Indian Transformation Unit (Mitra) and National Entrepreneurial Group Economic Fund (Tekun).
The carnival was officially opened last night by Deputy National Unity Minister R. Yuneswaran. — Bernama

f2b920ea5a70163b: BRUSSELS, Nov 1 — The European Union slapped a €2 (RM9) handling fee on packages from outside the 27-nation bloc today in a bid to curb the influx from China.
The new levy — coming just weeks before the Black Friday, Cyber Monday, and Christmas season shopping rushes — will be on top of the EU’s €3 fee on small parcels.
How will it work?
The fee will apply to each type of item in a package sent directly to consumers from outside the EU, regardless of the parcel’s value.
For example, if there are 10 T-shirts in a package, the handling fee will be €2. But if a package contains two hats and 10 T-shirts, the fee will be €4.
The handling fee comes on top of the €3 duty imposed in July on small packages worth less than €150.
European consumers are not expected to pay the handling fee, insists the EU, but online retailers and sellers can add a €2 charge before a sale.
The European Consumer Organisation (BEUC) said it was “concerned that some platforms may try to pass these new costs onto consumers at the final stages of the purchase.”
It added: “That would be illegal under EU law, which requires the full price to be shown upfront.”
Why is the EU introducing the fee?
Nearly six billion small packages entered the EU last year, according to official data.
Some 93 per cent of the cheap packages that arrived in Europe came from China, usually via popular Asian platforms such as AliExpress and Temu.
Brussels says this is putting increasing strain on customs authorities, thereby raising their costs too. The handling fee will compensate their efforts.
Since the EU imposed the €3 duty on small parcels in July, imports have fallen by around 64 per cent — although officials warn it is too early to draw firm conclusions.
Europe has also expressed concern about “unsafe” non-EU products such as toys that violate the bloc’s rules arriving via Chinese e-commerce platforms.
“For years customs have been asked to take on illegal imports with limited resources while small parcels have multiplied out of control,” BEUC’s Agustin Reyna said.
What’s next?
The €2 handling fee is a permanent levy but the €3 duty on low-value packages is a temporary measure in place until July 1, 2028.
From that date onwards, standard, product-specific customs tariffs will apply.
The EU will have to assess the handling fee’s amount every two years to ensure it remains proportional to the cost of customs operations in the bloc. — AFP

df29daa140c2b789: SEOUL: South Korea's exports nearly doubled in October, the sharpest jump in more than 50 years, as robust global demand for AI investment boosted shipments of the country's chips, government data showed on Sunday.

Exports from Asia's fourth-largest economy, a bellwether for global trade, rose 93.7% from the same month last year to US$115.28 billion, slightly higher than a median 93.2% rise forecast in a Reuters poll of economists.
The surge, boosted by having more working days than a year earlier due to the timing difference in the Chuseok holidays, exceeded September's 83.7% gain and was the strongest since January 1974.

"With exports continuing solid growth of more than US$110 billion in October, it is becoming certain that annual exports of US$1 trillion will be reached within November," said Kim Jung-kwan, the minister of trade, industry and resources.

South Korea's exports for the January-October period totalled US$930 billion. Annual exports of more than US$1 trillion will make South Korea the fourth country in the world to reach the milestone, after the US, China and Germany.

Overseas sales of semiconductors jumped 259.4% in October to US$56.44 billion, as prices and volume remained high on continued facility investment by global big tech firms in the competition for AI industry leadership, the trade ministry said.
Computer sales spiked 496.6% on increasing server demand for AI services.
Shipments to China rose 133.6%, while those to the US grew by 185.8%, to Europe by 56.4% and to Southeast Asia by 128.0%.

South Korea's imports rose 36.0% to US$72.78 billion, after rising 26.0% in September, to post the biggest annual increase since January 2022 on higher crude oil prices, as well as demand for semiconductor manufacturing equipment and automobiles.
The nation posted a monthly trade surplus of US$42.50 billion, narrower than a record US$49.97 billion surplus in the previous month.
8c13b9185c9104d9: NEW YORK, Nov 1 — The FBI yesterday accused North Korea of stealing more than US$6 billion (RM24.3 billion) in virtual assets from the cryptocurrency exchange Binance in what is thought to be the biggest-ever crypto heist.

The US law enforcement agency’s statement came as Binance offered reassurances it was covering the losses from the hacking attack, saying it has used company funds to buy tokens to replenish 90 per cent of what was stolen.
Binance is the world’s largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes. News of the cyberattack caused the prices of most major cryptocurrencies to fall sharply on Friday.
The FBI confirmed earlier suspicions from private investigators and analysts that a North Korea-affiliated group called TraderTraitor was behind the hack.
TraderTraitor is the same group blamed for a US$1.5 billion theft from the Bybit platform in February last year.

“The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is releasing information advising the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than US$6 billion USD in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about October 29, 2026,” the statement said.

The FBI added that it had observed “TraderTraitor actors” converting stolen assets into Ethereum, and expected those assets to be laundered further by converting them using decentralized finance and instant swap services.
It said it was urging private sector entities “to block transactions with or derived from addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder these stolen assets.”
Binance said yesterday it has set aside more than US$6.34 billion in company funds to cover losses in the hack.
“Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident,” the company said on X.

It said it has used company money to buy tokens to replenish 90 per cent of the stolen funds, while the remaining 10 per cent of tokens are “less liquid, which means they may take longer to source in the required amounts.”
Binance suspended user withdrawals after the hack, but said in its latest update they were on track to resume today.
The attack on Binance came as many observers express worries that the ever-expanding capabilities of artificial intelligence models could compromise cryptography and IT security protocols.
Bitcoin plunged nearly five per cent after the news of the hack, while Ethereum dropped nearly six per cent and BNB, native to Binance, tumbled nearly 10 per cent.
Binance said Friday it was working to resolve what it called a “complex attack” with several “points of breach.”

The sheer scale of the hack has put a spotlight on the capacity of North Korea — which faces extensive international sanctions over its nuclear and missile programs — to find illicit means to capture revenue.

TraderTraitor is believed to be part of the Lazarus Group, which gained notoriety in 2014 when it was accused of hacking into Sony Pictures as revenge for The Interview, a film that mocked North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. — AFP

0747ff0d7149d6f2: Google on Friday celebrated receiving a poem from its first experimental orbital AI datacenter satellite.

The company's Suncatcher satellite, launched at the start of the month and put into low Earth orbit, has responded to a ground station prompt to "Write a haiku from the perspective of a TPU orbiting Earth, with the wonderful world spinning beneath you."

Travis Beals, senior director of Google's interdisciplinary Paradigms of Intelligence research team, said that with Suncatcher's host and TPU trays powered up and machine learning tests completed, the onboard Gemma 4 model achieved its "Hello World" milestone by sending an inference response from orbit.
"During a ground-station pass, we uplinked our first prompt to our onboard Gemma 4 open model, asking it to generate a haiku about being in space," wrote Beals in a blog post.
And as the satellite passed over Svalbard, Norway, the orbiting AI model responded over the downlink:

Those roughly 20 tokens would cost about $0.000012 if generated through the Google Cloud API, based on Gemma 4 26B's pricing of $0.15 per million input tokens and $0.60 per million output tokens, excluding input costs.
Add in a satellite weighing perhaps 500 kg, based on the mass of SpaceX's Starlink satellites, and a retail launch price of around $7,000 per kg, and you have a very expensive haiku.

According to Google's calculations, if the cost of getting a satellite into low Earth orbit can be brought down to $200/kg, the launch cost amortized over the satellite's useful life (~$810–7,500/kW/year) could be comparable to current electricity spending for terrestrial datacenters in the US (~$570–3,000/kW/year).
Google predicts that SpaceX could achieve that by 2035, more or less, and considers it strategically beneficial to prototype well in advance of that actually happening.

After the haiku, Beals said, "we tested space-themed limericks and telemetry prompts reporting the technical status of the payload systems." Next up: tests for evaluating how TPUs perform under thermal stress and radiation.
Google has already done some laboratory testing of its Trillium Cloud TPU and AMD host server to see how well they can withstand a 67 MeV proton beam.

The system's high-bandwidth memory shows the most sensitivity in terms of the total ionizing dose – it exhibits irregularities after a cumulative dose of 2 krad(Si), which is about 3× Google's minimum requirement for TID survival of 750 rad(Si).

"For typical transformer workloads, the observed SDC [silent data corruption] rate of approximately one event/17 rad, at an estimated orbital dose of 150 rad(Si)/year, translates to a very low failure probability on the order of 1 per 3 million inferences, assuming 1 inference per second," Google researchers said in a paper published earlier this month.
"While this error rate is likely acceptable for inference, the impact of SEEs on training jobs, and the efficacy of system-level mitigations, requires further study."

Indeed, the study will continue. Next year, the plan is to test a pair of interconnected satellites. Rather than lofting large satellites into orbit, Google anticipates sending a constellation of many smaller satellites that communicate with one another. ®

c4847b9309dd62fe: Their most pressing challenge is solving the long-standing water shortage in the village
Originally published on Global Voices
Participants of the project in Qyzylsay, Kazakhstan. Photo by Nazgul Aidabossynova. Used with permission.

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

Women in the rural areas of Kazakhstan are among those most affected by climate change, energy deficit, and poor governance. They bear the heavy burden of water shortages, especially in the southern parts of the country, where this problem is the most acute due to dense population, economic reliance on agriculture, and water losses related to outdated irrigation infrastructure.

In the village of Qyzylsay, located in the southern Jambyl region, the water shortage has become a major issue affecting the daily lives of women. It forces them to spend multiple hours a day outside their homes to secure water for their households, gardens, and animals. Their grueling work often goes unnoticed and unpaid, and their geographical remoteness places limits on access to information and government services, exacerbating their situation.

In 2026, Nazgul Aidabossynova, a local activist, implemented a project to help local women improve their livelihoods by training them to engage with the government more effectively and efficiently, calculate the cost of their labor and products, and mobilize collective efforts to solve community problems. Global Voices conducted an email interview with Aidabossynova to learn more about her initiative. The interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.
Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Sparks project.

Nazgul Aidabossynova (NA): I represent a community-based initiative led by rural women in Qyzylsay. Our work focuses on supporting women who manage households, small farms, livestock, and care responsibilities, while also facing limited access to information, public services, and opportunities for civic participation.

We chose to participate in the Digital Sparks project because digital tools can make a direct, practical difference in women’s daily lives. Many women already own smartphones, but previously used them mainly for calls and WhatsApp.

The project created an opportunity to turn these devices into tools for accessing eGov services, documenting community problems, managing farm and household responsibilities, protecting digital security, and communicating with local authorities.
GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?

NA: The key challenge is unreliable access to water in Qyzylsay. Water often disappears from the pipes during the day, particularly in summer. This affects gardens, livestock, household work, and the health and well-being of families.

The burden falls disproportionately on women. They wake early to store water, carry water for household and agricultural needs, care for the livestock, and wait for irrigation turns. Much of this work is unpaid, time-consuming, and rarely recognized.

Women also faced barriers in reporting water problems: they knew what was happening, but often lacked the knowledge, evidence, and confidence needed to raise concerns effectively with local institutions.
GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?
NA: The project delivered four practical training sessions for ten rural women.

The first one, titled “Your Phone is More Than WhatsApp: Smartphone as Your Household Assistant”, taught them how to use smartphone reminders, photo-diaries for farm and livestock work, eGov services, strong passwords, and basic digital-security practices.

In the second workshop, titled “Smart Water: When Your Garden Tells You It’s Thirsty”, participants learned about water rights, the responsibilities of relevant local authorities, and water-supply mapping using timestamped and GPS-tagged photographs.

The third session, titled “Numbers Don’t Lie: When You Count Everything, You Earn More”, covered how to track unpaid work and calculate the real cost of agricultural products such as milk. It also discussed the economic value of time saved through smart irrigation.

In “Honest Agreement: When Technology Helps Us Trust Each Other”, the fourth and final session, participants prepared time-to-income plans, mapped local support networks, discussed peer mentoring, and agreed to begin work toward a cooperative approach to water advocacy and shared smart-irrigation infrastructure.
GV: How did your participation in the project impact your organization’s beneficiaries and the community that you serve? Please provide examples.
NA: The project helped participating women see smartphones as tools for independence, civic participation, and practical problem-solving, rather than only communication devices.
For example, women learned that they can use eGov services to request certain official documents online, reducing the need to spend time and money traveling to administrative offices.

They also learned to create structured evidence of water problems. A photograph of a dry canal, broken pipe, or contaminated water source becomes more useful for advocacy when it includes the date, location, and a written description.

The training on unpaid labor and production costs was especially meaningful. Participants calculated the value of their time and better understood the real cost of milk production and irrigation work. The discussion showed that manual irrigation may take up to 60 hours per month.
This helped participants recognize that their time has economic value, and that shared smart-irrigation solutions could create more time for income, education, rest, and community participation.
The group also began a peer-learning process. Three participants started sharing the knowledge gained during the training with neighboring women.
GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed, thanks to your participation in the project?
NA: My understanding of digital democracy has become much more practical. Before this project, digital tools could be viewed mainly as a way to communicate or access information.
Through Digital Sparks, I saw how digital tools can strengthen people’s ability to exercise rights, access public services, collect evidence, engage with local authorities, and organize collectively.
I also gained a stronger understanding of the link between digital inclusion, women’s unpaid labor, climate-related water challenges, and civic space.

For rural women, digital capacity is not only about technical skills. It is about having a voice, being able to document problems, understanding their rights, and participating in decisions that affect their families and community.
GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?

NA: The most valuable lesson is that digital literacy has the greatest impact when it is directly connected to people’s real, daily needs. In Qyzylsay, water shortages, agricultural work, unpaid care responsibilities, and access to public services were the issues that made digital tools relevant and useful.

Another important lesson is that women need not only information, but also confidence and collective support. When participants understood their rights, calculated the value of their labor, and learned how to create reliable evidence, they became more prepared to speak with local authorities and work together.
The project also showed the value of peer learning. Participants are more likely to trust and learn from women in their own community who face similar challenges.
GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built in your future work and within your community?
NA: We will continue the peer cascade model, with trained participants sharing basic smartphone, eGov, digital safety, and evidence documentation skills with other women in Qyzylsay.

The group intends to develop a cooperative approach to the village’s water challenges. The planned cooperative would support joint advocacy, shared learning, and exploration of funding opportunities for smart-well or shared irrigation infrastructure.

In future work, we will continue combining digital skills with women’s economic empowerment, rights awareness, and local civic participation, so that rural women’s work, knowledge, and needs become more visible.
Written by Nurbek Bekmurzaev

a336ab677a302b8c: Microsoft senior software engineer Raymond Chen has explained what Windows is doing when you hold down the power button, and shared a story about the time a customer accidentally created a Goth Mode for Windows 3.1.

There's a section in The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy (actually, page 116 of this writer's dog-eared copy of The Restaurant at the End of the Universe) in which Zaphod Beeblebrox observes of a ship's interior: "Every time you operate one of these weird black controls that are labeled in black on black background, a little black light lights up black to let you know you've done it."
The same turned out to be true of a user who called Microsoft customer support to complain that after Windows 3.1 booted up, all that remained after the product logo disappeared was a blank screen.
It turned out the customer liked black a little too much and, according to Chen, made themself a Goth theme.

The customer support engineer on Microsoft's end pieced it together. The customer had, according to Chen, "set the wallpaper color to black. They set the title bar color to black. They set the button color to black. They set the window background color to black. They set the window text color to black.
"Every possible color you could pick in the Colors control panel was set to black."

We suspect the mouse pointer, at least, would have stuck around, unless the customer had also managed to change some settings around this. And then there are the icons… However, Windows 3.1 was a long time ago, and this writer's attempts at theming then were the consequences of growing up in the '70s and '80s, which resulted in some interesting neon, orange, and brown combinations.

As for Goth mode, Chen said, "Once you get yourself into this situation, it’s hard to get out because you can't see anything." One solution he suggested was deleting the [colors] section from the win.ini file.

Chen told the anecdote as a coda to the question – what exactly is modern Windows doing when you hold down the power button on a PC? According to Chen, after eight seconds of holding the power button, the Windows kernel realizes a forced power-off is happening and tries to take a kernel dump for diagnostics.

He explained that the kernel dumps were classified by Microsoft as "long power button hold" (LPBH) failures, with one of the bits of information captured indicating if all the pixels on the screen were black. The video driver might therefore be the culprit. Or whatever was responsible for drawing to the screen.
Today's Windows struggles with dark mode. But in the dim, distant past, every pixel being black might mean the user was either Hotblack Desiato or had done something very silly indeed. ®
124eb8a4808f667b: Flying across several time zones often causes jet lag, a feeling when the body insists it's the middle of the night while the clock says it's lunchtime. Now it turns out this nuisance is not exclusive to humans.

A new Science study on Manx shearwaters, seabirds that can fly hundreds of kilometers a day over the North Atlantic, shows they jet-lag themselves during their excursions. And because these birds navigate by the Sun, that jet lag leaves a measurable mark—it skews their compass.

Patrick Lewin is a behavioral and sensory ecologist at the University of Oxford and lead author of the study. “Manx shearwaters are medium-sized birds, about the same size as a pigeon,” Lewin said. “They are white underneath and black on top, but they have very long wings, and they are closely related to albatross.” Manx shearwaters nest in burrows on coastal islands around the North Atlantic. Most breed around the UK and Ireland, with about half of their population living in Wales.

493d74a6bcb2f43a: There's a ridiculously simple test you can use to figure out whether AI mandates at a given company are well-considered, or are being shoved out the door by out-of-touch buffoons: What happens when an engineer documents that AI made a task worse? Are they taken seriously, or are they marginalized and eventually managed out?

Conveniently, this week Amazon published a treatise by Terk Terkowitz, a VP/Distinguished Engineer/Final Boss of Their Independent Contributor Technical Career Track, on the role of the developer in the age of AI. It was originally an internal missive sent to their software engineers and their managers back in September, which is an interesting lag for a document that sounds this confident. It also maps exceedingly well to what other organizations are struggling with.

I think it's a good document, but I can't help but view it with a somewhat cynical eye. I see it as an attempt to make the future of the profession of software engineering feel less bleak. And it's feeling mighty bleak for a lot of folks right now.

This treatise comes at a time of dramatic upheaval. Tech as an industry is no stranger to change (usually at 3AM, heralded by the pager), but something about the current AI-ification of the world strikes many of us as fundamentally dissimilar from previous revolutions. Folks are scared about their career prospects. "Should I give up tech and get into farming?" is a sincere question multiple people have asked me. I don't know! Tech is already a goat rodeo, so you've got a leg up if you do?

This anxiety isn't theoretical. In May, Amazon wisely shut down KiroRank, an employee-built cash incineration leaderboard that ranked people by token usage, after the obvious thing happened: people spun up junk tasks to climb the ranks. This is now called "tokenmaxxing," and the Terkowitz treatise specifically calls it out as being at odds with "frugality." Meta did the same thing with "Claudenomics" and 85K employees that same week. And Amazon reportedly announced another 250 job cuts this week. I can't tell you that these things are related. But I can tell you that every engineer who read the memo assumes that they are.

This document contains a lot of great stuff. I have a tremendous level of respect, both personal and professional, for Amazon's Principal Engineering community; I'm led to understand that that respect may not be reciprocated, but that's okay. I am, by their standards, a lapsed engineer who ran away to join the circus as one of its lesser clowns.

Terkowitz's memo emphasizes customer outcomes and engineering judgement, two things I would absolutely not delegate to AI any time soon. (Note: I am writing this in October of 2026, with the full understanding that previous comments on the capabilities where AI falls short tend to age like fine milk.) It documents work that (today) AI tools aren't improving. That's way better than assuming that every objection to AI inherently comes from some self-interested Luddite who's scared of being replaced. It also says something smart about measurement: look at the 90th percentile of AI adoption, at those teams burning the most tokens, and check whether their delivery actually went up commensurately. This is great! Shout it from the rooftops; we should all be doing such things.

The memo says “If your work does not benefit from current AI tooling, that is a finding, not a failing.” Document it, bring it to your manager, work through the problem. I agree with every word of that! The question is whether anyone's promo doc is gonna survive citing it.

Here's what happens next. The memo concedes that input metrics are "deeply flawed," but then in the next paragraph says to go ahead and use them anyway, carefully. It then warns that non-adopters are falling behind. Those are three different positions within three sentences and they're not at all aligned with one another.

That's not muddled; I think it's cover. A manager can cite "a finding, not a failing" when a strong engineer skips the AI tool, and then cite "falling behind" when it's time to PIP someone. Both are congruent with their stated policy; you get to decide which interpretation you want to go with in a given situation.

How will managers handle justified AI non-use? Are promotion and performance decisions being made in a way that rewards these long term outcomes? Or are they instead taking the easy weasel way out, optimizing for what's cheap to measure, and rewarding tool activity? Because if you give me a metric, I will turn it into a target. So will an overwhelming majority of employees. When that happens, everyone loses — it's how KiroRank happened in the first place.

I write this after two days of attending GitHub Universe, where they talked about how agents start roughly 40% of PRs now. And yet, Jay Parikh’s keynote argument was that useful output wasn't "more code," but rather completed outcomes: features shipped, bugs fixed, security issues addressed, loudmouth columnists silenced, etc. The problem here is that their entire business model cuts against that; they're billing in a model that charges customers on a consumption basis, not an output basis. There's nothing, today, that ties "AI spend" to "output that was worth the effort."

Which brings us back to Amazon. The memo says tokenmaxxing is at odds with frugality, and for Amazon’s internal cost line, it is. Meanwhile AWS bills Bedrock and Kiro customers by the token. Inside the building, tokenmaxxing is a problem to be stamped out. Outside it, it’s the revenue plan. ®
