<!--kg-card-end: html--> Welcome back to the Abstract—and Happy Halloween! Here are the studies this week that smashed into Earth, put aliens on ice, drank mummy wine, and hugged it out.

First, a century-old theory that comets enriched Earth with the stuff of life is upended by new models of ancient impacts. Then: the case for life in extraterrestrial sea ice, a Halloween-coded medieval concoction, and a scientific embrace.
As always, for more of my work, check out my book First Contact: The Story of Our Obsession with Aliens, or subscribe to my personal newsletter The BeX Files.
Did the seeds of life come from above or below?
Anslow, Richard J. et al. “Cometary impacts are an unlikely pathway towards the origins of life on Earth.” Scientific Reports.

Carl Sagan eloquently said that we are all made of “star stuff,” but just how much of us is really comet vomit? This is a hotly debated question in science due to the popular theory that comets delivered essential ingredients for life to Earth during impacts more than four billion years ago, paving the way for the curious emergence of Earthlings.

But scientists have thrown cold primordial water on this idea in a new study that challenges “the long-held assumption that cometary impacts played an important role in the origins of life on Earth.” By running more than 100,000 advanced simulations of comet impacts, the team found that key prebiotic molecules found in comets, such as hydrogen cyanide, would be smashed to smithereens during impacts with Earth’s ancient surface in most cases.

Moreover, while Earth was pummeled by these snowballs during its youth—relatable!—this bombardment doesn’t neatly line up with the timeline of abiogenesis, the term of the origin of life. For these reasons, it’s much more likely that life assembled from earthly molecules that leaked out from our planet’s interior, according to the study.

“The most probable timing of successful cometary impact is in the early Hadean…more than 100 [million years] earlier than the estimated emergence of the last universal common ancestor (LUCA) at 4.2 [billion years ago],” said researchers led by Richard Anslow of the University of Cambridge.

“Taken together, the rapid decline in Earth’s cometary impact bombardment and the efficient destruction of fragile cometary organics indicate that the successful delivery of prebiotic feedstock molecules was an exceedingly rare event,” the team added.

The researchers didn’t rule out the possibility altogether, but concluded that any impact that had a direct influence on abiogenesis would be an edge case. That said, comets might serve as prebiotic wellsprings on other planets, such as Mars, where key molecules might have faced better odds of survival upon impact due to the red planet's smaller mass and thin atmosphere.

“Mars would have been the more favourable target for the cometary delivery of prebiotic feedstock molecules” which “strengthens the possibility that life could have emerged on Mars,” the study concluded.
In other news…
The tip of an alien iceberg
Barrier, Edouard et al “Sea Ice as an Origin of Life Location for Hycean and Ocean Worlds.” Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society.

While we’re on the topic of prebiotic feedstock molecules—a household conversation, no doubt—let’s speculate about their accumulation on weird exoplanets. In a new study, scientists suggest that these molecules might build up in sea ice on a variety of extraterrestrial ocean worlds, providing a pathway to the emergence of aliens.

“Water worlds with potential deep oceans are at the forefront of currently observable exoplanetary habitability,” said researchers led by Edouard Barrier of the University of Cambridge. “Here we outline a location where nutrients could be concentrated in sufficiently high quantities to make abiogenesis possible—at the interface between the open ocean and the surface ice shelf.”

The team studied the dynamics of sea ice on Earth, and modelled how similar features might form on a range of different exoplanets, including hypothetical “Hycean” planets. These are worlds more massive than Earth, but smaller than Neptune, making them part of the “sub-Neptune” class of exoplanets.

The results revealed mechanisms that “may plausibly provide concentrated chemical feedstock for prebiotic chemistry” on many of these exoplanets, suggesting they could be a substrate for the emergence of alien life. This “rich avenue of research…has the potential to significantly advance our understanding of aquaplanet habitability, and particularly to improve the prospects of abiogenesis on sub-Neptunes,” the team concluded.

What a week for the prebiotic feedstock beat! Taken together, these studies point to multiple onramps for life on worlds like Earth, Mars, exotic sub-Neptunes, and more, upping odds that life exists elsewhere in the universe—regardless of whether we ever find it.
Drink the mummy wine
Berger, Tim, and Naimi, Amira et al.“New molecular and historical evidence on ancient Egyptian embalming.” Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

To celebrate Halloween, here’s a trick and a treat all wrapped up in one delightfully grotesque story about mummies. Roughly 700 years ago, someone had the interesting idea of grinding up parts of Egyptian mummies, mixing the residue with wine or other liquids, and prescribing it as a medicinal elixir for people to drink.

This resulting product, known as Mumia vera aegyptiaca, circulated in Arabic and European markets for centuries, but its exact composition and pharmacology remain unclear. You know what that means: It’s time to do science on the medieval mummy cocktails.

Researchers analyzed historical Mumia vera products, mummified body parts, embalming residues, bandages, and two mummified skulls. The team discovered a wide range of formulas for this medicine, including one powdered product that appears to have been derived from a mummified head.

The results demonstrate that “an apparently uninformative powdered material can be chemically linked to a specific mummified head,” said researchers co-led by Tim Berger and Amira Naimi of Marburg University. “This study shows that linking historical texts, material culture, molecular composition, and bioactivity, can open new routes for decoding historical medicines and reconstructing the material biographies of human remains and museum objects.”

So if you are really committed to the spirit of this season, break out some Mumia vera aegyptiaca to pair with your Halloween candy and witches’ brew. Bottoms up—or more accurately: mummified-heads up.
Advances in hug science
Dueren, Anna Lena et al. “Why we hug: Individual differences predict emotional touch memories.” PLOS One.
What better way to close out this chilling spooky season than with the warm embrace of science? So come on, bring it in for a hug—or, in this case, roughly 15,000 of them.

Hugging is an incredibly common form of affection among humans, and even some other animals, including Halloween favorites like vampire bats. But little is known about “how individual differences shape the remembrance of such experiences,” according to a new study.

To fill this cuddly gap, scientists analyzed survey responses from 15,049 adult participants in the United Kingdom who were recruited in a public broadcasting campaign that included the BBC. The volunteers reported that their most memorable hugs were “for comfort, support, and understanding” and there was a noticeable gender split, as men were more likely to remember hugs that were “arousing” than women.

“Regarding hugs, men have shown different lateralisation and arm crossing patterns when hugging other men compared to women,” said researchers led by Anna Lena Dueren of the University of Bristol. “Furthermore, women were found to experience a stress buffering effect of hugs that was absent in men.”

And for anyone who considers themselves not a “hugger,” you are not alone. Plenty of participants expressed that they found hugs difficult or unpleasant. So whether you love bear hugs or cannot bear hugs, this study has something for you.
Thanks for reading! See you next week.

cccccd681779cc0e: Today's bit of signage silage is either Windows 10 protesting that it is not part of London's Oxford Street pedestrianization, or someone failing to heed an alert before the public is made all too aware that things aren't going well…

Eagle-eyed Register reader Aaron Colwill spotted the sign outside the food hall entrance of a Marks & Spencer store on London's Oxford Street. It usually entices passersby through the doors with promises of treats inside, but today it appears to require a different kind of feeding. Disk space is running low.

Marks and Spencer (also known as M&S and Marks and Sparks) is no stranger to cyber whoopsies, having been the victim of an attack in 2025 in which crooks made off with customer data. Later that year, it reckoned cleanup costs would be about £136 million.
That's quite a lot, but not enough to buy a bigger hard disk for Windows 10, it seems. Storage prices have increased over the years, but surely not that much?

Colwill reckoned that Windows 10 21H2 LTSC was behind the problems. It could well be. While support for 21H2 ended for many users in 2023, Windows 10 LTSC 2021 will carry on until Jan 12, 2027, meaning engineers might have an exciting festive period ahead of them. Windows 10 IoT Enterprise LTSC 2021 will receive extended support until Jan 13, 2032.
Either way, using Windows to advertise the Food Hall's wares seems slightly overkill. Simple posters, for example, never run out of disk space or attract the bork fairy's attention.

d27b8284b36d94fe: Nvidia is more than just a leader in graphics and AI hardware. It has also become a titan of the networking industry with bigger datacenter Ethernet sales than any other vendor.
In Q2, Nvidia's networking revenues topped $17.5 billion. To put that in perspective, Cisco's revenue during that same period, across all products, was $17.3 billion.
GPUzilla's arrival as a networking power feels sudden, yet Jensen Huang started working towards this status in 2019 with the $6.9 billion acquisition of long-time networking partner Mellanox .

At the time, Mellanox wasn't a big name in Ethernet switching. The company was mostly known for its ConnectX NICs and InfiniBand switches. Outside of high-performance computing (HPC) and supercomputing clusters, and a big deployment at Microsoft, InfiniBand wasn't widely deployed in hyperscale datacenters.

Buying Mellanox allowed Nvidia to reposition itself as a system builder, which means something different in the context of distributed compute. Nvidia understood its datacenter customers weren't interested in buying GPUs or even servers; they wanted clusters of systems. For that, Nvidia needed interconnect and Mellanox's InfiniBand fit the bill.
Relentless co-design

Over the years, Huang has talked about co-design – designing components and software to work together for specific set of jobs rather than to be the best GPU, switch, or NIC. Its work with Mellanox is a prime example of that approach.
According to Dell'Oro Group analyst Sameh Boujelbene, Nvidia's decision to integrate compute and networking became key to the company's success.

"Customers choose Nvidia for its tightly integrated compute and networking architecture, optimized for AI workloads," she told The Register. That integration makes deployments easier and speeds time to market.
Ben Mabey, CTO of pioneering AI and machine learning company Recursion, told The Reg Nvidia's integration schemes won him over.
Founded in 2013, nearly a decade before ChatGPT made AI the subject of dinner-table discussion, Recursion sought to apply machine learning running atop GPUs to the problem of drug discovery.
This work involved churning through massive datasets which, Mabey tells us, now total more than 50 petabytes in size.
"When you think about our workloads, it makes LLMs workload training seem easy compared to the amount of data that has to be moved around," he told The Register.

"In the biological space and sciences in general, it's not well appreciated just how big the data actually is," he added. "The internet's big, but in the grand scheme of things, the text that people are training on is actually pretty small, versus the petabytes of data that we have of these images."

Recursion's first cluster was a system called BioHive Zero which it cobbled together from GTX 1080 graphics cards originally intended for gaming systems. It used Ethernet to connect GPUs and ran into the limits of conventional networking.
So, for its second cluster, an A100-based machine with around 300 accelerators, Recursion went with Nvidia's Quantum InfiniBand switches and ConnectX NICs.

As Mabey explains it, buying its compute and interconnects from the same vendor vastly simplified optimization and troubleshooting. When Recursion reached out to Nvidia for help tuning the system, they were able to consider it as a single system, rather than discrete compute and networking resources. This level of integration had only previously been offered by boutique supercomputer builders like Cray or Atos (Eviden/Bull/whatever it gets renamed next).
A wider Spectrum
Nvidia hasn't always listed networking revenue as a single line item in its financials. However, based on CFO commentary and a little back of the napkin math we can fill in the blanks.
Nvidia's networking revenues have grown steadily since the Mellanox acquisition. At two moments, its revenue shot up suddenly.
The first came in the 2023 calendar year (FY24) after OpenAI kicked off the AI gold rush with the launch of ChatGPT.
The second spread across 2024 and 2025, when Nvidia started selling Blackwell-generation GPUs and then started to ship them in large quantities.

"I see two major inflection points, both coinciding with the Blackwell platform ramp: the introduction of NVLink switches and the accelerating adoption of Spectrum-X Ethernet switches for AI back-end networks, driven by growing deployments of Nvidia GPU clusters and increased attach rates of Nvidia switches, NICs, optics, and cables," Boujelbene said.
It was around this time that users started deploy to Ethernet switches in large volume across Nvidia clusters. Elon Musk's Colossus supercomputer was one of the earliest examples.

As we reported at the time, the first half of the 200,000-chip H100 and H200-based cluster came online in 2024 and, at the time, was among the largest ever clusters deployed using Nvidia's Spectrum-X Ethernet switches.
Meta has also made extensive use of Nvidia's Spectrum switches in its own training clusters, including at its million-GPU Prometheus site in New Albany, Ohio.
There are a couple reasons Nvidia's Spectrum-X offering is doing so well.

First, through a combination of Spectrum Ethernet switches, superNICs, and some clever software optimizations, Nvidia was able to replicate many of the qualities that made InfiniBand so attractive while also benefiting from significantly higher radix and interoperability.
Ethernet switches, including Nvidia's own, have historically offered more ports. The higher the radix, the fewer switches are necessary to support a cluster at a given port speed.

This often gets misconstrued to mean that InfiniBand can't scale beyond clusters of a certain size, which isn't necessarily the case. But for clusters exceeding a certain number of GPUs, Ethernet is often more economical because it requires less equipment while achieving similar utilization.
That said, Nvidia's Spectrum-X isn't exactly unique. Broadcom, Cisco, AMD and others have managed to achieve utilization similar to InfiniBand through various investments in smartNICs and switches.
Nvidia's main differentiator, as Mabey and Boujelbene noted earlier, is the level of integration between the compute and networking.
The next frontier
Then Blackwell hit the market, enabling much greater scale and creating a surge in Nvidia's networking revenue.

Prior to Blackwell, Nvidia's NVLink and NVSwitch interconnect tech had largely been limited to single systems with up to eight GPUs. With the launch of the GB200 NVL72, these NVSwitches were broken out into dedicated appliances. (And yes, we remember GH200 NVL256 and NVL32, but from what we can tell these were never shipped in any meaningful volume, if at all.)

For every NVL72 rack system sold, Nvidia also sold nine NVSwitch trays, which enabled the system's six dozen GPUs to function as a single enormous GPU. This effectively guaranteed steady networking revenue growth: even if customers didn't buy Nvidia's scale-out switches, if they wanted NVL72 racks, they were automatically buying NVSwitch.

"We estimate that NVSwitch now accounts for roughly one-third of Nvidia’s networking revenue, up from virtually zero less than two years ago," Boujelbene told El Reg. "This underscores how quickly NVLink switching has become a major growth engine for Nvidia’s networking business."
Nvidia is now moving to grow its networking business even further with a new licensing program.

Until recently, Nvidia's NVSwitch tech was limited to its own accelerators. However, with the introduction of NVLink Fusion early last year, Nvidia opened the interconnect tech up to third parties to license.

Many chip designers, including Marvell, Qualcomm, Arm, Fujitsu, MediaTek, and d-Matrix, have announced plans to develop CPUs and XPUs using NVLink Fusion. The adoption of the interconnect opens the door to additional NVSwitch sales, as the chips using NVLink Fusion still rely on them for chip-to-chip communications, and there's no other place to get them, as Nvidia has yet to license out NVSwitch.

"NVLink Fusion allows Nvidia to extend its networking footprint beyond its own GPUs into the rapidly growing custom accelerator market. I see it as a strategic move to capture a larger share of AI networking spending, even in clusters that do not use Nvidia GPUs," Boujelbene said.
Nvidia's networking ambitions don't stop there.

"Nvidia continues to pursue opportunities in emerging networking domains as network requirements evolve to keep pace with increasingly demanding AI workloads," Boujelbene added. "The latest example is scale-in networking, designed to address the new requirements of agentic AI, while innovations such as CPO will help overcome growing bandwidth, power, and scalability challenges." ®

6d6ace8f977196fc: SAN FRANCISCO, Oct 31 — OpenAI, Google, Microsoft and Anthropic pledged on Friday to give media outlets and other websites a single way to prevent their content from being scraped to train artificial intelligence (AI) models, amid growing criticisms and legal battles from news publishers.

Publishers currently have to implement multiple blocking commands for every bot that crawls the web to collect data, but the new proposed solution will allow them to enter a single, standardized instruction that’s recognised and honored by any AI company that adopts the protocol.
The solution will not fully take effect for months, though.

Microsoft will implement it beginning February 1, 2027, and Google sometime in 2027. ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said it will roll it out “in the coming months,” while Claude-maker Anthropic said it has “already started” rolling it out.
The announcement comes as publishers are facing a surge in bots that scrape their articles to feed AI models. Some, like the New York Times, have taken the matter to court.

In December 2023, the Times sued OpenAI and Microsoft for allegedly using millions of its articles without authorisation or payment to train ChatGPT. The two tech companies are invoking an exception to copyright law known as fair use.

Meanwhile, internet infrastructure provider Cloudflare has blocked AI bots by default on new customer sites since July 2025, and a standard called Really Simple Licensing already allows publishers to charge bots that visit their pages.

The new setting will apply only to future training of models but does not prevent bots from crawling otherwise, and content scraping will be allowed by default until the setting is changed by a publisher, Microsoft said in a blog post.
Opting out of AI training could reduce the chances that a publisher’s content will surface in AI apps and experiences, Microsoft and Google said in separate blog posts.

“We believe creating a common signal that conveys such preferences to multiple providers at once is an important step. And we look forward to working with other AI companies on the standards and their implementation across the industry,” Meta spokesperson Andy Stone wrote on X, conveying his support for the effort. — AFP

6f2278fea9c4ba0b: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 31 — A primarily US-owned startup is planning a US$600 million (RM2.4 billion) investment in a Malaysian rare-earth refinery, aiming to develop a new critical minerals supply chain as Washington moves to reduce its reliance on China.

DTEC Mineral and Metal Technology expects to establish the facility within three years, chief executive officer Milan Perlly said in an interview. The startup recently became the first company to receive permission under Malaysia’s relaxed export regulations to ship unprocessed rare-earth material to the US, Bloomberg reported.
“The larger goal is to make Malaysia the rare-earth elements processing hub for ionic clay in the region,” Perlly said.

Much of Malaysia’s identified rare-earth wealth lies in ion-adsorption clay deposits. These elements bind loosely to clay rather than locking into hard rock, making extraction cheaper and more efficient. Crucially, they contain the heavy rare earths vital for electric vehicles, wind turbines, and advanced military technology.
DTEC Mineral plans an initial processing capacity of 5,000 tonnes annually. The company ultimately envisions two facilities in Malaysia with a combined output of 10,000 tonnes a year.
“The US wants us to build 10,000 metric tons output,” he said. “My goal is to put one plant on the east coast for 5,000 metric tons, a second plant on the west coast.”

Perlly noted the firm is evaluating sites after holding discussions with state officials in Kedah, Terengganu, Perak, and Negeri Sembilan. These new facilities would expand Malaysia’s rare-earth footprint beyond the existing Pahang operations run by Australia’s Lynas Rare Earths Ltd.

Moving forward, DTEC Mineral intends to develop locally sourced ionic-clay deposits and eventually operate its own mine. While government data places Malaysia's rare-earth resources at an estimated 16.1 million tonnes, much of this remains commercially unproven.
To determine the most suitable processing technology, the company is preparing to ship 30 tonnes of unprocessed material to the US for research, having secured approval to export up to 700 tonnes.

Perlly, a Malaysian-born US citizen and former Capital One executive, holds a 51 per cent stake in DTEC Mineral alongside business partner David Greer. Local firm DTEC Engineering and Construction owns the remaining 49 per cent.
The startup harbours ambitions for a dual listing on Bursa Malaysia and either the Nasdaq or New York Stock Exchange.
DTEC was part of a critical minerals pact signed between US President Donald Trump and Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim last year.

According to the company's website, the agreement makes DTEC eligible for funding from the Export-Import Bank of the United States, the US International Development Finance Corporation, and the Department of Defense.
1fb4bfe9bce21a7a: BEIJING: China's factory activity slipped back into contraction territory in October, official data showed Saturday, despite sustained growth in high-tech industries, as the market for consumer goods weakened.
The manufacturing purchasing managers' index (PMI), a closely watched gauge of industrial health, came in at 49.3 this month, below the 50 mark separating expansion from contraction.

The fall in manufacturing activity was in part driven by a week-long national holiday at the start of the month, as well as a "complex and volatile international environment", according to NBS statistician Huo Lihui.
The figure, from the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS), missed the forecast of 49.9 by a Bloomberg survey of economists and was below the 50.1 and 49.8 recorded in September and August respectively
However, it was above the 49.2 recorded in July.
Prices for international crude oil have continued to climb, hiking up the prices of coal, rubber and plastic products, Huo said.

Despite "positive development momentum" within the high-tech sector fuelling the artificial intelligence boom, the PMI for the consumer goods industry in October was down 1.9 percentage points from the previous month, showing that "market activity has somewhat weakened", he added.
Beijing is hoping for annual growth this year of 4.5 to 5.0 percent, its lowest goal in decades, as sluggish domestic demand weighs on its export strength.
"Strong exports alone are not enough to boost the economic momentum," said Zhiwei Zhang, chief economist at Pinpoint Asset Management.
"If the external demand weakens in 2027, China will need more significant policy support to boost domestic demand," he added.
The non-manufacturing PMI, which measures activity in other areas including services and construction, came in at 49.7 in October, the data showed.
That was lower than a Bloomberg forecast of 50.0, and down from the 50.2 recorded in September.

Huo, the NBS statistician, said the drop was "influenced by factors such as a decline in (business) prosperity within certain service sectors," particularly the financial sector, but did not elaborate.
There was also a slowdown in construction activity compared to the previous month, Huo said.

8f9e81279e5a8c4d: From Moaz Nair
If you ever feel ignored at work, underappreciated by your friends or are generally invisible to the human eye, take comfort. You could be the Malaysian Indian People’s Party (MIPP) or Gerakan.
In the grand corporate hierarchy of Perikatan Nasional (PN), these two are the interns who don't get invited to the lunch table, yet somehow believe they are next in line for the CEO's position.
To say that MIPP and Gerakan bring no clout to PN is a profound insult to the word clout.

They are the political equivalents of plastic indoor plants – supposed to add a splash of "multiracial colour" to a very green room – except the plants have withered, the owners keep forgetting to water them and the landlords are currently trying to evict the entire building.

The political future of these minority component parties in PN has become one of the most ironic talking points in modern Malaysian politics. Critics, political analysts and observers frequently debate their position, although "debate" might be too active a word. It is more akin to watching two passengers argue over who gets the window seat on a bus that has already driven off a cliff.
MIPP: from bold newcomers to zero-vote club

Let’s start with MIPP, the bold newcomers whose political future in PN is currently the hottest topic among three guys at a coffee shop. MIPP entered the scene with the explosive energy of a damp firecracker. At its grand electoral debut in Johor, it contested five seats and managed a spectacular, flawless clean sweep of losing their deposits in all five.

MIPP’s standing within a major coalition remains precarious precisely because it has demonstrated a rare, mathematically impressive lack of an independent base. Yet, MIPP’s confidence remains unshaken by minor details like numerical reality.

Recently, the party announced it would completely sit out the Nov 14 Melaka state election after seat distribution talks with the PN leadership broke down. The official reason? President P Punithan bravely declared that the party refuses to compromise its dignity or accept "irrelevant" seats just to field candidates.

Translation: PN offered it a constituency consisting entirely of three palm trees and a stray cat, and MIPP chose "dignity" over another hefty loss of deposit. This breakdown signals deep friction over how minority component parties are treated by the dominant Malay-Muslim parties in PN.

The ideological mismatch here is staggering. MIPP is trying to pitch a minority-interest narrative in a coalition heavily dominated by PAS’s religious and conservative Malay narratives. It’s like trying to sell vegan burgers at a Texas steakhouse and acting surprised when the chef throws a spatula at you. It is incredibly difficult for a minority-interest party like MIPP to gain genuine traction among non-Muslim voters while standing next to politicians who view secularism as a design flaw.

Ultimately, MIPP’s decision to bypass Melaka highlights the ongoing, tragicomic struggle for minor non-Malay component parties to find an equal voice in a house that doesn't even know they are in the room.
Gerakan: master of the secular submissive

Then we have Gerakan, the veteran master of political irrelevance. The argument that Gerakan has no future in PN is a view increasingly shared by political analysts, critics, and even internal party factions who have grown tired of buying antacids in bulk.

Political observers highlight several compounding crises that threaten Gerakan's long-term viability in the coalition. First and foremost is its utter inability to attract non-Malay voters. Gerakan originally joined PN to serve as its non-Malay face, a bridge to the cynical urban electorate. Instead, it has become a cautionary tale, repeatedly failing to win over non-Malay voters from Pakatan Harapan, particularly DAP.

This has trapped it in the "shadow dilemma" – a polite academic term for operating entirely in the shadow of its larger partners, PAS and Bersatu. Because Gerakan brings minimal electoral data or seat victories to the table, its leverage in PN is roughly equivalent to a discount voucher that expired during the Asian financial crisis.

The ideological friction between Gerakan’s secular principles and PAS’s Islamic stance peaked hilariously during the school brewery donation saga. When PAS attacked the fund-raising, Gerakan deputy president Oh Tong Keong threatened to exit the coalition over "extreme" demands. PAS responded with a collective yawn, and Gerakan naturally stayed – proving that its red lines are drawn in invisible ink.

Naturally, this masterclass in political submission has triggered an internal rebellion. High-profile departures – such as the resignation of 31-year veteran and party treasurer Hng Chee Wey – underscore a growing internal revolt against sacrificing core principles for political expediency. These exits expose deep cracks under president Dominic Lau, as grassroots members grow tired of watching their leadership nod politely while being publicly sidelined.
PN's burning house

To make matters funnier, the house that Gerakan and MIPP are clinging to is literally on fire. The broader PN coalition is undergoing severe structural shocks, with PAS announcing the end of its political cooperation with Bersatu, triggering a chaotic power struggle and the sudden resignation of top PN leadership.

The Registrar of Societies even ordered the coalition's deregistration, and while a temporary court reprieve saved it from legal oblivion, persistent internal rifts cloud the bloc's political future. It is a civil war where the big boys are throwing live grenades, and Gerakan and MIPP are caught in the crossfire armed with plastic cutlery.

What is Gerakan’s next move? Political analysts suggest that leaving the coalition may be a risk worth taking compared to staying and enduring further humiliation. Yet, Lau has indicated that Gerakan is trying to pivot by backing a broader PN-Barisan Nasional electoral tie-up for future stability.

Yes, you read that correctly. While PN is on the verge of structural collapse and PAS is actively exploring independent realignments with Umno, Gerakan is trying to build a bridge to a party that doesn't know it exists, using a blueprint that is already out of date.
Conclusion

Gerakan risks being completely left behind unless it thoroughly recalibrates its political alignment. But that would require a sense of direction, and right now, both Gerakan and MIPP seem perfectly content to sit in the back seat of a driverless car heading straight towards a cliff, arguing over who gets to hold the auxiliary cable.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.

d84808b6057ac5b3: The Hubble Space Telescope still shines in the eyes of astronomers after 36 years in orbit, but it is not as nimble as it once was. Left alone, the observatory will plunge back into the atmosphere in the early-to-mid-2030s, closing the book on one of the most famous scientific instruments of the century.

NASA last raised the orbit of Hubble in 2002, when the Space Shuttle Columbia visited the observatory for a servicing mission. The final shuttle servicing flight in 2009 did not reboost the telescope's orbit, and with the retirement of the shuttle fleet two years later, Hubble has steadily lost altitude with no way to stave off eventual destruction.

The space agency released a Request For Information (RFI) on Thursday asking commercial companies for ideas on how to reboost, service, or a controlled disposal of Hubble. Responses are due November 30. Specifically, NASA is looking for information about companies' current and near-term capabilities for capturing Hubble and boosting it to an altitude of at least 373 miles (600 km), enhancing the telescope's performance, or guiding Hubble to a controlled reentry.
68f2fe60ad7543ba: Washington’s decision to order non-emergency American diplomatic personnel and their families to leave Saudi Arabia is more than a precautionary measure. It signals a dangerous deterioration in the security environment of West Asia.
For Malaysia, the implications are immediate, strategic and potentially costly.

Saudi Arabia is not merely another oil-producing country. It is a pivotal power in the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), the custodian of Islam’s two holiest cities and an indispensable pillar of global energy security.
When Washington begins withdrawing diplomatic personnel from Riyadh, Kuala Lumpur must pay attention.
The decision follows increasingly audacious attacks by Yemen’s Houthis against Saudi airports, energy installations and civilian infrastructure.
The recent targeting of Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport and Saudi Aramco’s Shaybah oilfield demonstrates how asymmetric warfare can undermine even a militarily sophisticated state.

Saudi Arabia possesses advanced Western weapons systems, extensive financial resources and powerful international partnerships. Yet relatively inexpensive drones and missiles continue to penetrate or challenge its defensive arrangements.
This carries five important lessons for Malaysia.
First, energy security cannot be separated from national security.
Although Malaysia produces petroleum and natural gas, its economy remains vulnerable to disruptions in global energy markets.
Higher transportation costs, expensive imported industrial inputs and renewed inflationary pressures could weaken domestic purchasing power.
Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s unity government has worked to preserve economic stability amid considerable international uncertainty.
A prolonged crisis in Saudi Arabia could undermine these efforts, especially if disruptions spread across the Persian Gulf and Red Sea.
Second, maritime security must be understood as an interconnected strategic system.
The Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb are indispensable arteries of international commerce.
If both become increasingly dangerous, shipping companies will face higher insurance premiums, longer journeys and mounting operational costs.
Malaysia, strategically positioned along the Strait of Malacca, cannot remain insulated from these developments.
Disruptions in West Asia can eventually affect Malaysian ports, manufacturers, exporters and consumers.
Third, the Houthis have demonstrated the growing effectiveness of asymmetric warfare.
Military superiority no longer guarantees comprehensive security.
Drones, missiles, cyberattacks and sabotage can inflict enormous economic damage without requiring conventional military parity.
Malaysia and Asean must therefore strengthen the protection of airports, ports, energy installations and communications networks.
The strategic lesson is straightforward: resilience matters as much as deterrence.
Fourth, Saudi instability carries serious implications for Malaysian pilgrims.
Mecca and Madinah remain central to the religious lives of Malaysian Muslims.
Any deterioration in aviation security or airport operations could complicate haj and umrah arrangements.
Wisma Putra, Tabung Haji and Malaysia’s diplomatic missions must strengthen contingency planning, particularly regarding evacuation procedures, flight disruptions and consular assistance.
The safety of Malaysian citizens must remain paramount.
Fifth, the American decision exposes the limitations of excessive dependence on external security guarantees.

The United States remains militarily formidable. Nevertheless, its decision to reduce diplomatic exposure demonstrates that even Washington cannot eliminate every security threat confronting its allies.
Malaysia must therefore deepen its strategic relationships with Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Pakistan, China and other influential powers.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
d55bb61639ca65ed: PARIS: The Fitch ratings agency on Friday maintained France's credit rating at A+ but downgraded its outlook from "stable" to "negative" as it raised new concerns over the cost of paying for the country's debt mountain.

"Weaker growth, renewed fiscal deterioration and higher yields have increased the challenge of delivering the necessary sustained fiscal consolidation to arrest France's worsening debt trajectory," it said.

The country will hold a two-round presidential election in April-May next year, and Fitch said the prospects for debt reduction after the vote were "uncertain".

"The emerging policy debate ahead of the presidential election has not materially strengthened Fitch's confidence in the prospects for durable deficit reduction that could lead to debt stabilization. 256141e19a66337a: Dalam dunia moden, masyarakat sering merasakan mereka bebas membentuk pendapat sendiri. Namun, seperti dihujahkan oleh Edward S Herman dan Noam Chomsky dalam karya penting Manufacturing Consent (1988), pendapat umum sebenarnya dibentuk melalui hubungan rapat antara elit politik, elit korporat dan pemilik media.

Herman & Chomsky menunjukkan media arus perdana tidak benar-benar bebas; sebaliknya, ia mengikuti struktur kepentingan pemilik, pengiklan, kerajaan, dan rangkaian ekonomi-politik yang mengawal aliran maklumat. Apabila masyarakat bersandar kepada elit kerajaan, agensi dan tokoh berpengaruh, keputusan menjadi lebih mudah ‘diurus’ kerana rakyat bergantung kepada sumber yang sudah dianggap sah dan berautoriti.
Jika pada era lama pemilik media ialah syarikat akhbar, konglomerat penyiaran dan stesen televisyen nasional, hari ini ‘pemilik media’ telah berubah wajah menjadi pemilik platform digital.

Herman & Chomsky menekankan sesiapa yang menguasai infrastruktur penyampaian maklumat akan menguasai ruang fikir masyarakat. Dalam konteks abad ke-21, kuasa itu bukan lagi dimonopoli oleh kerajaan atau syarikat media tradisional, tetapi oleh gergasi digital seperti Meta (Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp), Google (YouTube), X (Twitter), TikTok, dan aplikasi mesej peribadi seperti Telegram.
Mereka bukan sahaja menyebar kandungan, tetapi mengawal algoritma iaitu sistem yang menentukan apa yang rakyat lihat, baca dan bincangkan setiap hari.

Inilah versi baharu manufacturing consent dalam era digital: persetujuan tidak lagi dibentuk melalui editorial akhbar, tetapi melalui newsfeed, trending list dan algoritma cadangan yang direka untuk memaksimumkan masa tontonan.

Sebagai contoh, Facebook boleh mengangkat isu tertentu sehingga kelihatan seperti ‘suara rakyat’, walaupun ia sebenarnya digerakkan oleh kumpulan kecil belakang tabir yang mengeksploitasi sistem perkongsian. Begitu juga YouTube, yang boleh mempercepatkan penyebaran ideologi tertentu melalui cadangan video yang memerangkap pengguna dalam echo chamber.

Walaupun kerajaan masih mempunyai kuasa kawalan, yang menurut saya terhad kepada kandungan. Mereka kini bergantung pula kepada platform digital untuk menjangkau rakyat, menjadikan pemilik platform sebagai rakan strategik atau ancaman senyap dalam pembentukan pendapat umum.

Hubungan ini dapat dilihat dalam pilihan raya moden. Di Amerika Syarikat, kempen Donald Trump 2016 bergantung kepada Facebook Ads yang menyasarkan kelompok tertentu dengan mesej emosi, membuktikan bahawa pemilik data kini lebih berpengaruh daripada pemilik media tradisional.

Di Malaysia, penyebaran naratif politik di TikTok menjelang PRU15 menunjukkan bagaimana anak muda membina pandangan politik bukan daripada ucapan rasmi, tetapi daripada video pendek yang dikuasai algoritma. Ini menunjukkan kuasa mengurus masyarakat kini bergantung kepada gabungan kerajaan + elit korporat + pemilik platform digital, bukannya kerajaan sahaja.
Secara keseluruhan, apabila masyarakat terlalu bersandar kepada elit berkuasa baik kerajaan, media tradisional atau pemilik digital maka proses membuat keputusan menjadi lebih mudah dimanipulasi.

Masyarakat percaya kerana mereka menganggap sumber-sumber ini ‘natural’ dan neutral, sedangkan Herman & Chomsky membuktikan setiap sistem media sebenarnya mempunyai struktur kepentingan yang tersusun. Dalam era digital hari ini, propaganda menjadi lebih halus kerana ia bukan lagi disampaikan oleh editor manusia, tetapi oleh algoritma yang memutuskan apa yang wajar ditonton.
Pemahaman ini penting supaya masyarakat sedar bahawa ‘kemudahan membuat keputusan’ selalunya datang dengan harga: penyerahan sebahagian kebebasan berfikir kepada elit yang mengawal aliran maklumat.
Bagaimana ekosistem ini mempengaruhi fikiran dan tindakan masyarakat

Ekosistem yang dibina oleh kerajaan, pemilik media tradisional dan pemilik platform digital hari ini membentuk satu sistem pengaruh yang hampir total. Masyarakat yang bergantung pada sumber-sumber rasmi dan platform digital untuk memahami dunia akan mengikuti aliran maklumat yang telah ‘ditapis’ sebelum sampai kepada mereka.

Dalam kerangka Herman & Chomsky, ini ialah proses penyusunan agenda di mana apa yang dianggap penting oleh rakyat sebenarnya ditentukan oleh struktur kuasa di belakang media. Platform digital menambah satu lapisan baharu: maklumat bukan sahaja disaring oleh pemilik media, tetapi dipilih oleh algoritma yang mengutamakan interaksi popular dan bukan atas agenda kepentingan negara.
Akibatnya, isu yang paling banyak mendapat perhatian bukanlah isu yang paling penting, tetapi isu yang paling menguntungkan dari segi trafik dan emosi.

Ekosistem ini mempengaruhi cara masyarakat berfikir dengan mencipta ilusi bahawa maklumat datang secara organik, sedangkan ia sebenarnya hasil kawalan sistemik. Contohnya, seseorang mungkin percaya sesuatu isu ‘hangat dibincangkan rakyat’ kerana ia tular di TikTok, walhal algoritma hanya menolak kandungan serupa berulang kali sehingga mencipta kesan majoriti palsu.

Ini disebut Herman & Chomsky sebagai manufactured perception, persepsi yang dibuat, bukan dilahirkan secara semula jadi. Begitu juga dalam konteks politik: apabila naratif tertentu diulang melalui media arus perdana dan disokong oleh kemunculan semula video pendek di laman sosial, masyarakat mula melihat naratif itu sebagai ‘kebenaran kolektif’. Mereka percaya bukan kerana bukti, tetapi kerana kekerapan dan kebiasaan.

Ekosistem ini juga mempengaruhi emosi kolektif. Kerajaan mungkin menetapkan nada optimistik seperti ‘ekonomi stabil’, media tradisional mengulanginya melalui laporan rasmi, dan platform digital memanjangkan emosi itu melalui konten yang dipromosikan oleh algoritma seperti infografik, meme, video pendek, atau klip ucapan pemimpin. Pada masa sama, algoritma meminggirkan suara yang dianggap tidak menguntungkan atau bertentangan dengan arus popular.

Apabila masyarakat hanya dibenarkan melihat satu sisi, mereka percaya itulah keseluruhan cerita. Keadaan ini menjadikan propaganda lebih efisien kerana ia tidak memaksa masyarakat menerima sesuatu naratif, tetapi membentuk persekitaran maklumat yang membuatkan naratif itu kelihatan seperti pilihan paling logik.

Selain fikiran dan emosi, ekosistem digital juga mempengaruhi tingkah laku. Di Malaysia, kita dapat lihat bagaimana pola pengundian anak muda berubah secara drastik apabila mereka terdedah kepada video politik TikTok dan bukan kerana hujah rasional, tetapi kerana naratif visual yang dikuatkan oleh algoritma.

Di peringkat global, kempen Trump 2016 dan Brexit menunjukkan bagaimana data pengguna digunakan untuk menyasarkan mesej individu mengikut ketakutan, minat dan kelemahan masing-masing. Apabila algoritma mengetahui apa yang mencetuskan kemarahan, ketakutan atau harapan seseorang, ia boleh mempengaruhi tindakannya tanpa individu itu sedar mereka sedang dipengaruhi.

Akhirnya, ekosistem ini menjadikan masyarakat lebih mudah diurus. Herman & Chomsky menyebut media moden sebagai ‘sistem propaganda’ yang tidak kelihatan seperti propaganda kerana ia berfungsi dalam suasana kebebasan. Dalam era digital, sistem ini menjadi lebih kuat: masyarakat percaya mereka bebas memilih, tetapi pilihan mereka telah dibentuk oleh infrastruktur maklumat yang dikuasai oleh kerajaan, pemilik media, dan pemilik platform digital global.

Kesimpulannya, apabila aliran maklumat dikawal oleh jaringan elit ini, masyarakat bukan sahaja terpengaruh, malah diarahkan tanpa sedar untuk berfikir, merasa dan bertindak mengikut kepentingan pihak yang menguasai sistem.

0a7c6a7f6988f770: In calling on Malaysians to reject the politics of hatred based on race and religion on Oct 25, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said some people were attempting to “distort history by claiming that this country can only be saved through the victory of a single race”.
“If our ancestors succeeded in building the Melaka Malay Sultanate into a great empire, we can do the same through peace, unity among all quarters, and sound development strategies,” he said.
I couldn’t agree more. And history proves him right.

In recent decades the tension over whose country this is has taken on a life of its own, with those arguing for ketuanan Melayu or calling non-Malays pendatang gaining in strength. So much so that it has put many non-Malay citizens on the defensive.
It is as if Malay political strength and cosmopolitan composition are rivals for the same space.
They need not be, as Melaka’s history shows.

For roughly a century, the most important port in the Malay world was simultaneously the most thoroughly Malay polity in the region and one of the most diverse places on earth. Both facts were true at once. Neither diluted the other.

The Sultanate of Melaka was unambiguously Malay and Islamic. The court spoke Malay, kept Malay adat, drew its ceremonial rituals from Hindu-derived concepts filtered through centuries of courtly tradition, and derived legitimacy from control of the Strait of Melaka.

And yet the city’s population was staggering in its variety. Tomé Pires, writing within living memory of the sultanate’s fall, described traders from around the world who spoke somewhere around eighty-four languages in the port.

Gujarati Muslim traders and Tamil merchants from India traded here; Hokkien and Cantonese-speaking Chinese merchants ran warehouses; and Javanese, Siamese, Cham, Ryukyuan, Arab, Persian and Filipino traders also maintained quarters here.
There were resident communities with temples, mosques, shrines and headmen of their own.
This diversity was not incidental to Melakan power. It was Melakan power. The sultanate’s wealth came from being the place where the South China Sea met the Indian Ocean.

And that could only work if an Indian Muslim or Tamil merchant, a junk owner from Quanzhou and a pepper shipper from Java could all find or agree on the same weights, the same credit practices and the same language of contract.
Cosmopolitanism was not a value Melaka upheld. It was the economic base.

Melaka’s answer to governing this population was administrative rather than ideological. The state appointed a Shahbandar — the chief port master — to oversee all traders and revenue. The Shahbandar managed distinct trading quarters, registered merchants, collected taxes, settled internal disputes, and liaised with the government.

In practice this gave each community customary autonomy over its own affairs (marriage, inheritance, temple and mosque management), while the Bendahara handled internal Malay affairs. All commercial, criminal and appellate jurisdiction, however, rested with the sultanate.

The arrangement deserves attention precisely because it looks superficially like what colonial administrators later built and what Malaysian coalition politics later imitated — separate channels for separate communities. But the difference is structural, and it matters for how we think about unity today.

Under colonial rule, communal separation was the point. British policy froze categories through census classification, partitioned schooling by language, segregated employment by race, and treated intermixture as a management problem. Communities coexisted economically while remaining socially sealed, held together from above by an administration that belonged to none of them.

Melaka’s system separated for the purpose of incorporation. The Shahbandar registered you so you could trade, marry, inherit and litigate inside Melaka’s order. The Undang-Undang Melaka and the maritime code recognised community customs while reserving commercial, criminal and appellate jurisdiction to the state.
Malay was the lingua franca of the market and the court, and participation in that common life was the price and the reward of belonging.

Movement across lines was expected and routine. Chinese traders married locally and produced Baba-Nyonya culture. Indian Muslims settled into quarters that became permanent neighbourhoods, as did the Tamil merchants. And Arab Syed families entered Malay genealogies.
Conversion to Islam opened the fullest paths into the elite, and did so without erasing the commercial networks converts had brought with them.

Unity here meant a shared sovereign frame, a shared commercial language and a shared legal horizon — not shared blood, shared schooling or shared culture. Diversity was not accommodated at the margin. It was administered at the centre.

Against this record, the claim that non-Malay presence in the peninsula is a colonial residue awaiting digestion does not survive contact with the evidence. The ancestors of today’s Malaysian Chinese and Malaysian Indian communities were not confined to nineteenth-century steamships.

Long before Penang, Singapore and Melaka passed to Britain, there were resident Chinese, Tamil, Indian Muslim, Gujarati and Arab populations under Malay sovereignty here. They were registered, taxed, and adjudicated; and they even intermarried.
They were not guests awaiting permanent permission and the Shahbandar was not a manager of ethnicities.
That historical fact dismantles the foundational premise of ethnic exclusivism — that Malayness and non-Malay residence are, in principle, incompatible claims on the same land.
Five hundred years of Malay statecraft say otherwise, in Jawi script, in the records of a Malay court.

Honesty, however, requires stating the limits. Melaka was a transit entrepôt with a small population, perhaps tens of thousands, many of them sojourners, governed as subjects rather than citizens, and ranked by status and religion in ways no modern Malaysian would want restored.

So Melaka is not a blueprint. Nobody should propose reviving the Shahbandar offices. But it is something more useful than a blueprint: it is a refutation. It removes the alibi. If exclusion is defended on the grounds that Malay civilisation has always been exclusive, the fifteenth-century record contradicts the defence.
If assimilation is defended on the grounds that diversity requires uniformity to be governable, the fifteenth-century record contradicts that too.

What survives the comparison is a definition. Melaka shows that this region produced a working model of unity in diversity in which unity meant shared sovereignty, shared law and shared language, while diversity meant real autonomy of custom, belief and association.
The unity did not require the diversity to dissolve. The diversity did not threaten the unity.
This is an opportune time to remember this historical fact, as voters prepare to go to the polls in Melaka next month.

Some politicians will surely tell voters that they must choose between affirming Malay identity and embracing the country’s plural character; that they must unite to save their race or religion. Others may say voters need to come together to defend their rights.

The city’s own history says the choice being thrown at them was invented by colonial administrators who preferred divided subjects to a mixed populace. Before the colonialists came, the most successful Malay state in history proved the two were never opposites.

It would be asking a great deal of a banner-waving election season to engage with that. But the evidence sits there, in plain sight, in the very state being fought over — and it is worth saying out loud, in Melaka, before the voting: this country’s diversity is not a problem Malay civilisation inherited from outsiders. It is an achievement Malay civilisation once mastered.

14797c52cd6d8406: MUMBAI: Indian conglomerate Reliance Industries on Friday reported its highest ever quarterly revenue, saying net profit rose 41% in the third quarter, helped by strong performances from its core oil-to-chemicals arm and digital services division.

Reliance's July-September numbers come days after the impressive debut of Jio Platforms, the conglomerate's digital services arm, which raised more than US$3 billion in the country's biggest initial public offering earlier this week.
The retail-to-refining giant led by billionaire tycoon Mukesh Ambani is India's most valuable company by market capitalisation.
The conglomerate reported revenue of 3.62 trillion rupees (US$38 billion), up 27.8% year-on-year and its highest ever quarterly sales figure, according to a company statement.
Reliance has aggressively expanded into telecom and green energy businesses over the last decade, but it still relies on its traditional oil business for profits.
The conglomerate owns and operates the world's largest refinery complex in the eastern Indian state of Gujarat.
The sector has faced multiple challenges, with the ongoing Middle East conflict affecting supplies, but Reliance has managed to diversify crude imports.
Reliance "delivered a strong performance despite a complex operating environment", Ambani said in the statement.
"Our ability to optimise feedstock sourcing and product placement along with operations across the value chain enabled us to improve margin capture," Ambani added.
Jio's strong listing has also pushed the growth.
Launched a decade ago, Jio's wireless service disrupted the market with steep discounts that helped it rapidly win customers from rival telecom firms Bharti Airtel and Vodafone.

With more than 530 million subscribers, the firm currently makes most of its money from telecoms, but has expanded in recent years into newer areas including digital services and artificial intelligence.
Analysts see Jio as the key to Reliance's strategy to evolve beyond its traditional business and a touchstone of its future tech ambitions.
Ambani said Reliance has set "multiple global benchmarks."
"It demonstrates the depth of confidence investors place in Jio’s solid foundation and strong growth visibility," he added.
a77f1d52cf7d1709: For a genuine fright this Halloween, you can turn your gaze to the southern border, where ravenous, flesh-eating maggots are festering and have taken to eating people's pets.

This week, the country's New World Screwworm (NWS) infestation spread to a third state, Arizona, which joins New Mexico and Texas in being plagued by the horrifying parasites. To date, 74 animal cases have been identified in the US since the flies re-invaded the country in June.

The flies lay hundreds of eggs in wounds and moist orifices of animals, and the resulting voracious maggots feast on their victims. The maggots resemble screws and tortuously bore and twist into living flesh, causing severe, sometimes fatal wounds, before dropping to the ground to develop into adults.

9868ed317ba92ea5: Declining token prices have prompted Darkbloom, a distributed inference network, to reassess its business plans.

Darkbloom, a project from Seattle-based tech biz Eigen Labs, has developed software that allows anyone with a sufficiently capable macOS device to rent their GPU through the Darkbloom network for interference jobs. In return, they get paid.

Through this network, 800 or so participants – including as of two days ago this reporter – have been able to collect a few cents to a few dollars per day by having their hardware handle AI model prompts submitted through OpenRouter, an AI model gateway.

In theory, someone running one of Apple's recently released Mac minis with an M5 Pro chip and 64 GB of RAM could earn as much as $192 per month handling incoming inference jobs, per the company's estimate.

That assumes full 24/7 utilization during this period on a sought-after model like Qwen3.6 35B A3B, which sells for $0.065/M input tokens, $0.75/M output tokens. But not every network participant has fully surrendered their Mac hardware to the network.

The median earnings of the 50 people on the leaderboard amount to about $5.26 per day, $159.86 per month, or $1,918.50 per year. So the best case estimate presented by Darkbloom looks plausible. But it may not be sustainable.

The price of tokens – the unit of AI work – has declined, reportedly down 54 percent since May. Ramp's AI Token Price Index, which tracks the price of tokens from Anthropic and OpenAI, shows similar slippage. For Anthropic, the price per million tokens went from $2.65 on May 1, 2026 to $0.62 on October 22, 2026, a decline of 77 percent.

In a message shared with Darkbloom participants on the company's Slack channel, Kydo, one of the Eigen Labs researchers working on the distributed inference network, celebrated the network's processing of its trillionth token while attempting to moderate expectations about the project's viability.
"Earnings have been low," said Kydo. "For most providers, I don't expect that it is going to recover soon."
Pointing to the computational prowess of DeekSeek's DeepInfer framework, he explained that structural changes in the inference market have affected the supply of tokens.
"Data centers have become cheaper," he said. "Output per NVIDIA cluster is up ~20x this year, and their margins are wide enough to cut prices 90 percent and still profit at 50 percent."

The flood of tokens in turn has washed away the price advantage Darkbloom had previously. "The market caught up to our price," Kydo explained. "We could go lower, but then most of you would earn even less nothing."
Finally, he said, the inference routing market is changing, with OpenRouter moving away from price-based routing and putting more emphasis on decode speed, quantization, and prefill speed.
For network participants with older or less powerful Mac hardware – those without top of the line Max or Ultra Apple Silicon – "inference won't be worth running," he said.

Kydo went on to outline how Darkbloom aims to adapt to the commoditized token market. This involves analyzing model demand to steer participants toward more sought-after models, and looking at ways to provide other kinds of compute work, like distributed CI/CD jobs.
For Mac hardware, the focus now appears to be on clusters of high-end Mac Studios (now available with up to 512 GB of RAM), using Apple's Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) over Thunderbolt.

The CI/CD work, based on the observation that AI agents now make pull requests faster than CI/CD pipelines can handle them, will require sandboxing — something the biz expects to begin testing soon. And Darkbloom also aims to improve the performance of its network (in terms of time to first token) and to look for other token buyers beyond OpenRouter.

"The next stretch will be a fight, and I expect many machines will leave and Slack will get quieter," Kydo concluded. "But those who stay will be first in line when new earning opportunities come along. We are a driven team and well capitalized. We will not give up." ®

be8bb047a425a21d: A significant number of patients in the US lie to their doctors to get antibiotics they likely don't need, according to two new studies. While that may not be a startling revelation, the studies drills down on the phenomenon, finding that the lies patients tell are generally bad ones—and yet, they work almost all the time.

In the two linked studies published Friday in JAMA Network Open, a team of researchers led by Alistair Thorpe at the University of Utah analyzed online survey data from over 1,000 adults. They found that over a quarter of people reported having lied to a clinician at least once to get an antibiotic prescription for themselves or a child in their care. Patients lied by either exaggerating symptoms, making up symptoms, or—most often—both.

But interestingly, the lies people told to get antibiotics involved making up or exaggerating symptoms of infections that wouldn't be treated with antibiotics. For example, the most common falsehoods were symptoms associated with colds, such as fever, cough, and sore throat. That's despite the fact that colds are caused by viruses, not bacteria—which antibiotics treat.

72c93f4405f050cb: When you're ordering food from your phone, even time spent navigating the app is time wasted. At the P99 2026 virtual conference, Elvis Chidera, a staff engineer at Germany-based global delivery service Delivery Hero, explained how the company moved most of its user base to HTTP/3, and consequently cut its apps’ total end-to-end response time of the home screen by 17 percent.
Chidera, who managed the project, explained that, as promised on the tin, HTTP/3 delivers the web faster than HTTP/2, though it has slow bits that need to be adjusted to work properly.
Uber eats Delivery Hero

Delivery Hero is all but unknown in the US, which is dominated by Uber Eats and DoorDash. But it is a company with global reach outside the US, with an estimated user base of 60 million across Europe, Latin America, Africa, the Middle East, and Asia. Uber is currently acquiring Delivery Hero for $14.8 billion, with plans to unite the company with Uber Eats.

With this purchase, Uber would expand the number of markets where it offers both ride-hailing and delivery services, though not necessarily under the Uber Eats nameplate. Delivery Hero centrally manages separate apps for different regions, all of which it built or acquired. Asians can order poke bowls and sundries through Foodpanda. Turks can order kebabs through Yemeksepeti. Throughout Spain, Italy, Poland, Romania, Ukraine, and much of Africa, the Glovo app is where to ring up the late-night deliveries. And in Latin America, users dial in to PedidosYa to get what they need from nearby farmacias, restaurantes, and mercados.
All these regions have widely varying network connectivity, a problem Delivery Hero wanted to minimize.

Last mile networking was most often the bottleneck. Apps in Pakistan, for instance, could take nearly a second (at p90) to establish a secure handshake with a server. The engineering team looked at HTTP/3 as a way to lower, even eliminate, that latency.
A QUIC-er HTTP

The Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) formally introduced the third version of the internet’s Hypertext Transfer Protocol in 2022. HTTP is the application layer protocol that connects browsers and other resources connected to servers over the Internet.

The previous versions of HTTP were built on the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP), which offered guaranteed delivery and flow control. In conjunction with the Internet Protocol (IP), TCP/IP built the modern internet.
HTTP/3 replaced TCP with Quick UDP Internet Connection (QUIC), developed by Google, to address some of TCP’s perceived sluggishness as a transfer protocol.

UDP stands for User Datagram Protocol and, unlike TCP, it does not guarantee packet delivery or flow control. UDP is faster because it doesn’t wait around for a signature (QUIC adds in its own flow control on top of UDP).

But the UDP-based HTTP/3 reduces, and sometimes eliminates, the round trips needed to secure connections. The app can cache a session ticket and, on a later connection, use QUIC's 0-RTT capability to start sending eligible application data while the handshake is still underway, rather than waiting for it to finish.

“Essentially, you can eliminate that one second” of latency that plagued slower networks, Chidera said. “You don't want to pay the cost of two round trips just to exchange data, if you could do it faster.”

And unlike HTTP/2, HTTP/3 doesn’t get hung up when packets are lost or delayed. There’s no head-of-line blocking because packets are sent in multiple streams, not just the single string that HTTP/2 offers.
Multitask during initialization

Setting up HTTP/3 turned out to be surprisingly easy, Chidera found. Delivery Hero used Cloudflare’s content delivery network to serve its global user base, so moving to HTTP/3 involved a simple reconfiguration.
Adding HTTP/3 support to the clients, mostly mobile, proved almost as straightforward. Apple has supported HTTP/3 since iOS 15 and most native browsers already support HTTP/3 out of the box.

Android proved a bit trickier. The engineers used Google’s Cronet library for the networking stack, initially wired into their Android apps with the Cronet Transport for OkHttp wrapper to minimize rewriting their existing code, originally written for the OkHttp HTTP client.

Out of the box, Cronet helped support the HTTP/3 rollout, which reduced network-level request failures. But it also came with a significant catch: the engine took approximately 800 milliseconds to initialize at P90, eating into some of HTTP/3's 0-RTT speed benefits. So the team forked the code into their own bridge using a library called OKCronet. They also did some additional engineering work, which involved overlapping Cronet initialization with other background tasks.
Overall, they slashed the P95 latency time from 1.2 seconds to 120 milliseconds, achieving a 10x improvement in read latency.
Choose your congestion control algo wisely

Overall, the engineering team moved 95 percent of the users over to HTTP/3. Those devices that couldn’t use the protocol (largely due to networks blocking UDP traffic) automatically fell back to HTTP/2. Handshake latency between the apps and the server was cut by 51 percent. Pakistan’s response time was cut in half.

One hurdle remained, however. Secondary screens on some of the apps (pages/screens that aren’t the home page) experienced latency issues. These issues only happened in certain markets that were known to be prone to packet loss, such as Pakistan.

Delivery Hero’s engineers attributed the issue to Cloudflare’s choice of the congestion control algorithm for HTTP/3, Cubic, which historically has not handled packet loss well. The engineering team tested some of its traffic with Google HTTP/3-aware servers, which use another congestion protocol, Bottleneck Bandwidth and Round-trip propagation time (BBR), and did not get hung up on the packet loss.
Delivery Hero is currently working with Cloudflare to resolve this specific congestion algorithm issue, Chidera said.

5516c01947fa6ce1: A n0n ransomware operator tried to break into 23 organizations across 14 countries, but couldn't secure its own front door, leaving its server exposed with all of its methods on view.

The criminals used a mix of new (AI) and old (stolen credentials) tooling during their data-theft spree, and in some cases not only stole and encrypted files, but also deleted data and backups, eliminating victims’ ability to recover their information.

And despite the fear and hype around the breachpocalypse, with AI finding and developing exploits for critical vulnerabilities affecting most organizations across the globe, these crooks did not exploit a single bug to gain entry into any of their victims’ IT environments.
“In every documented compromise in this investigation, access relied on weak or stolen credentials,” said Ensar Seker, chief information security officer of threat intelligence firm SOCRadar.

“What stands out is the combination of AI-assisted development and very conventional entry points,” Seker told The Register. “We found no evidence of vulnerability exploitation in the cases examined.”

The gang breaks into organizations at scale using widespread Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) scanning and automated FortiGate SSL-VPN credential stuffing. To access US-based IT managed services provider ChiBiTek, the crew used a 15-thread residential SOCKS5 proxy pool to test credentials (ip:port:user:password) against FortiGate portals (GET /remote/login).

The operators also gained entry using exposed cloud credentials and reused hosting portal sessions. In one case linked to e-commerce site Fanatics, SOCRadar found that n0n used an exposed AWS access key with permissions to list, read, and delete objects in S3 buckets. The criminals then used this key to pull data from 40 S3 buckets, with up to 110 GB per bucket, and ultimately deleted data, including bank-transaction archives, and purged keys across 12 sensitive buckets.
AI-assisted extortion

While the threat hunters didn’t find any evidence of a fully autonomous attack system, the ransomware operator did use AI to assist with these intrusions, incurring more than $7,216 in AI usage costs by October 22.

Specifically: the criminal or criminals used OpenCode, an open-source AI coding agent, configured with 154 model entries across seven providers. Models included Gemini, Mistral, Nemotron, Llama, Claude, GPT-5.x, Grok, Kimi, GLM, DeepSeek, MiniMax, Qwen, and many, many others, some with safety training removed and others marketed as “uncensored” models.
“The operator used AI to write and debug hundreds of scripts. That shows how AI can help an attacker turn basic access into a broader, tailored operation,” Seker said.

“The destructive behavior is equally significant,” he added. “The operator did more than steal and encrypt files: in some cases, it deleted data and backups, and in one case changed firewall policies to block traffic. That creates a recovery problem that a decryption key alone cannot solve.”

SOCRadar’s threat hunters found the operator’s workspace - a publicly accessible Python HTTP file server hosted in Sweden at 185.157.161[.]148 on port 8877 - last month, and documented the exposed directory in snapshots on September 25 and 26.

“Across those snapshots, we identified 1,719 files, including attack scripts, ransomware source code, extortion infrastructure, and an AI coding agent environment,” Seker said. “This gave us visibility into the operation behind the victim listings, including how the operator prepared attacks and handled stolen data.”
Meet n0n
It also provided a close look at n0n, a newcomer to the data-theft and extortion game that has claimed 108 victims since it emerged last month.

On October 12, the group added 38 maritime, port and logistics organizations across 18 countries to its leak site in a single batch. Researchers have linked at least 21 of them to customers of South Korean maritime software provider CyberLogitec, although the software provider has not confirmed an intrusion.

The crooks set an October 19 deadline for the maritime firms, with ransom demands ranging from $400,000 to $28 million, payable in Bitcoin. After the deadline, however, none of the 38 listings were marked “settled” and none of their payment addresses showed any transaction. All affected organizations’ stolen data was published.

While a handful of the gang’s claimed victims have been marked “honored - data destroyed” on n0n’s leak site, indicating the victim orgs paid the ransom demand, SOCRadar hasn’t validated any transactions on-chain. In its profile details, the security shop rates the gang a 10 out of 10 for "aggressiveness" and a zero out of 10 for “lethality.”

The group is believed to be based in Russia, although the server uncovered by SOCRadar, which it attributed to a single operator or small team, didn’t provide any definitive geographic or national attribution.

Every case that the exposed server documented followed the same lifecycle, moving from initial access to establishing persistence and credential collection via hidden admin accounts disguised as services, covert proxies, credential and session-token theft, mailboxes and emailed multi-factor authentication codes.

The crooks then collected sensitive data and sent everything to the operator’s central storage with the attack impact shifting between data-theft, encryption, destruction, and network disruption, depending on the targeted organization.

After breaking into Transcom, a Netherlands-based financial services provider, the crims sent a secondary ransom alert directly to PayPal's security team, even though the compromised data was only on Transcom's network.
Stupid mistakes and n0n security basics

Finally, the crims send ransom notes, post a countdown clock on the leak site, establish negotiation rooms and emails for victims - and then leak the stolen files or destroy backups when the organizations don’t pay up. In some cases, and to apply increased pressure on victimized companies, n0n also broadcasts automated countdown warnings to businesses’ service providers, clients, and media outlets.
Despite its aggressive tactics, the operator in this case - as with other stupid criminals The Register has gleefully documented in earlier stories - still struggles with basic security hygiene.

“There is a striking gap between operational ambition and security discipline,” Seker said. “The operator invested thousands of dollars in AI services while leaving its own workspace exposed. The locker also contained hardcoded encryption keys, with evidence suggesting reuse across victims. An operation can have serious destructive capability while still making fundamental mistakes.”®
