071e826394b5b671: For centuries, infrastructure has evolved alongside technology. New materials and engineering techniques enabled taller buildings, longer bridges, and larger cities. Computing and digital technologies later transformed how infrastructure was designed, monitored, and operated. Now, the pace of change is accelerating, and challenges are arriving simultaneously. Climate change is increasing pressure on water, energy, and other resources. Artificial intelligence is beginning to transform engineering and design, and its energy needs, along with aging grid infrastructure, is creating significant challenges, as well as new opportunities. In addition, geopolitical complexity is exposing vulnerabilities in global supply chains, and demand for infrastructure is rising, particularly in the developing world. The result is a fundamental challenge: How can the world build the infrastructure it needs without simply repeating the extractive, carbon- and resource-intensive model of the 20th century? In this interview, Ali Jadbabaie, JR East Professor and head of the MIT Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, says the answer will require rethinking not only how infrastructure is designed and built, but how it is financed and operated, and bringing together the many stakeholders who shape those decisions. On Oct. 28, Jadbabaie will join experts from around the world in Madrid to explore these topics at the World Infrastructure Forum, which was co-founded by MIT’s Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, UPM, the World Bank Group, and the University of Texas at Austin. Q: Infrastructure has always evolved in response to technological advances. What makes this era different? A: In the 18th century, civil engineering emerged as the civilian counterpart to military engineering, building the dams, bridges, and canals of its time. Industrialization in the 19th century brought railways and sewage systems. In the early 20th century, the focus scaled up to buildings, highways, tunnels, and metro systems, and by mid-century the infrastructure needed to support megacities and skyscrapers. Every time technology has changed, with information technologies, computing, sensing, and, more recently, digital transformation, it has changed the shape of infrastructure. It has even changed the definition of what infrastructure is. Today, we consider the power grid, semiconductor manufacturing plants, and data centers part of infrastructure, along with wireless infrastructure like cellphone towers and the infrastructure for high-speed internet, just as much a part of our critical infrastructure as roads, water systems, and power grids.  What is different now is the combination and speed of the changes we're facing. Climate change, resource constraints, and geopolitical instability are putting pressure on the way we designed infrastructure in the 20th century. At the same time, many people are moving out of poverty because of recent economic growth in the developing world. In fact, according to models, by 2028, for the first time in the history of humanity, the median human inhabitant of the planet will live off $10 a day. As more people move out of abject poverty, there will also be an increase in the demand for infrastructure. If we try to meet that demand using the same resource-intensive model we used in the 20th century, we simply won't have the resources to do it. The question then becomes: How do we use the remaining resources more efficiently? We need to find a way to provide more infrastructure while using less water, energy, and materials, and produce less carbon. This is where digital transformation and AI become potentially transformative. Faster and cheaper sensing, greater access to data, and better sensing, actuation, and control can help us make infrastructure decisions more efficiently. AI is slowly permeating the physical world, and we expect it to revolutionize the engineering design process, allowing us to explore many more possibilities, much faster and at a lower cost.  But the story of that hasn't been written yet, and the outcomes could still be very positive, depending on what we do. Q: Can you give an example of infrastructure systems becoming more interconnected in a way that changes how we build or manage them? A: The revolution in information technology and digital transformation over the past 30 years has made infrastructure systems more interconnected. You see this in cities. If the power goes out, water and gas systems can stop functioning, internet fails, and transportation system comes to a halt. If communications networks fail, many other services are affected. We saw this during Covid, when disruptions in supply chains affected energy networks, critical materials, and manufacturing. We see it when geopolitical conflicts disrupt oil and energy markets and those disruptions propagate through other parts of the global economy. Infrastructure systems that were once managed separately are increasingly dependent on one another. As we connect more things together for more efficiency, we also increase systemic risk and expose the systems to rare but catastrophic failures. They have become rare, but when they happen, they're much bigger and more consequential. The really tricky thing is that developing infrastructure involves much more than designing and building it. The whole value chain includes financing and operating it, as well as understanding who will use it and what those users need and prefer. So, designing infrastructure is a highly transdisciplinary, sociotechnical endeavor, involving social, technical, and economic considerations. Understanding how these systems are designed is increasingly important because they are becoming more complex, making decision-making particularly difficult. There’s also so much uncertainty in large infrastructure projects. They’re very capital-intensive, the business is lower margin than many other industries, and projects take a long time. Combine all of that, and it has historically made the industry very conservative. But the transformations coming from AI and digital transformation are potentially offering a new way forward. What that new way looks like, no one has quite delineated it yet. Q: How are you and your colleagues working to change how these decisions get made?   A: We realized that if we're going to develop a new approach to infrastructure, no single discipline, company, or country can do it alone. Infrastructure value chain is too interconnected, and the challenges are too large. That's why MIT’s Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering co-founded the World Infrastructure Forum with the World Bank Group, the Universidad Politécnica de Madrid, and University of Texas at Austin. The goal is to bring together academia, industry, governments, and financial institutions across the infrastructure value chain and create an ongoing dialogue about how infrastructure should be designed, financed, built, and operated in the decades ahead. This is particularly important because the biggest opportunities for new infrastructure development are not necessarily in the United States or other countries with mature infrastructure systems. Those countries still face significant needs for modernization and new investment. But over the coming decades, much of the world's population growth, and much of the infrastructure that will need to be built, will be in countries where infrastructure systems are still developing.  Those countries have an opportunity to benefit from modern infrastructure without simply repeating the model of the 20th century. But capturing that opportunity will require new approaches to technology, financing, engineering, and governance. We're trying to create an ecosystem rather than just a forum, a mechanism for continuing the conversation among the different stakeholders across the infrastructure value chain. We've established five working groups and an advisory group of more than 30 leaders from across the infrastructure value chain, including engineering and construction, materials, finance, multilateral institutions, and academia. Ultimately, the question is not whether we need a new way of developing infrastructure. The question is how we create it and who is going to execute it. There is no single person, company, or country that can solve this problem, because infrastructure itself is interconnected. We need to build the new model together.
133598f3f99fbe16: Donate to our Justice as infrastructure Spotlight issue, and get more of the coverage you value!

All images via Canva or fair use. Screenshots of Peacekeeping circle (bottom left) and Duterte protest (top center) via YouTube. International Criminal Court building (top right) via Wikimedia CC BY-SA 4.0. St. Louis courthouse under construction (center middle) via Picryl CC0 1.0.

Often portrayed as abstract, large, formal, distant, and quite technical, justice is a moral and ethical area, tied to institutions and legal statutes, and can seem a long way from mundane daily experience. But it is also a deeply practical underpinning for how most societies function. Without justice systems that work and are understood at the most fundamental level, economic mobility is threatened, socially marginalized groups have no recourse, and lack of trust hampers institutions and interpersonal interactions alike.

Justice is the grease in the motor of social functioning. Nobody will contest the importance of justice to holding people to a collective moral code of conduct, but the often overlooked next-level function justice plays is that, when justice is fair, fast, and reliable, it makes everything in a society run better. It allows for a society to fulfill its economic, social, and creative potential. Copyright law protects ideas and innovation; land law protects resources and livelihoods; labor law supports humane and effective use of our work — as long as those laws are enforced. When you know that it will be straightforward and predictable to get all the permits, you are more likely to start a business. When you know that fraud will be punished, you are more likely to invest your capital. When you know that you will be caught, you’re less likely to evade taxes. When you know that there will be fair and fast prosecution, you are more likely to report injustice and less likely to perpetrate it.

In this spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to make visible the ways in which justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society, and how countries with a justice deficit can work towards stronger protections that will enable economic and social benefits.

ad8a7bfc37201941: Patients who think they're getting an annual checkup often end up with an unexpected bill. The Good Brigade/DigitalVision Collection via Getty ImagesI was teaching health economics when a student raised his hand. We were discussing the Affordable Care Act, or ACA, which requires most health plans to cover certain recommended preventive services at no additional cost to patients. I explained that preventive care could cost nothing. The student had expected that, too. Instead, he said, he received a bill for more than US$500 after his checkup. He was so frustrated that he said he would never go back for another annual checkup. I suggested he contact his insurer to find out why he had been charged and whether his visit had been billed as preventive care. Then another student spoke up. Her husband had paid several hundred dollars for what he thought would be a free checkup too. The very next day, I received a $78 bill for my own Pap smear. I expected my insurance to cover this cervical cancer screening without cost-sharing because it is among the preventive services recommended by the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force and generally covered under the ACA. When I called my insurer, I learned that the visit had been billed as a regular outpatient office visit, with no mention of the Pap smear. I then called my primary care provider’s office. The clinic acknowledged a coding error and corrected it. My bill dropped to zero. As an assistant professor of health policy and addiction studies at Penn State Harrisburg, I know whom to call and what questions to ask when I receive an unexpected medical bill. Many of my graduate students worked full time and took evening classes. Would they know how to dispute a bill, or have time? Those experiences led me to investigate how often patients pay out of pocket for annual checkups. I teamed up with fellow researchers Erin Duffy and Max Crowley to examine this question. In our analysis of a Pennsylvania survey, nearly 1 in 4 insured respondents reported paying for their most recent checkup. Why a preventive visit may come with a bill Many health care services covered by insurance are subject to copayments or deductibles. A copayment is a fixed amount patients pay for a covered service, while a deductible is the amount they generally must pay for covered care before insurance starts paying. The ACA, however, requires most health plans to cover certain recommended preventive services, including screenings for high blood pressure and certain cancers, vaccinations and counseling to help people quit smoking. These should come at no cost to patients. Generally, this applies when patients see providers who are in their insurance plan’s network. But that doesn’t mean every annual checkup is free. If a patient discusses a new symptom or asks the clinician to manage an existing condition during their annual checkup, it can result in a separate office-visit charge. A test may be billed as diagnostic rather than preventive, and coverage varies by plan and provider. Sometimes, as in my case, a coding error is responsible. Not every charge is inappropriate. The challenge is that patients often cannot tell which services should be covered, why they were billed, or whether a mistake occurred. What our survey found Previous studies have found, using insurance claims, that patients sometimes face out-of-pocket costs during preventive visits. But these records show how visits were billed, not necessarily what patients believed they were receiving. We wanted to know whether people who thought they were getting annual checkups also reported paying out of pocket. Our study, published in August 2026 in the peer-reviewed journal Prevention Science, used the 2024 Penn State Lion Poll, an online survey of Pennsylvania adults. We analyzed responses from 912 insured adults who reported an annual checkup within the preceding 10 years. Most had one in the past year. Of those respondents, 23.5% reported paying out of pocket for their most recent checkup. Among those who paid, the average reported out-of-pocket amount was $68.50. After accounting for other characteristics such as age, gender, insurance type, income and education, we found that respondents who were not familiar with ACA preventive-care protections were about 12 percentage points more likely to report paying than those who were familiar with the protections. That difference is equivalent to roughly 12 more people paying out of every 100. Those who considered healthcare unaffordable were about 13 percentage points more likely to pay than those who found it affordable. Because our survey relied on patients’ reports rather than billing records, we could not determine why individual charges occurred, or whether they were appropriate. The findings show associations, not causation, and our nonrandom sample cannot provide a precise statewide estimate. How doctor visits are billed doesn’t always match what service patients think they are receiving. adamkaz/E+ Collection via Getty Images Why these bills matter I kept thinking about the student who said he would never return for another checkup. Research has shown that even modest out-of-pocket costs can discourage people from getting recommended screenings. Delaying preventive care could mean missing opportunities to detect health problems early, when treatment may be more effective. Our survey did not find a statistically significant association between paying for a previous checkup and planning another one. However, respondents who were unfamiliar with ACA protections or considered healthcare unaffordable were less likely to plan a checkup. These findings suggest that uncertainty about costs may discourage people from seeking preventive care. What patients can do Before a visit, ask your insurer which preventive services are covered without cost-sharing and confirm that your provider is in-network. Ask the clinic whether discussing other health concerns or receiving additional tests could trigger a charge. If a bill arrives, compare it with your insurer’s explanation of benefits, which you can typically find in your online insurance account or receive by mail. Ask the provider’s billing office which services and codes were submitted and request a correction if something appears wrong. You can also contact your insurer to question or appeal a coverage decision. A colleague told me she challenged a $20 or $30 copayment requested at check-in for an annual visit after remembering our conversations. The charge was removed. Patients should not have to become experts in insurance billing to receive preventive care. Clearer coverage information and more transparent billing could help people seek care without fearing unexpected costs. 1084f4473e021767: Paying for childcare remains one of the biggest costs for households, often costing as much as housing. AP Photo/Craig MitchelldyerWhile affordability pressures are hitting Americans in many facets of their lives, from groceries to gas prices to housing costs, one important expense often gets less attention – childcare. After a huge infusion of federal funds into childcare dried up at the end of the Biden administration, experts warned that this sharp cutoff, sometimes dubbed the “childcare cliff,” would force parents to either scale back work to handle the extra caretaking or pay steep costs out of pocket. The potential effects of the federal cuts are hard to estimate, in part because states took different approaches in the aftermath. In some cases, they offset the sharp cuts in part by redirecting other funds to childcare. But several states, including Vermont, New Mexico and Kentucky, have gone further and innovated on their own to shore up support for working parents and their young children. Meanwhile, New York City is expanding free toddler slots for lower-income families, following Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s announcement to build a universal early childcare system. Taken together, these experiments point to bipartisan ways to support working parents, especially if the results of the November 2026 midterms signal a new willingness to tackle one of the biggest cost burdens for families. As researchers of sociology and childcare policy with six children from 1 to 16 years old between us, we have also gained insights from our own data gathered over 75 interviews with parents in St. Louis, Missouri, over the past few years. We see them struggling with a fragmented childcare system that’s in need of a deep strategic investment. These families face limited choices and soaring costs for an essential good that allows a parent to go to work. Out-of-pocket expenses for parents using center-based care in childcare centers and private preschool programs have more than doubled since 2019. In 2024, the national average price of childcare was US$13,128 annually, which rivals housing as the most expensive item in family budgets. States go their own way The disruption caused by the COVID-19 pandemic laid bare the critical role that reliable, high-quality childcare plays for working families. But we believe it also presented an opportunity for innovative investments in the nation’s fractured childcare landscape. Pandemic relief legislation in 2021 directed nearly $40 billion to shore up the supply and quality of childcare. This funding increase, which was a fourfold jump over previous levels, supported childcare staff with higher wages and allowed for other investments to improve the quality of care. The reach was vast, with stabilization funds flowing to 220,000 providers serving 9.6 million children. Many states also provided grants to create new slots and improve how providers got paid. As those funds began drying up in September 2023, some states started to address these shortfalls on their own. In some cases, they took significant steps at a policy level to channel more support to working parents. We believe these investments could serve as examples for the rest of the country. One is Vermont, which in 2023 became the first state to pass a law establishing a childcare entitlement. Following more than a decade of advocacy and bipartisan support, the law established a near-universal public childcare system, funded partially through a payroll tax of 0.44% split between employers and employees. Through an expansion of subsidies along income tiers, the number of families covered rose by 55% from July 2022 to May 2025, while flexible grants increased the number of providers and focused on improving the quality of care. About 12,000 children are now covered under this program. New Mexico went even further. In November 2025, the state became the first in the nation to offer universal childcare. Based on an older program that provided free childcare to low-income families, the initiative expanded support to all working parents regardless of income. Children draw at a daycare center in Albuquerque, N.M., which has gone further than any other state in expanding subsidies for working parents. AP Photo/Susan Montoya Bryan Before the expansion, 32,000 children were covered, a number the state aims to double by 2028. On average, the state estimates that the program will save families $12,000 a year. Meanwhile, the Kentucky legislature in April 2026 passed a measure with strong bipartisan support to make major investments in the state’s childcare infrastructure. Key provisions include free childcare for the children of childcare center employees, increased state-subsidized reimbursement rates, and required training to support very young special needs children. The Kentucky measure also loosened regulations that had made it tough for employers to share costs for care, such as renting facilities, while pitching a pilot program to open one-room “microcenters” in communities that lacked sufficient childcare options. In addition, Gov. Andy Beshear launched a complementary Pre-K for All pilot program in several counties. Another example is New York City, where Mamdani has announced an expansion for toddlers as young as 2 years old in all five of the city’s boroughs, building on the city’s programs for free childcare for 3-K and pre-K. To date, this effort has increased some slots, although the rollout in September hit bumps. The childcare crunch by the numbers Given the skyrocketing costs, over 70% of families who sought care say it’s difficult to find childcare – and that doesn’t count the 11% who fail to find any at all, according to a 2023 government survey. That report found that families with Black or Hispanic children or infants, and those living in the South and West, are more likely to run into cost as a barrier. On the supply side, three-quarters of providers say they have to turn many families away or put them on waiting lists. Center-based care for an infant costs more than in-state college tuition at a public university in 32 states, yet childcare workers, who are overwhelmingly women of color, earn the same as parking lot attendants and dog walkers. That makes them some of the lowest-paid workers in the entire economy. Amid soaring costs and scarce supply, roughly half of all U.S. families live in so-called childcare deserts – areas where there are three children under 5 for every licensed-care slot. The answer for many families in these cases is to rely on ad hoc and irregular informal care. Some parents told us they’re turning to relatives and neighbors for help. Others resorted to using unlicensed, and potentially unsafe, childcare providers because they found no other viable options. And for some remote workers, the daunting solution is to care for their kids themselves while working. The problem with such makeshift arrangements is that they tend, on average, to offer fewer of the learning opportunities linked to children’s long-term development and social mobility. And even these arrangements can be tough to afford: One single mother we interviewed told us she paid for a week’s childcare in kind with her own breast milk, which went to feed the care provider’s grandchildren. We also spoke to parents who reported choosing between childcare bills and heat, electricity or rent. Another mom told us about a more unconventional solution. She and her husband work full time but can’t afford the childcare options in their community, so she decided to join a gym that provides free childcare while its members exercise. She brings her laptop and works, rather than working out, while her toddler plays. These parents are scraping by in the absence of the affordable, subsidized childcare options commonplace in other countries. But this crunch is also a lose-lose proposition for the economy. The U.S. could lose as much as $290 billion per year by 2030 in forgone economic activity due to women not working or not working as much due to childcare pressures, according to the consultancy BCG. A path forward The Trump administration has laid out its own vision. Vice President JD Vance announced in September 2026 a preliminary proposal to repurpose existing funds for childcare subsidies as a cash transfer to married parents, provided that one spouse stays home. We believe, however, this approach fails to reflect the real needs of the millions of U.S. parents who can’t pay their bills if they only get one paycheck. In fact, under the subsidy program that Vance cited, only 16% of eligible children are reached today anyway. We believe, based on our research, that any comprehensive overhaul has four important components. First is a robust national policy for paid family leave, which would let families make the best care decisions for newborns, infants and parents themselves rather than sprinting back to work. Paid family leave would also ease demand for scarce infant care in the market. Second is an expansion of early childhood care and education programs. By publicly subsidizing childcare, particularly for low-income families and special needs kids, policymakers can help close the affordability gap for high-quality care. Third is a greater investment in childcare workers. Qualified caregivers are the cornerstone of high-quality childcare. If their wages and working conditions improve, it means fewer will have to take side hustles or quit for better jobs. Finally, providers will need more incentives to open in underserved areas. Childcare is expensive to provide and runs on thin margins. In low-income and rural areas, many families can’t pay prices that cover the true cost of care, and subsidy payments are often set below that cost. So opening a center there doesn’t make much financial sense. Startup grants, higher subsidy rates and operating support help close that gap, which makes it possible to open and stay open where need is greatest. 04f101fb6f68cf59: If you're going with a lower-cost health insurance plan, make sure to read the fine print. Pla2na/iStock via Getty Images PlusHealthcare costs are a major concern for Americans, and health insurance premiums are a primary fuel for that anxiety. Shrinking federal subsidies for Affordable Care Act plans led to large premium increases for millions of Americans in 2025, causing many people to drop coverage. With premiums expected to rise further and Medicaid work requirements set to begin in January 2027, many Americans are left scrambling for affordable options. We are health economists who study public policies aimed at expanding health insurance coverage. When it comes to our own health insurance, we are fortunate: We are among the roughly 160 million Americans who receive coverage through their employers. But if you don’t work for a large employer that provides health benefits, finding coverage for your family can be confusing and, increasingly, expensive. People looking for low-cost alternatives have no doubt encountered several options. They may look appealing and, in some cases, may be appropriate, but they can also carry real risks. Navigating trade-offs Historically, people who didn’t have access to employer-sponsored coverage had limited health insurance options. Before the Affordable Care Act went into effect in 2014, insurers could charge you a higher premium based on your health status, exclude coverage for preexisting medical conditions, or deny you coverage altogether. The ACA eliminated this kind of discrimination, established a minimum standard of 10 essential benefits that health insurance plans had to cover, and required plans to fully cover the cost of preventive care. It also introduced income-based subsidies that could be used to purchase coverage in newly established online marketplaces. Americans who are not insured through an employer-sponsored plan must find coverage through sources like the ACA marketplaces. mixetto/E+ via Getty Images Low-cost plans that aren’t available through ACA marketplaces are essentially vestiges of the pre-ACA health insurance landscape. Regardless of where you get coverage, choosing health insurance involves trade-offs. The more you pay in premiums, the more comprehensive your coverage will be in terms of how much you must pay when you need care and the breadth of the network of covered providers. Some trade-offs are clear when you choose a plan, but some lower-cost options may have limitations that are not immediately obvious. Less costly short-term plans As their name suggests, short-term, limited-duration plans are designed for people with temporary gaps in coverage, such as those who are between jobs or months away from qualifying for Medicare. These plans, which can be purchased for periods of up to six months, tend to be cheaper than marketplace coverage for two reasons. First, because they are not subject to ACA rules, they may not provide the full range of essential health benefits. Short-term, limited-duration plans often do not cover maternity care and commonly don’t have an annual limit on out-of-pocket costs. In fact, these plans may cap how much they will pay in a year, leaving policyholders stuck with large, unexpected expenses. Second, unlike plans offered through the ACA marketplaces, short-term, limited-duration plans are allowed to deny coverage based on your health status. Screening out higher-cost consumers reduces premiums, but if you are not in perfect health, you may not be able to find an insurer that will sell you one of these more limited plans. Because of a concern that they destabilize the market by siphoning off healthy consumers, short-term, limited-duration plans are banned in five states. Alternatives that look like insurance Another seemingly affordable option is healthcare sharing ministries, arrangements through which consumers with common religious beliefs agree to share medical expenses. Their websites resemble those of health insurance companies – for example, they often present different plan options offering different levels of benefits – but they avoid using standard insurance terms like “premium” or “deductible” because these offerings are not insurance. Because they are not regulated as insurance companies, healthcare sharing ministries are not subject to consumer protections or other state or federal requirements. There is also no guarantee that the ministry will cover your medical expenses when you submit a claim. Like short-term, limited-duration plans, healthcare sharing ministries may deny coverage based on your health history, exclude coverage for preexisting conditions and put a limit on the dollar amount they will pay in benefits. Another lower-cost option available in 14 states is health coverage offered by a farm bureau. These plans are similar to healthcare sharing ministries in that they are limited to a certain group of people – to enroll, you must be a member of the state’s farm bureau, though that does not mean you necessarily have to work in agriculture. These plans are also not subject to federal or state insurance regulations. This means that, like short-term, limited-duration plans, they can offer lower prices by not offering certain benefits required by the ACA and by screening out high-cost consumers. Unlike short-term, limited-duration plans, there is no limit on how long you can hold farm bureau coverage. Choosing a health insurance plan often requires fighting through a thicket of jargon. What should you do? Although the cost of marketplace coverage has increased dramatically since 2025, for many consumers who need coverage for more than six months, it remains the best option. If you are single with an annual income below US$64,000, a couple with an annual income below $87,000, or a family of four with an annual income less than $132,000, you should still be eligible for a premium subsidy. And you will know that the plan you are purchasing is real insurance that covers a standard set of benefits and is subject to robust consumer protections. If you are considering an alternative to marketplace coverage, there are a few things you should do to protect yourself: Make sure you ask for a summary of benefits and coverage. This is a plain language summary of a health plan’s benefits and coverage with examples of how much the plan would cover for two specific conditions – diabetes and childbirth. Insurers and employers who offer coverage are required to provide this document to anyone applying for coverage. If they cannot provide one, what they are selling may not actually be insurance. If they do provide a summary of benefits and coverage, read it carefully. As we noted earlier, one reason some options might be less expensive than a marketplace plan is that they provide much less coverage. Don’t assume that they cover all the benefits you would expect from a health insurance plan, or that they will cover the full cost of the care you receive. Finally, never enter your phone number into a “do you need insurance” website. This area is rife with fraud, including multiple cases in which telemarketers misled consumers into paying hundreds of dollars per month to purchase sham health insurance. Health insurance is expensive because healthcare is expensive – which means that consumers have to make difficult trade-offs. There is no easy answer, but beware of options that look too good to be true. They very well might be. Thomas Buchmueller is a Non-Resident Senior Fellow at the Brookings Institution. O2O Creative/E+ via Getty ImagesAfter 10 states began to add new restrictions to what people could buy with Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits in early 2026, the number of convenience stores authorized to accept those benefits was 1.4% lower than would be expected based on trends in states without the policy change. That’s what we found in our study, published in October 2026 in Health Affairs Scholar – a peer-reviewed journal. SNAP, a federally funded program administered by the states, helps about 36 million low-income Americans afford groceries with government benefits that can be used at more than 250,000 stores to buy fresh fruit, ground beef, canned beans and other groceries. Using the benefits for many items, including hot food, alcohol, toiletries and pet food, has long been prohibited. States can now obtain federal waivers to prohibit SNAP benefits from being used to buy other products. The 10 states with waivers that we studied had a mix of rules. Some only barred the sale of soda and other sugary drinks. Other prohibitions applied to energy drinks, candy, cake and other prepared desserts. In states like Oklahoma and Florida that have adopted these new SNAP restrictions to discourage unhealthy diets, the number of convenience stores participating in the program has fallen relative to other states that haven’t made these changes. That was especially notable in areas with high numbers of low-income people where a large share of the population gets SNAP benefits. We analyzed the number of stores participating in SNAP from January 2025 through June 2026 for the 10 states. We compared changes to that number before and after the waivers took effect with what happened in the rest of the country. We found no clear evidence that the number of supermarkets or superstores was declining in waiver states. Although it’s slightly lower than otherwise expected, this effect is not statistically significant. Because the restrictions vary, we also investigated whether the type mattered: sugary drinks only, or sugary drinks plus other products that state officials wanted to discourage. We found the largest declines in the number of SNAP-authorized convenience stores in states restricting both drinks and candy: an average of 2.2%. Why it matters Stores in waiver states may need to update their checkout systems and train employees to prevent purchases that are no longer allowed with SNAP benefits – potentially a time-consuming burden for some retailers. That may help explain why the number of SNAP-authorized convenience stores is declining. Although most people use SNAP benefits to buy food at big stores, they also purchase some groceries at convenience stores, especially in neighborhoods where there are few supermarkets. Other federal policies are also changing how SNAP works due to provisions in the big tax and policy legislation that Congress passed in July 2025. It changed some eligibility rules and how much states pay to administer the program. Even before all those changes take effect, many people who are likely eligible for SNAP benefits are having a harder time getting them, due to the steps states are taking to prepare for the new rules. The number of Americans enrolled in the program is falling fast despite no sign that their needs are shrinking. What still isn’t known We focused on changes to the number of stores authorized to accept SNAP in states with waivers. We didn’t study whether stores closed, or exactly why stores left the program. We also don’t know what role court rulings will play. On June 22, near the end of our study, a federal court invalidated SNAP food restrictions in five states: Colorado, Iowa, Nebraska, Tennessee and West Virginia. Waiver programs in other states – Indiana, Utah, Idaho, Oklahoma, Louisiana, Texas and Florida – were allowed to continue. Four states had similar restrictions in the works: South Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio and Virginia. Those plans are on hold. Beginning in November 2026, most U.S. stores will also have to meet new requirements of a different kind to participate in SNAP. They’ll need to stock a wider variety of staple foods, such as grains, dairy products and produce. These requirements could pose additional challenges for convenience stores. Further research is needed to see if the effects we found change over time, including in states that introduce these restrictions after the period we studied. That will require autonomous robots, nuclear power, and a way to use the moon’s resources to keep the base operating. But the chief obstacle may be one of political will.

9e57b3c7cb0d7eb2: The crack of a bat accompanied by a roar from the crowd can capture a baseball fan’s attention, even if they miss seeing the home run. Humans may be visual creatures, but we also perceive the world around us by listening to it.  To improve artificial perception, MIT Professor Paris Smaragdis SM ’97, PhD ’01 seeks to make machines that can hear and understand sound even better than humans. A machine with super-human hearing could rapidly pinpoint the location of a traffic accident by listening for squealing tires and crunching metal, or identify when an industrial drill might break while it is boring through dense bedrock to dig a geothermal well. “I like to say that I do the same thing the computer vision folks do, but instead I do it for hearing,” says Smaragdis, a professor in the Music and Theatre Arts program of the School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Sciences holding an MIT Schwarzman College of Computing shared position with the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science. His research group explores areas like machine learning for sound source separation, smart devices that can augment the audio surroundings of humans, and better tools to help people understand, manipulate, analyze, and create music. “Having had a musical background, I’ve been interested in examining these ideas. What does it take to make machines understand sound? There is a huge domain of applications for machines that can listen,” says Smaragdis, who joined MIT in 2025 and is also part of the Music Technology program and a member of the Research Laboratory of Electronics. A musical prelude Smaragdis, who grew up in Greece, began playing classical guitar at a young age. He enjoyed playing traditional pieces but reached a turning point in his musical journey when his father brought home a small synthesizer. “That little synthesizer had a function that allowed you to make your own sounds, and I became completely captivated by the possibilities,” he says. Synthesizers were taking a more prominent place in pop music during the 1980s, adding to his fascination with the technology. As he advanced through school, Smaragdis wanted to study music made with synthesizers. But this was not an educational path offered by the more traditional European conservatories at the time. Instead, he enrolled at Berklee College of Music in Boston, into a program where he could explore the use of computers and synthesizers to shape and manipulate sound. “With computers and synthesizers, I could make new sounds that have never been heard before,” he says. At the same time, Smaragdis became immersed in jazz fusion. He declared bass as his major at Berklee since it would allow him more opportunities to play with jazz ensembles. “I found the bass to be sonically more interesting than the guitar. It was a more unexplored domain, and I’ve always gravitated toward unexplored domains,” he says. That interest in the unexplored carried over into his coursework. He and mentor Richard Boulanger, a professor of electronic production and design, created new tools to help people use computers to write, produce, and enhance music.  Through his studies at Berklee, Smaragdis embarked on a collaborative project with Professor Barry Vercoe (who passed away in 2025) at the MIT Media Lab to create software synthesizers for music creation. Building on that project, Smaragdis pursued graduate studies in Vercoe’s group, where he completed his master’s degree and PhD, followed by a postdoc. “In the Media Lab, I got exposed more to the computer part of computer music. That’s where my attention shifted a bit. Now I really wanted to make computers that could understand sound,” he says. Tuning in to unexplored domains At that time, many students in the Media Lab were using signal processing techniques to help machines handle sound. Smaragdis chose a less explored approach — machine learning — to separate himself from the pack. He found that training machine-learning models to understand sound offered advantages that couldn’t be attained with traditional signal processing techniques. “Over time, it became really clear to me that we need to teach computers how to listen. We can’t just tell them how to listen. If anything, we don’t even know how we humans listen,” he says. “We don’t have a vocabulary to explain what it means to listen, or how to tell the difference between a cat’s meow and the sound of a violin.” After finishing his postdoc, Smaragdis began a career at Mitsubishi Electric Research Labs, where he worked on artificial intelligence systems that could scan video soundtracks and understand what is happening on screen.  “What if you record an entire soccer game, but you only want to watch the highlights? In computer vision, it is very difficult to identify what a highlight is. But on the other hand, if you only listen to the sounds, then when the crowd goes crazy you would know that something interesting is happening,” he says. That system was eventually incorporated into electronic devices, including a personal video recording system Mitsubishi was developing at the time, and into traffic monitoring systems and cell phones. Smaragdis later joined Adobe, where he created the audio research team that built user-friendly tools to help artists, musicians, and producers manipulate sound without needing a lot of expertise. “As we did that work, I kept coming up with deeper technical problems that needed to be resolved. I jumped into academia to address that itch,” he says. Smaragdis joined the faculty at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, where he and his group incorporated the latest machine-learning techniques into audio-processing systems. One of the technologies they developed utilized neural networks for separating individual sounds from audio mixtures. That project caught the attention of the team working on the 2021 documentary mini-series “The Beatles: Get Back.” The production team enlisted Smaragdis to help clean up some archival Beatles recordings. “That was a very different way of audio processing than what I was doing in academia. Now, I had to do something that sounded good but didn’t necessarily have to look good on paper. We didn’t have a formula we could optimize,” he says. Every recording involved different challenges. For instance, in one clip John Lennon was playing music while Paul McCartney was horsing around, reading headlines from newspapers and making fun of George Harrison. “We were trying to come up with a technological solution that could help us do everything, as opposed to addressing each problem on its own,” he says. His contributions helped the team win an Emmy Award for sound editing for a nonfiction or reality program, in 2022. A concerted effort After 15 years at the University of Illinois, Smaragdis decided to join the faculty at MIT to tackle the thorny, interdisciplinary problems that were emerging in the field.  His group now focuses on two main areas. For one, they develop systems that make computers more useful tools for musicians.  One project in this area is enabling machines to understand how to listen to music, so they can provide constructive feedback to musicians. “We want to enhance the toolbox a musician has. We don’t want to use computers to replace musicians,” he says. On the other side, his group focuses on the fundamental tools scientists and artists alike can use to process, analyze, and manipulate audio. For instance, his team has recently been exploring algorithms that allow sophisticated signal processing where traditional frames of reference, such as sampling rates, frame sizes, or context-windows, are not fixed — or even defined.  That implies different computational structures that are yet unexplored, despite their potential for more efficient processing, Smaragdis says. “That requires rethinking a lot of the basics, but once you have that ability, you can start getting much more flexible and more powerful systems,” he adds. They also explore ways to incorporate the latest techniques, like large language models, into speech recognition and audio enhancement. “AI is an immensely powerful tool, but I don’t think we have found the ideal way to use it for sound and music yet,” he says. He also enjoys mentoring students and helping them materialize their visions for research projects. Since few of his students have experience using computation in sound, he emphasizes hands-on lessons so they see and hear how to transform equations into something tangible. Smaragdis still feels a thrill from making music, whether with a computer or a more traditional instrument. Off campus, he tries to play jazz bass whenever he can find the time, and enjoys exploring the rich musical community of Boston with his wife and 15-year-old son. Outside the musical realm, he plays and coaches underwater hockey — a sport where players wear diving masks and use sticks to push a heavy puck across the bottom of a pool toward their opponent’s goal. He coached the underwater hockey team at the University of Illinois, and is hoping to revive the MIT underwater hockey club soon and start hosting tournaments on campus. While underwater hockey may be a lesser-known sport, it fits with Smaragdis’ lifelong interest in pursuing the underexplored. “I’ve always like doing things that were different from what everyone else was doing. If you can create a new sound that no one has heard before, what does that mean about your ability to create new things? I still find these questions completely fascinating,” he says.
a3c1ecdc3562be0b: Sultan Selangor yang menyambut jubli perak pemerintahannya tahun ini ada mesej tajam kepada golongan pembakar sentimen perkauman yang melihat diri sendiri sebagai wira sesuatu bangsa .
Sultan Sharafuddin Idris Shah dengan lantang menegur golongan itu - hentikan eksploitasi bangsa dan agama untuk mendapat keuntungan politik dan jangan mengheret istana ke dalam pertikaian mereka.

Titah baginda datang ketika arena politik Malaysia dicengkam permainan sentimen ras dan agama dimana hak Melayu, identiti Islam dan kedudukan masyarakat bukan Melayu berulang kali diketengahkan, secara negatif.

Lihat sahaja PRN Johor dan Negeri Sembilan yang diadakan tahun ini. Sentimen perkauman ditiup dan dibakar. Ferociously – to a level never seen before. Selain dua PRN itu, hampir semua perkara dijadikan isu bangsa dan agama di merata tempat. Politik perkauman (atau kata sesetengah orang politik identiti) dimainkan sewenang-wenangnya.

Daripada kempen pilihan raya, dibawa ke perdebatan di Parlimen, menembusi platform media sosial naratif politik berkisar tentang siapa yang konon akan kerugian, kehilangan hak, diancam dan terancam serta siapa yang benar-benar wira mempertahankan bangsa dan agama tertentu.
Retorik politikus mencetuskan naratif perkauman melampau dalam kalangan warganet yang merupakan ‘rakyat biasa’ dan pastinya golongan yang digelar atau mahu dianggap ‘laskar siber’.
Kata kolumnis politik, Lim Hong Siang, negara berada dalam situasi kebangkitan kumpulan sayap kanan ekstrem yang mengancam realiti kepelbagaian dan kebebasan.

Pada 15 Okt lalu, Ahli Parlimen Puncak Borneo Willie Mongin berkongsi maklumat di Dewan Rakyat seorang guru baru-baru ini memberitahunya, ada dalam kalangan anak sekolah yang tidak mahu duduk sebelah rakan sekelas bukan sebangsa dan seagama dengan mereka.

Daripada mana atau daripada siapa anak-anak ‘belajar’ tabiat tidak baik begitu? Kemungkinan besar daripada ibu bapa yang termakan kata-kata berbaur perkauman sang politikus dan dakyah negatif dimainkan di media sosial.

Mongin tidak beritahu di mana sekolah perkara itu berlaku. Bagi saya jika ia berlaku di Borneo yang terkenal dengan muhibah dan toleransi antara kaumnya, saya tidak terkejut jika itu juga ada berlaku di Semenanjung.
Semua ini mengancam perpaduan rakyat – merenggang hubungan antara kaum. Ramai pandai menyakiti dan ramai pula yang disakiti.
Dengan PRN Melaka pula akan diadakan tidak lama lagi pasti atau hampir pasti taktik eksploitasi ras dan agama akan diulangi politikus sebagai jalan pintas untuk mendapat kemenangan di peti undi.
Sememangnya memperalatkan isu bangsa dan agama mudah menarik perhatian dan sekali gus mendapat sokongan.

Lantas teguran Sultan Sharafuddin tepat pada masanya. Baginda tidak menamakan sesiapa. Namun, kita tahu siapa yang dimaksudkan. Kita tahu siapa penggemar permainan politik perkauman. No prizes for guessing.
The Sultan’s patience is wearing thin. “Seperti rakyat, beta juga bosan,” titah Sultan Sharafuddin yang dilapor Malaysiakini, Isnin lalu.

Baginda menyeru semua ahli politik Selangor memberi fokus terhadap serving the people, perkhidmatan baik untuk rakyat, menjana pertumbuhan ekonomi dan memastikan perpaduan yang terjalin dalam kalangan rakyat terus dipupuk dan dijaga .

Demi memastikan Selangor maintains it’s leading position in the country. Titah baginda kekuatan Selangor ialah pada rakyatnya. “Kita dianugerah masyarakat berbilang bangsa, kebudayaan dan agama yang generasi ke generasi telah hidup dan bekerja bersama dalam harmoni mencapai kemakmuran.”

Titah baginda, sememangnya boleh dirujuk atau diguna pakai untuk seluruh Malaysia bukan sahaja Selangor. Dan saranan Sultan Sharafuddin kepada ahli politik memang boleh dituju kepada semua ahli politik di semua negeri. Politikus pemain politik perkauman are everywhere in the country.

Sebenarnya, memang raja Melayu lain juga seperti Sultan Sharufuddin mahu permainan politik perkauman dinyahkan. Kita pernah dengar saranan, teguran serta nasihat mereka. Cuma politikus degil tetap degil. Yang gemar main sentimen ras untuk kemenangan pilihan raya meneruskan kegemaran mereka. Tanpa hirau nasihat raja tanpa menghiraukan kesejahteraan rakyat dan negeri masing-masing dan juga negara.

Sehingga kini, seperti Sultan Selangor, raja-raja tidak atau belum namakan sesiapa. Namun, mungkin akan tiba masa Sultan Selangor dan raja-raja lain akan menamakan politikus yang terus-menerus jadikan bangsa dan agama isu untuk dapat manfaat peti undi konon atas nama bangsa dan agama.
Mungkin akan tiba masa raja-raja mendedahkan identiti mereka kepada rakyat meskipun rakyat tahu siapa mereka .

Ini tidak mustahil berlaku, kerana bak titah Sultan Sharafuddin yang dinyatakan tadi baginda sudah bosan dengan gelagat politikus meniup sentimen perkauman. Saya yakin the other rulers are equally fed up. Their patience are also wearing thin.

6f20fa3677e84710: From Cheli Tamilselvam Nadarajah
A school should be a place where children feel safe, friendships flourish, differences are respected, and every child knows that someone cares.
It should be a place where teachers inspire, parents trust, and children grow not only in knowledge but also in character.
Yet we read about tragic incidents of violence, bullying and the loss of young lives in our schools.
Could these tragedies have been prevented? Were there red flags? Did these children have someone to turn to?
Time to act
As an educator, I believe that a school’s greatest achievement is not simply excellent examination results, but the kind of human beings it nurtures.
What does academic excellence mean if a child is afraid to attend school, humiliated by classmates, or feels invisible within its walls?

I have had parents standing before me with tears in their eyes, asking for just one thing: that their children grow up to be good people. Their plea has stayed with me. Every child deserves an excellent education in a safe, caring and supportive environment.
Bullying is not merely a disciplinary issue that children will eventually outgrow. It can damage confidence, emotional wellbeing and a child’s sense of belonging.
While those who bully others must be held accountable, punishment alone may not change the attitudes and beliefs behind their behaviour.
We cannot condemn our children for displaying behaviours that we, as adults, have modelled, tolerated or failed to challenge.
We must protect victims, support affected children, address harmful behaviour and help every child learn responsibility, empathy and respect.
This requires more than occasional motivational talks or campaigns launched after a tragedy. It requires a sustained transformation of our school culture.
A lesson from SMK Bandar Kuching No 1

In 2006, while serving at SMK Bandar Kuching No 1 in Sarawak, I introduced the Attitude Breakthrough Challenge (ABC) to demonstrate that positive attitudes can be developed, and character strengthened through consistent practice and shared responsibility.
The initiative went beyond punishing misconduct.
It sought to empower teachers, engage parents and encourage students to take ownership of their behaviour. Students were encouraged to support one another in making better choices.
The aim was not to shame children or make them police their peers, but to build a community where positive behaviour was valued and everyone had a part to play.

Its key elements included peer accountability, teacher empowerment and parental engagement, supported by a structured system of merit and demerit codes, focusing more on the recognition of positive behaviour, and graduated responses to misconduct.

Student suspension cases recorded by the education ministry (MoE) fell from 136 in 2005 to fewer than 40 in 2006, followed by 16 in 2007, fewer than 10 in 2008, eight in 2009, six in 2010 and three in 2011.
For me, the greatest lesson was this: Negative behaviour need not be accepted as inevitable.
When teachers are empowered, parents are involved, students are accountable and positive behaviour is recognised, meaningful change becomes possible.
Making positive attitudes a way of life
The ABC, now rebranded as Positive Attitude Builds Character (PABC), must be more than a short-term programme or a slogan on a school wall; it must become a way of life.
Children need opportunities to practise positive values, supported by adults who model them and systems that reinforce them consistently.

While PABC is not a magic solution to every school safety challenge, its principles and practical experiences offer valuable lessons for a comprehensive approach to prevention, accountability, character development and student wellbeing.

We must distinguish between holding children accountable and labelling them as failures. Children who make mistakes need appropriate consequences, guidance and opportunities to change, while victims must be protected and serious misconduct addressed promptly.

A positive school culture does not happen by accident. It requires committed leadership, empowered teachers, engaged parents, responsible students and effective systems to identify problems early, monitor concerns and ensure timely follow-up.
A safe school is not one where no complaints are made. It is one where children feel safe enough to speak up and trust that adults will act.
I appeal to the MoE, school heads, parents and communities to make safe, happy and inclusive schools a national priority.
When a child feels safe, valued and happy at school, learning becomes more meaningful, relationships flourish, and every child has a greater opportunity to thrive.

Let us make the main thing the main thing: the wellbeing, character and future of our children. Amid the many demands, distractions and competing priorities that bombard us daily, we must never lose sight of what matters most.
Every child must know that someone cares
After more than four decades in education, I remain passionate about the potential of every child.

I believe in the teacher who encourages a struggling student, the school head who refuses to ignore a problem, the parent who sacrifices for a child’s future, and the child who can grow into a responsible and caring person when given the right guidance and support.

Children should not have to remember school as a place where they were afraid. They must remember it as a place where they discovered their abilities, built friendships, learnt to respect others and found adults who believed in them.
Teachers should not feel that they must fight these battles alone. They deserve to feel empowered, supported and valued.
We may not be able to prevent every difficulty a child faces in life, but we can do far more to ensure that school is never a place where a child has to live in fear.
Our children deserve better. They deserve schools that are safe, happy, caring and inclusive. The time to act is now.
Cheli Tamilselvam Nadarajah is a fomer school principal and an FMT reader.
